會試錄序

皇上御極之十有二年，為正德丁丑，復當會試之期。春二月，禮部尚書臣李遜學、侍郎臣石珤、臣王瓚以考試官請。上命臣貴、臣清往主校文之任。同考則洗馬臣霄、侍讀臣銑、修撰臣臯、編修臣嵩、臣琛、臣棟、臣朴、臣襄、檢討臣臯、臣憙、臣維藩、都給事中臣泰、給事中臣臯、臣夔、郎中臣頤、臣廷、主事臣道。監試則御史臣宗儒、臣鼇充。暨諸執事，皆推擇惟允。時臣貴以疾在告，方疏請
translation_en:
Preface to the Metropolitan Examination Record

The twelfth year after His Majesty ascended the throne, the dingchou year of the Zhengde reign [1517], again marked the time for the Metropolitan Examination. In the second month of spring, Li Xunxue, Minister of Rites, and Shi Bao and Wang Zan, Vice Ministers, petitioned for the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded us, Gui and Qing, to undertake responsibility for evaluating the examination essays. The Associate Examiners were Xiao, Librarian to the Heir Apparent; Xian, Reader-in-waiting; Gao, Senior Compiler; Song, Chen, Dong, Pu, and Xiang, Junior Compilers; Gao, Xi, and Weifan, Examining Editors; Tai, Chief Supervising Secretary; Gao and Kui, Supervising Secretaries; Yi and Ting, Bureau Directors; and Dao, Secretary. The Censors Zongru and Ao served as examination monitors. They and all the other functionaries were recommended and selected with due care for their suitability. title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
謝事
上慰留未允而又遣醫来視
恩至渥也尋承是
命則拜手稽首曰求賢
國家重務莫有急焉者而人臣
攄忠報
國亦惟此為大是惡敢辭乃力
===
疾從事曩者辛未禮闈臣貴
實承乏主試事嘗得盡觀天
下之文今獲再至再觀較諸
前益有加焉擇其純以俟
宸斷得三百五十人盖于時就試
之士三千九百有奇雖言人
人殊而其本經術達治體類

謝事。上慰留未允，而又遣醫来視，恩至渥也。尋承是命，則拜手稽首曰：「求賢，國家重務，莫有急焉者；而人臣攄忠報國，亦惟此為大，是惡敢辭？」乃力疾從事。
曩者辛未禮闈，臣貴實承乏主試事，嘗得盡觀天下之文。今獲再至再觀，較諸前益有加焉。擇其純以俟宸斷，得三百五十人。盖于時就試之士三千九百有奇，雖言人人殊，而其本經術、達治體，類
translation_en:
…to retire from office. His Majesty graciously urged me to remain and did not grant my request; he also sent a physician to attend me. His favor was exceedingly generous. Soon afterward, upon receiving this appointment, I bowed with clasped hands and knocked my head to the ground, saying: “Seeking worthy men is a weighty task of the state; nothing is more urgent. For a subject, too, no greater task affords the opportunity to express his loyalty and repay the state. How could I dare decline?” Thus I exerted myself despite my illness and undertook the work.
At the Metropolitan Examination in the xinwei year (1511), I, your servant Gui, had indeed filled the position of presiding over the examination, and had the opportunity to survey writings from throughout the realm. Now, having the opportunity to return and survey them once more, I find that they have improved still further over those of the previous examination. We selected those whose work was sound, to await His Majesty’s judgment, obtaining 350 men. At that time, more than 3,900 candidates sat the examination. title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
皆彬彬可觀誠有取之而不
能盡者嗚呼盛哉夫天下未
嘗無才而所趨實係乎時前
代取士非止一科進士之科
唐宋始重然自他途顯者尚
多有之我
祖宗監古定制養士於學校而取
===
之一於科目四海嚮風故凡
材質之秀而志於用世者莫
不趨而歸之天下無遺才焉
皇上懋昭大德守成右文所以鼓
舞招徠之者又與日俱新則
人才之衆多固勢所不得不
然者豈才之盛哉時之盛也

祖宗監古定制養士於學校而取
===
之一於科目四海嚮風故凡
材質之秀而志於用世者莫
不趨而歸之天下無遺才焉
皇上懋昭大德〔守成右文所以鼓〕
舞招徠之者又與日俱新則
人才之衆多固勢所不得不
然者豈才之盛哉時之盛也
punctuated: 皆彬彬可觀，誠有取之而不能盡者。嗚呼，盛哉！夫天下未嘗無才，而所趨實係乎時。前代取士，非止一科，進士之科，唐宋始重，然自他途顯者，尚多有之。我祖宗監古定制，養士於學校，而取之一於科目，四海嚮風，故凡材質之秀而志於用世者，莫不趨而歸之，天下無遺才焉。皇上懋昭大德，守成右文，所以鼓舞招徠之者，又與日俱新，則人才之衆多，固勢所不得不然者。豈才之盛哉？時之盛也！
translation_en: …all were refined and worthy of admiration; indeed, there were deserving candidates whom we could not all select. Ah, how flourishing an age! The realm has never lacked talent, but the direction in which talented men turn depends upon the times. Former dynasties recruited men through more than one category of selection. The metropolitan graduate (jinshi) examination first gained prominence under the Tang and Song, yet many still rose to distinction by other routes. Our imperial ancestors, taking antiquity as their guide, established a system that nurtured scholars in schools and recruited them exclusively through the examinations. All within the four seas followed their example. Thus, all men of outstanding natural ability who aspired to serve the world turned to this path, leaving no talent in the realm overlooked. His Majesty assiduously manifests his great virtue, preserves the achievements of his forebears, and honors letters. The means by which he inspires and attracts scholars are renewed daily. The abundance of talented men is therefore an inevitable consequence of these circumstances. Is this merely a flourishing of talent? It is a flourishing of the age!

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
雖然
國家之所望於士者則厚矣古
者治化之盛莫過虞周舜之
臣五人武王之臣十人孔子
亟稱之曰才難則夫所謂盛
者固不惟其衆惟其人耳而
士之所以自待者又可輕乎
===
孔子曰事君先資其言拜自
獻其身以成其信今茲所試
之文固諸士子自獻先資之
言也而果能一一以成其信
乎今夫堯舜其君而使無一
夫不獲夫人能言之然君子
莫之許而獨謂伊尹為然豈

獻其身以成其信今茲所試
之文固諸士子自獻先資之
言也而果能一一以成其信
乎今夫堯舜其君而使無一
夫不獲夫人能言之然君子
莫之許而獨謂伊尹爲然豈
punctuated:
雖然，國家之所望於士者則厚矣。古者治化之盛，莫過虞周。舜之臣五人，武王之臣十人，孔子亟稱之，曰：「才難。」則夫所謂盛者，固不惟其衆，惟其人耳。而士之所以自待者，又可輕乎？

孔子曰：「事君，先資其言，拜自獻其身，以成其信。」今茲所試之文，固諸士子自獻先資之言也，而果能一一以成其信乎？今夫堯舜其君，而使無一夫不獲，夫人能言之，然君子莫之許，而獨謂伊尹為然。豈
translation_en:
Nevertheless, the state’s expectations of its scholars are indeed weighty. In antiquity, no age surpassed those of Yu and Zhou in the flourishing of good government and moral transformation. Shun had five ministers, and King Wu had ten. Confucius repeatedly praised them, saying, “Talent is hard to find.” Thus, what is called flourishing depends not simply on their numbers, but on the men themselves. Can scholars, then, take lightly the standards they set for themselves?

Confucius said, “In serving a ruler, one first pledges one’s words, then bows and offers oneself in service [?], thereby making good one’s trustworthiness.” The essays examined on this occasion are precisely the words with which these candidates offer themselves and pledge their service. But can they indeed make good every one of these pledges? Anyone can speak of making his ruler a Yao or a Shun and ensuring that not a single person goes without his due. Yet the exemplary man grants this achievement to no one else, saying that Yi Yin alone accomplished it. Could it be …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
非其為德為民功業所到真
能充其志以信其言故耶今
諸士子論道必曰堯舜論治
必曰唐虞凡百家功利之說
一切屏棄不齒其言美矣其
志亦畧見矣不知登崇之後
果能充其志以信其言如有
===
商阿衡否也夫有其言而無
其志是謂自欺有其志而行
之不力是謂自畫二者之弊
生而人才視古益遠甚矣士
而以是自處其如
國家求賢圖治之意何哉夫以
國家重務莫急於斯而微臣區

之不力是謂自畫二者之弊
生而人才視古益遠甚矣士

國家求賢圖治之意何哉夫以
國家重務莫急於斯而微臣□
punctuated: 非其為德為民，功業所到，真能充其志以信其言故耶？今諸士子論道必曰堯舜，論治必曰唐虞，凡百家功利之說，一切屏棄不齒。其言美矣，其志亦畧見矣。不知登崇之後，果能充其志以信其言，如有商阿衡否也？夫有其言而無其志，是謂自欺；有其志而行之不力，是謂自畫。二者之弊生，而人才視古益遠甚矣。士而以是自處，其如國家求賢圖治之意何哉？夫以國家重務，莫急於斯，而微臣區
translation_en:
…was it not because, in cultivating virtue and serving the people, his achievements truly fulfilled his aspirations and bore out his words? Now, whenever these examination candidates discuss the Way, they invariably invoke Yao and Shun; whenever they discuss governance, they invariably invoke Tang and Yu. They utterly reject the various schools’ doctrines of achievement and profit, disdaining even to mention them. Their words are admirable, and their aspirations, too, are somewhat apparent. Yet we do not know whether, after being promoted to high office, they will truly fulfill their aspirations and bear out their words, as did the Aheng, the chief minister of the Shang dynasty, Yi Yin.

To utter such words without having such aspirations is called deceiving oneself; to have such aspirations but fail to pursue them vigorously is called setting limits on oneself. When these two failings arise, men of talent fall ever further short of the ancients. If scholars conduct themselves in this way, how can they answer the state’s intention to seek worthy men and achieve good government? Among the weighty affairs of state, none is more urgent than this; and your humble servant’s modest…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
區圖報之忱又以此為大也
敢弗慎歟如得其人則不惟
國家之慶而貴等猥承任使之
責亦可少塞萬有一焉徒得
自欺自畫者而無裨於上下
則不職之愆亦何逭哉貴用
是懼比試事告成既錄其言
===
以獻於
朝矣而又為是說以勵之
光祿大夫柱國太子太保戶
部尚書兼
武英殿大學士靳貴謹序
alt_text:
匪圖報之忱又以此為大也
敢弗慎歟如得其人則不惟
國家之慶而貫等猥承任使之
責亦可少塞萬有一焉徒得
自欺自畫者而無裨於上下
則不職之愆亦何逭哉貫用
是懼比試事告成既錄其言
===
以獻於
朝矣而又為是說以勵之
光祿大夫柱國太子太保戶
部尚書兼
武英殿大學士靳貫謹序
punctuated:
區圖報之忱，又以此為大也。敢弗慎歟？如得其人，則不惟國家之慶，而貴等猥承任使之責，亦可少塞萬有一焉。徒得自欺自畫者，而無裨於上下，則不職之愆亦何逭哉？貴用是懼。比試事告成，既錄其言以獻於朝矣，而又為是說以勵之。
光祿大夫、柱國、太子太保、戶部尚書兼武英殿大學士靳貴謹序。
translation_en:
…in my humble devotion to repaying imperial favor, I likewise regard this as a matter of the greatest importance. How could I dare to be careless? If we obtain the right men, it will not only be a blessing for the state: my colleagues and I, unworthily entrusted with this responsibility, may also discharge some tiny fraction of our obligation. If we obtain only men who deceive themselves or set limits on their own efforts, bringing no benefit to those above or below, how could we escape the blame for failing in our duties? This is what I, Gui, fear. Now that the examination has been completed, we have recorded their writings and presented them to the court; I have also composed these remarks to exhort them.
Preface respectfully composed by Jin Gui, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Revenue, and concurrently Grand Secretary of the Hall of Military Glory.

第壹塲

四書

夫仁者，己欲立而立人，己欲達而達人。

敬大臣則不眩，體群臣則士之報禮重，子庶民則百姓勸，來百工則財用足，柔遠人則四方歸之，懷諸侯則天下畏之。

易

剛過而中，巽而說行，利有攸往，乃亨。大過之時大矣哉！

大壯利貞，大者正也。

成性存存，道義之門。

懼以終始，其要无咎。

書

佑我烈祖
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The benevolent person, wishing to establish himself, establishes others; wishing to attain success himself, helps others attain success.

By honoring the great ministers, one avoids confusion. By showing consideration for the assembled ministers, one elicits a generous response from the officers in return for such courtesy. By treating the common people as one's children, one encourages them to exert themselves. By attracting the various artisans, one ensures sufficient wealth and resources. By treating people from afar with kindness, one wins the allegiance of the four quarters. By cherishing the regional lords, one inspires awe throughout the realm.

There has never been a ruler who failed to become a true king when the aged wore silk and ate meat, and the common people suffered neither hunger nor cold.

Book of Changes

The firm is excessive, yet occupies the center. Acting with yielding gentleness and joy, it is beneficial to have somewhere to go; thus there is success. Great indeed is the significance of the time of Great Exceeding!

Great Strength: beneficial to be steadfast and correct. What is great is correct.

Continuously preserving one's fully realized nature is the gateway to the Way and righteousness.

Maintain apprehension from beginning to end; the essential aim is to remain without blame.

Book of Documents

How enlightened is the head! How worthy are the limbs! How well ordered are all affairs!

“If I cannot make my sovereign a Yao or a Shun,” he felt shame in his heart, as though he were being flogged in the marketplace. If even one man failed to obtain his due, he would say, “This is my fault.”

Assist our illustrious ancestor …

彤弓弨兮，受言藏之。我有嘉賓，中心貺之。鍾鼓既設，一朝饗之。

穆穆文王，於緝熙敬止。

綏萬邦，屢豐年。天命匪解，桓桓武王，保有厥士，于以四方，克定厥家。於昭于天！

translation_en:
…reached august Heaven.

May you yourself enjoy health and strength, and may your descendants encounter good fortune.

Greatly illustrious were Kings Wen and Wu. They carefully cultivated their luminous virtue; its radiance rose above, and its renown spread below.

Book of Odes

Look at those birds: even they seek the answering calls of companions. How could human beings fail to seek friends?

The red bow is unstrung; I receive it and store it away. I have an honored guest; from my heart I bestow it upon him. Bells and drums are set out, and at a morning banquet I feast him.

Solemn and reverent was King Wen. Ah, how unceasingly radiant was his reverence!

He brought peace to the myriad states, with plentiful harvests year after year. Heaven’s mandate did not slacken. Martial King Wu secured his warriors, took possession of the four quarters, and firmly established his house. Ah, how glorious in Heaven!

Spring and Autumn Annals

Jizi came home. 〔First year of Duke Min.〕

The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, and representatives of Jiang and Huang covenanted at Guan. 〔Second year of Duke Xi.〕 The men of Chu attacked Huang. 〔Eleventh year of Duke Xi.〕 The men of Zheng invaded Cai and captured Xie, a son of the duke of Cai. Zhen, a son of the king of Chu, led an army to attack Zheng. 〔Both in the eighth〕〔year of Duke Xiang.〕

A covenant was concluded at Shaoling. The men of Qi seized Yuan Taotu of Chen. 〔Both in the fourth〕〔year of Duke Xi.〕

〔俱文公三年〕
禮記
器用陶匏以象天地之性也
故知禮樂之情者能作識禮樂之文者能
述作者之謂聖述者之謂明

禮記
器用陶匏，以象天地之性也。
故知禮樂之情者能作，識禮樂之文者能述。作者之謂聖，述者之謂明。
故君使其臣得志，則慎慮而從之。
臣下竭力盡能，以立功於國，君必報之以爵禄。故臣下皆務竭力盡能，以立功。是以國安而君寧。禮無不答，言上之不虛取於下也。上必明正道以道民，民道之而有功，然後取其什一。故上用足而下不匱也。是以上下和親而不相怨也。和寧，禮之用也。此君臣上下之大義也。

translation_en:
Shusun Dechen joined men of Jin, Song, Chen, Wei, and Zheng in attacking Shen; Shen collapsed. Yang Chufu of Jin led an army to attack Chu in order to rescue Jiang. 〔Both in the third year of Duke Wen.〕

Book of Rites
The vessels used are of earthenware and gourd, to symbolize the natures of Heaven and Earth.
Thus, those who understand the essential meaning of rites and music can create them; those who recognize their forms can transmit them. Those who create are called sages; those who transmit are called discerning.
Thus, when a ruler enables his minister to fulfill his aspirations, the minister deliberates carefully and follows him.
When ministers exert their full strength and ability to render meritorious service to the state, the ruler must reward them with rank and emoluments. Thus, all ministers strive to exert their full strength and ability to render meritorious service. Consequently, the state is secure and the ruler is at peace. In ritual, nothing goes without a response: this means that those above do not take from those below without giving anything in return. Those above must clarify the proper Way to guide the people. Only after the people follow it and achieve results do those above take one-tenth of their produce. Thus, those above have enough for their expenses, while those below suffer no shortage. Consequently, those above and below live in harmony and affection, without resenting one another. Harmony and peace are the effects of ritual. These are the great principles governing ruler and minister, those above and those below.

Second Session
Discourse
What the sages follow is but a single principle.

translation_en:
Edicts, proclamations, and memorials 〔One topic from among these [?]〕
Compose an edict in the manner of the Han dynasty encouraging agriculture and sericulture and prohibiting the extraction of gold and jade.
Compose a proclamation in the manner of the Tang dynasty appointing Sun Fuga as Grand Master of Remonstrance.
Compose a memorial in the name of Academician Song Lian and his colleagues congratulating the emperor on having the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi) inscribed on the corridor walls of the inner palace hall.

Legal judgments 〔Five items〕
Children or grandchildren disobeying instructions and commands.
Officials exceeding the time limit for taking up their appointments.
Marriage between persons of free and servile status.
Junior family members privately using property without authorization.
Colleagues acting on another official’s behalf in rendering judgments and signing documents.

Third Session
Five Policy Questions
Question: The Book of Documents praises Yao, saying: “Both martial and civil.” These constitute the complete virtue of an emperor or king. In Yao, I can find no fault. Yet of King Wen and King Wu of Zhou, one was called “Civil” for his plans, and the other “Martial” for his achievements; neither could possess both virtues. Could it be that, although Wen and Wu were sages, they still fell short when compared with Yao? As for the rulers of later ages …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
不古若固也何漢有文帝武帝唐亦有
文宗武宗若是其多耶然此猶各就其
一時一莗稱之云爾唐之太宗乃得兼
稱二者不知其所謂功徳兼隆者進之
于周之文武二聖果若是班乎否也洪
惟我
聖祖高皇帝受
天明命驅逐夷虜復我帝王中國之土宇自起
淮右興弔伐之師不數年傳檄中原而

尚焉説者謂

translation_en:
…that they did not equal the ancients is certain. Why, then, did the Han have Emperor Wen and Emperor Wu, and the Tang likewise have Emperor Wenzong and Emperor Wuzong—so many bearing these designations of civil and martial excellence? Yet these names merely referred to a particular period or a particular undertaking [?] in each ruler’s reign. Taizong of the Tang, however, was accorded both designations. We do not know whether his supposed eminence in both achievement and virtue, when ranked alongside the two sages, Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou, truly placed him on an equal footing with them. Did it, or did it not?
We reverently consider how our Sagely Progenitor, the Exalted Emperor, received Heaven’s luminous mandate, expelled the foreign foes, and recovered the territory of China ruled by our emperors and kings. Rising from Huaiyou, he raised an army to succor the suffering and punish the guilty. Within a few years, his proclamations had spread through the Central Plain, and all under Heaven was firmly pacified. Wherever his righteous banners pointed, his might was like thunder; once his plans of state were settled, neither ghosts nor spirits could oppose them. This was surely what is called being endowed by Heaven. What martial excellence could equal his?
In moments free from the myriad affairs of government, he also personally wielded the imperial brush. The works now found in his Collected Imperial Writings, such as the Grand Pronouncements and the Text for the Great Sacrifice, all subtly probe fundamental principles and display profound and far-reaching understanding. They frequently reveal what earlier worthies had not revealed. What could surpass his civil excellence, thus innate and bestowed by Heaven? Commentators say that…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
聖祖掃胡元之亂復綱常正人紀舉一世而甄
陶之其道與帝王同而功則倍焉自生
民以来未之有也若然則我
聖祖文與武之全德止于斯而已乎諸士子其
鋪張揚厲以昭示萬世而
右文偃武之深意請并著于篇以為我
皇上法
祖之助
問先儒許魯齋有言傳記中人才傑然可
===
觀而血氣用事只是偏才豈非聖學不
傳無所持循依據以盡其性故耶子思
中庸一書固聖賢傳授之心法也自今
觀之蓋與堯舜禹授受之言如合符節
而尊德性道問學一章朱子乃謂聖賢
所示入德之方未有詳于是者且謂尊
德性所以存心而極乎道體之大道問
學所以致知而盡乎道體之細又以其
下八者俱為存心致知之屬不知于三

聖祖掃胡元之亂，復綱常，正人紀，舉一世而甄陶之，其道與帝王同，而功則倍焉，自生民以来未之有也。若然，則我聖祖文與武之全德止于斯而已乎？諸士子其鋪張揚厲，以昭示萬世，而右文偃武之深意，請并著于篇，以為我皇上法祖之助。
問：先儒許魯齋有言：「傳記中人才傑然可觀，而血氣用事，只是偏才，豈非聖學不傳，無所持循依據以盡其性故耶？」子思《中庸》一書，固聖賢傳授之心法也。自今觀之，蓋與堯、舜、禹授受之言如合符節。而「尊德性，道問學」一章，朱子乃謂聖賢所示入德之方未有詳于是者，且謂尊德性所以存心而極乎道體之大，道問學所以致知而盡乎道體之細，又以其下八者俱為存心致知之屬。不知于三
translation_en:
…the Sagely Progenitor swept away the disorder of the barbarian Yuan, restored the cardinal bonds and constant virtues, rectified human relationships, and molded an entire age. His Way was the same as that of the ancient emperors and kings, but his achievements were twice as great: nothing like this had occurred since humankind first came into being. If so, does the complete virtue of our Sagely Progenitor in civil and military affairs extend only this far? You candidates should expound and celebrate it, making it manifest to all generations. Please also set forth in your essays his profound intention in honoring civil culture and laying arms to rest, thereby assisting Our Emperor in emulating his ancestor.
Question: The earlier Confucian scholar Xu Luzhai said: “Among the men of talent recorded in biographies, some are outstanding and worthy of admiration, yet act under the sway of their physical passions and possess only partial talents. Is this not because the learning of the sages has not been transmitted, leaving them without anything to uphold, follow, or rely upon in fully realizing their nature?” Zisi’s Doctrine of the Mean is indeed the teaching of the mind transmitted by the sages and worthies. Viewed from the present, it accords with the words handed down from Yao to Shun and Yu as closely as the matching halves of a tally. Of the chapter beginning ‘Honor the virtuous nature and pursue inquiry and learning,’ Master Zhu said that no method shown by the sages and worthies for entering into virtue was more detailed than this. He further said that honoring the virtuous nature is the means of preserving the mind and reaching the utmost breadth of the substance of the Way, while pursuing inquiry and learning is the means of extending knowledge and exhausting the finest details of the substance of the Way. He also classified all eight items that follow under preserving the mind and extending knowledge. We wonder whether, with regard to the three…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
聖相傳之㫖亦有所據否乎朱子又嘗
謂子思之學傳之孟軻軻死而其傳泯
焉若然則荀揚諸子固不足論而董仲
舒能為正心以正朝廷之對韓退之又
能及乎大學誠意之說亦皆無可取耶
乃若孔明有學以廣才靜以成學之言
其所得者深矣而亦無與于斯何耶孔
明事業庶幾王佐槩以偏才目之不知
由玆心法而充其極其功用又當何如
===
其盛耶宋二程夫子生千五百年之後
始知尊信是書而表章之於是孟氏之
傳復續則其所言必有上契于子思者
今亦可得聞歟接程氏之傳者朱子也
其為存心致知之論亦有本于程氏否
歟性道之妙洙泗罕言朱子又為或問
以附章句之後得無與孔子之意異歟
然以言之如此其切說之如此其詳不
一再傳而雙峰饒氏乃有疑于存心致

一再傳而雙峰饒氏乃有疑于存心致
punctuated: 聖相傳之㫖亦有所據否乎？朱子又嘗謂子思之學傳之孟軻，軻死而其傳泯焉。若然，則荀揚諸子固不足論，而董仲舒能為正心以正朝廷之對，韓退之又能及乎大學誠意之說，亦皆無可取耶？乃若孔明有學以廣才、靜以成學之言，其所得者深矣，而亦無與于斯，何耶？孔明事業庶幾王佐，槩以偏才目之，不知由玆心法而充其極，其功用又當何如其盛耶？宋二程夫子生千五百年之後，始知尊信是書而表章之，於是孟氏之傳復續，則其所言必有上契于子思者，今亦可得聞歟？接程氏之傳者朱子也，其為存心致知之論亦有本于程氏否歟？性道之妙，洙泗罕言，朱子又為《或問》以附《章句》之後，得無與孔子之意異歟？然以言之如此其切，說之如此其詳，不一再傳，而雙峰饒氏乃有疑于存心致
translation_en:
…whether there is also a basis for this in the purport transmitted among the three sages? Master Zhu also once said that Zisi’s learning was transmitted to Meng Ke, and that when Meng Ke died, its transmission disappeared. If so, thinkers such as Xun Qing and Yang Xiong hardly merit discussion; yet Dong Zhongshu could offer a response concerning rectifying the mind in order to rectify the imperial court, and Han Tuizhi could also address the teaching of making the intentions sincere in the Great Learning. Is there likewise nothing worth accepting in any of these? As for Kongming, he said that learning broadens one’s abilities and tranquility brings learning to fruition. His understanding was profound, yet he too is excluded from this transmission. Why? Kongming’s achievements approached those of a worthy assistant to a true king, yet he is broadly characterized as a man of limited talents. Had he followed this teaching of the mind and developed it to its fullest extent, how magnificent might its practical effects have been?

The two Masters Cheng of the Song, born fifteen hundred years later, were the first to recognize that this book should be revered and trusted, and to bring it to prominence. Thereupon the transmission from Master Meng was renewed. Their statements must therefore have accorded with Zisi’s teaching of old. May we now hear how? Master Zhu carried on the transmission of the Cheng brothers. Did his account of preserving the mind and extending knowledge likewise have its basis in their teachings? The subtleties of human nature and the Way were seldom discussed in the school by the Zhu and Si rivers. Yet Master Zhu composed Questions and Answers to append to his Chapter and Sentence Commentaries. Might this differ from Confucius’s intention? Nevertheless, although his words were so pertinent and his explanations so detailed, scarcely one or two generations of transmission had passed before Master Rao of Shuangfeng came to doubt the teaching of preserving the mind and extending…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
知之說願為朱子□臣嗣後陳定宇史
伯璿以及保齋劉□□皆紛然辨論而於
朱子終不釋然道□□甫明而即晦全才
之不見于世又何□□哉茲二者正孔門
心法要旨所在使□□子猶有未融亦何
所持循依據以續□□學之傳乎諸士子
誦法之餘必有至□日歸一之論請極言
之以祛諸儒不決□疑使朱子立言之
意曉然大明于世□□于春闈深有望焉
===
嗚呼聖學明則□才出矣
問為治之道亦多□□矣究其急務則用人
安民二者此古今所同也以用人言之
古之時俊傑在位野無遺賢庶績咸熈
固其所也然九德以德稱而不聞短于
才元凱以才著而不聞歉于德盖未嘗
有才德之分焉則才德之分自何時始
歟官人者將惟德是庸而不計其才則
魏無知之所以進陳平者是或一道也

知之說，願為朱子□臣。嗣後陳定宇、史伯璿以及保齋劉□□，皆紛然辨論，而於朱子終不釋然。道□□甫明而即晦，全才之不見于世，又何□□哉？茲二者，正孔門心法要旨所在。使□□子猶有未融，亦何所持循依據，以續□□學之傳乎？諸士子誦法之餘，必有至□日歸一之論，請極言之，以祛諸儒不決□疑，使朱子立言之意曉然大明于世。□□于春闈，深有望焉。嗚呼！聖學明，則□才出矣！

問：為治之道，亦多□□矣。究其急務，則用人、安民二者，此古今所同也。以用人言之，古之時，俊傑在位，野無遺賢，庶績咸熈，固其所也。然九德以德稱，而不聞短于才；元凱以才著，而不聞歉于德。盖未嘗有才德之分焉，則才德之分自何時始歟？官人者將惟德是庸，而不計其才，則魏無知之所以進陳平者，是或一道也。
translation_en:
…the doctrine of extending knowledge, wishing to serve as Master Zhu’s [illegible] minister [?]. Subsequently, Chen Dingyu, Shi Boxuan, and Liu [two illegible characters], known as Baozhai, all engaged in a profusion of debate, yet their doubts concerning Master Zhu were never dispelled. The Way [illegible] had scarcely become clear before it was obscured again. Why, then, [illegible] should fully accomplished men of talent fail to appear in the world? These two matters are precisely where the essential purport of the teaching of the mind in Confucius’s school resides. If [illegible] still leaves something unresolved concerning the Master [?], what could one follow and rely upon to continue the transmission of [illegible] learning? Beyond your recitation and emulation of the texts, you candidates must have an account that [illegible] brings these matters into unity [?]. Please set it forth fully, to dispel the doubts left unresolved by the various scholars and make Master Zhu’s intention in formulating his teachings plainly evident to the world. [Illegible] places great hopes in this spring Metropolitan Examination. Alas! When the learning of the sages is made clear, [illegible] men of talent will emerge!

Question: The ways of governing are also many [illegible]. Yet when we examine its urgent tasks, they are these two: employing men and bringing peace to the people. This has been the same in antiquity and today. As for employing men, in ancient times outstanding men occupied office, and no worthy men were left undiscovered outside government; it was only fitting that all undertakings should flourish. Yet those characterized by the nine virtues were praised for their virtue, and we do not hear that they lacked ability; the Eight Yuan and Eight Kai were renowned for ability, and we do not hear that they were deficient in virtue. It seems there was never a division between ability and virtue. When, then, did this division begin? If those who appoint men to office are to employ them solely for virtue, without considering their ability, then the grounds on which Wei Wuzhi recommended Chen Ping may perhaps offer one approach…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
將惟才是使而不考其素則司馬温公
之所以斥吕惠卿者尤不可易也或謂
道不虚行是當責諸用人之人似矣而
不知擇用人之人而用之亦有其道否
歟以安民言之古之民耕食鑿飲不識
不知萬邦咸寧何其盛也然五方之土
宇不同何以能無貧富不均之嘆兆民
之稟賦不同何以能有比屋可封之俗
豈生斯世者適當雍熙太和之盛而上
===
之人可無為歟後世則異於是農桑非
不勸而民之貧富未必均學校非不建
而民之薄惡未必化或謂事在師古必
盡復古法而後可其果然歟抑猶有可
疑者漢高帝能用三傑任使當矣胡羣
屈羣策亦多吹簫屠狗之徒豈豪俊跅
弛之士亦不可棄歟文帝幾致刑措其
德化盛矣胡禮樂制度謙讓未遑豈愛
養元元教化非所急歟然一則成大業

punctuated: 將惟才是使，而不考其素，則司馬温公之所以斥吕惠卿者，尤不可易也。或謂道不虚行，是當責諸用人之人，似矣，而不知擇用人之人而用之，亦有其道否歟？以安民言之，古之民耕食鑿飲，不識不知，萬邦咸寧，何其盛也！然五方之土宇不同，何以能無貧富不均之嘆？兆民之稟賦不同，何以能有比屋可封之俗？豈生斯世者適當雍熙太和之盛，而上之人可無為歟？後世則異於是，農桑非不勸，而民之貧富未必均；學校非不建，而民之薄惡未必化。或謂事在師古，必盡復古法而後可，其果然歟？抑猶有可疑者：漢高帝能用三傑，任使當矣，胡羣屈羣策，亦多吹簫屠狗之徒，豈豪俊跅弛之士亦不可棄歟？文帝幾致刑措，其德化盛矣，胡禮樂制度，謙讓未遑，豈愛養元元，教化非所急歟？然一則成大業
translation_en:
…If, instead, one employs men solely for their talent without examining their previous conduct, then the grounds on which Sima Guang, Duke Wen, condemned Lü Huiqing are especially impossible to gainsay. Some say that the Way does not put itself into practice, and that responsibility therefore rests with those who employ men. This seems right; yet is there also a proper way to select and appoint those who will themselves employ others?

As for bringing peace to the people, in antiquity they ploughed for their food and dug wells for their drink, acting without conscious knowledge, and the myriad states were all at peace. How flourishing an age! Yet the lands of the five regions differed: how could there have been no complaints about inequalities of wealth and poverty? The innate endowments of the myriad people differed: how could their customs have been such that every household was worthy of receiving an enfeoffment? Could it be that those born into that age simply happened to enjoy an era of harmony, prosperity, and supreme concord, while their rulers could remain inactive?

Later ages differed from this. Agriculture and sericulture were indeed encouraged, yet disparities in the people's wealth did not necessarily disappear. Schools were indeed established, yet the people's mean and wicked ways were not necessarily transformed. Some say that the task lies in taking antiquity as one's model, and that only a complete restoration of ancient institutions will suffice. Is that really so?

There are, moreover, further points open to question. Emperor Gao of Han could employ the Three Heroes, and his appointments were fitting. Why, among those whose collective abilities and counsels he drew upon [?], were there also so many flute players and dog butchers? Does this mean that outstanding men of unrestrained conduct must not be discarded either? Emperor Wen came close to making punishments unnecessary: his transformation of the people through virtue was indeed flourishing. Why, then, did he modestly decline to undertake the establishment of rites, music, and institutions, saying that he had not yet had leisure for them? Does this mean that, when cherishing and nourishing the common people, moral instruction is not an urgent concern? Yet the one accomplished a great enterprise …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
于五載之間一則綿國脉于四百年之
久亦不可不論其故也兹欲尊賢使能
不失劑處之宜正德厚生同蒙至治之
澤真有以追盛治于虞唐而陋西京于
不居何修何為而可諸士子窮經有年
請稽諸經以對
問所貴乎稽古者非徒以資博辨盖將考
其盛衰之故以為經世之資耳姑以宋
事言之藝祖仁厚立國三傳至於仁宗
===
恭儉忠厚事先大體治道敦美而上下
因循綱紀漸隳吏治不振邊徼無功建
議者思欲更之而吕夷簡諸執政終不
以為然天下之事日入于弊而國勢因
之益弱豈老成謀國自有所見歟神宗承
積弊之後勵精圖治將欲大有所為以
復漢唐土宇之舊其志偉矣而耆舊大
臣多莫與共事獨一王介甫議與帝合
于是傾心信之創制立法講求富強之

punctuated:
于五載之間，一則綿國脉于四百年之久，亦不可不論其故也。兹欲尊賢使能，不失劑處之宜，正德厚生，同蒙至治之澤，真有以追盛治于虞唐，而陋西京于不居，何修何為而可？諸士子窮經有年，請稽諸經以對。
問：所貴乎稽古者，非徒以資博辨，盖將考其盛衰之故，以為經世之資耳。姑以宋事言之，藝祖仁厚立國，三傳至於仁宗，恭儉忠厚，事先大體，治道敦美，而上下因循，綱紀漸隳，吏治不振，邊徼無功。建議者思欲更之，而吕夷簡諸執政終不以為然。天下之事日入于弊，而國勢因之益弱，豈老成謀國自有所見歟？神宗承積弊之後，勵精圖治，將欲大有所為，以復漢唐土宇之舊，其志偉矣，而耆舊大臣多莫與共事，獨一王介甫議與帝合。于是傾心信之，創制立法，講求富強之
translation_en:
…within five years, while the other prolonged the dynasty’s life for four hundred years. The reasons for this, too, must be examined. Now we wish to honor the worthy and employ the capable, maintaining a proper balance in our arrangements; to rectify virtue and enrich the people’s livelihood, so that all may share the blessings of consummate government; and truly to emulate the flourishing rule of Shun and Yao, regarding the Western Han as too modest an achievement to rest content with. What must we cultivate and undertake to accomplish this? You candidates have devoted years to studying the classics thoroughly. Please consult them in framing your replies.
Question: What is valued in investigating antiquity is not merely its contribution to extensive learning and skill in argument. Rather, it is the examination of the causes of flourishing and decline, to furnish resources for governing the world. Take the affairs of the Song as an example. Its founding emperor established the dynasty through benevolence and generosity. After three successions, the throne came to Renzong, who was reverent, frugal, loyal, and generous. In affairs he gave priority to the essentials, and his governance was earnest and admirable. Yet superiors and subordinates alike followed established routines complacently; institutional order gradually deteriorated, civil administration languished, and no successes were achieved on the frontiers. Those submitting proposals wished to change this, but Lü Yijian and the other chief councillors never agreed. The affairs of the realm grew more troubled by the day, and the strength of the state consequently declined still further. Could it be that these seasoned statesmen had insights of their own in planning for the state?
Shenzong inherited these accumulated abuses and devoted his energies to achieving good government. He intended to accomplish great things and recover the former territories of the Han and Tang: his ambition was grand indeed. Yet few of the venerable senior ministers would join him in this undertaking. Wang Jiefu alone advanced proposals that accorded with the emperor’s views. Thereupon the emperor placed wholehearted trust in him, instituting new arrangements, establishing laws, and investigating means of achieving wealth and power…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
術風俗為之一新然天下騷然反不如
慶曆嘉祐之時豈更化善治别有道歟
眉山蘇氏蓋兩病之且于漢之文宣二
帝深加羨慕至謂漢文寬仁長者不聞
有怠廢不舉之患宣帝綜核名實不聞
有督責過甚之失信斯言也則二帝之
治敦大有功兩無所偏將遂可比隆於
有周成王之盛歟吾意蘇氏之言特以
警動當世非至論也獨惜夫忠厚有道
如仁宗勵精有志如神宗皆能信任其
臣而一聽其所為千載一時之會也而
為之相者顧不滿人望有遺憾焉此其
事夫人知之亦夫人能言之也然論事
易處事難諸士子設生二宗之世即授
以政如諸君子其何所施為建白乃為
善歟尚審其勢度其時深惟弊源所在
而各代為之處如或用爾執此以往可
也

眉山蘇氏盖兩病之且于漢之文宣二
帝深加羨慕至謂漢文寬仁長者不聞

有周成王之盛歟吾意蘇氏之言特以
警動當世非至論也獨惜夫忠厚有道
===
如仁宗勵精有志如神宗皆能信任其
臣而一聽其所為千載一時之會也而
為之相者顧不滿人望有遺憾焉此其
事天人知之亦夫人能言之也然論事
易處事難諸士子談生二宗之世即授
以政如諸君子其何所施為建白乃為
善歟尚審其勢度其時深惟弊源所在
而各代為之處如或用爾執此以往可
也
punctuated: 術，風俗為之一新，然天下騷然，反不如慶曆嘉祐之時，豈更化善治别有道歟？眉山蘇氏蓋兩病之，且于漢之文宣二帝深加羨慕，至謂漢文寬仁長者，不聞有怠廢不舉之患；宣帝綜核名實，不聞有督責過甚之失。信斯言也，則二帝之治敦大有功，兩無所偏，將遂可比隆於有周成王之盛歟？吾意蘇氏之言特以警動當世，非至論也。獨惜夫忠厚有道如仁宗，勵精有志如神宗，皆能信任其臣，而一聽其所為，千載一時之會也，而為之相者顧不滿人望，有遺憾焉。此其事夫人知之，亦夫人能言之也。然論事易，處事難。諸士子設生二宗之世，即授以政如諸君子，其何所施為建白乃為善歟？尚審其勢，度其時，深惟弊源所在，而各代為之處。如或用爾，執此以往可也。
translation_en:
…methods of enriching the state and strengthening its military. Customs were thereby renewed, yet the realm was thrown into turmoil, and conditions were worse than during the Qingli and Jiayou eras. Could there be another way to reform government and achieve good order? Master Su of Meishan found fault with both approaches. He also expressed profound admiration for Emperors Wen and Xuan of the Han, going so far as to say: “Emperor Wen of the Han was a generous and benevolent elder; we hear of no harm from negligent abandonment of affairs or failure to act. Emperor Xuan comprehensively scrutinized names and actual performance; we hear of no error from excessive demands and censure.” If these words are true, then the governments of these two emperors were magnanimous and effective, neither tending toward either extreme. Could they thus rival the flourishing reign of King Cheng of the Zhou? In my view, Master Su’s words were intended simply to rouse and admonish his contemporaries; they were not a definitive judgment.

It is especially regrettable that Renzong, so loyal-hearted, generous, and principled, and Shenzong, so diligent and ambitious, were both able to trust their ministers and give them full latitude to act—a conjunction of ruler and minister encountered once in a thousand years—yet those who served as their chief councillors failed to meet people’s expectations, leaving grounds for regret. These are matters that everyone knows and everyone can discuss. Yet discussing affairs is easy; handling them is difficult. Suppose you candidates had lived in the reigns of these two emperors and had been entrusted with government as those gentlemen were: what measures and proposals would you have put forward to achieve good government? Carefully examine the circumstances, weigh the demands of the times, and reflect deeply on where the abuses originated. Each of you should devise how you would have handled matters in their place. Should someone employ you, you may take these principles with you and put them into practice.

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
問古者聖人擬圓極以運璇璣列方輿而
配景曜以正天時以授民事以考災祥
黃虞迄兹世有專職今所宗者何人之
法歟九州十二野之分於天星各有所
繫而干支方位亦互有屬焉何所本而
言歟穹壤之相銜位固有相值者矣若
齊東而玄枵在子魯東而降婁在戌吳
越南而星紀在丑干支方位與此復相
戾焉可得聞其說歟或謂諸侯始封歲
===
星所在之辰而其國屬焉亦既有占驗
矣而或又以為非是何歟自古言天者
凡幾家論者謂惟渾天為近而或又以
為古人之意初不在是者何歟其說皆
可聞歟五星列宿隨其變而禍福應焉
以為不足畏者誠悖矣而亦直有其變
而無其應與宜有變而顧得其常者何
歟方今
聖人在上而四方郡邑天妖地異屢形奏章將

聖人在上而四方郡邑天妖地異屢形奏章朝
punctuated: 問：古者聖人擬圓極以運璇璣，列方輿而配景曜，以正天時，以授民事，以考災祥。黃虞迄兹，世有專職。今所宗者何人之法歟？九州十二野之分，於天星各有所繫，而干支方位亦互有屬焉，何所本而言歟？穹壤之相銜，位固有相值者矣。若齊東而玄枵在子，魯東而降婁在戌，吳越南而星紀在丑，干支方位與此復相戾焉，可得聞其說歟？或謂諸侯始封，歲星所在之辰，而其國屬焉，亦既有占驗矣，而或又以為非是，何歟？自古言天者凡幾家？論者謂惟渾天為近，而或又以為古人之意初不在是者，何歟？其說皆可聞歟？五星列宿，隨其變而禍福應焉，以為不足畏者誠悖矣。而亦直有其變而無其應，與宜有變而顧得其常者，何歟？方今聖人在上，而四方郡邑天妖地異屢形奏章，將
translation_en:
Question: In antiquity, the sages modeled the rounded heavens and their pole to operate the armillary sphere, laid out the square earth and correlated it with the celestial luminaries, thereby determining the seasons, assigning the people their tasks, and examining calamities and auspicious signs. From the Yellow Emperor and Shun down to the present, every age has had officials specifically charged with these duties. Whose methods are followed today? The divisions into Nine Provinces and twelve territories each have their corresponding stars in heaven, while the heavenly stems, earthly branches, and compass directions also have their respective associations. On what basis are these correspondences asserted? Where heaven and earth meet, their positions certainly have points of correspondence. Yet Qi lies in the east while Xuanxiao is at zi; Lu lies in the east while Jianglou is at xu; and Wu and Yue lie in the south while Xingji is at chou. The directions associated with the stems and branches thus conflict with these correspondences. May we hear an explanation? Some say that a feudal lord’s state was assigned to the celestial station occupied by Jupiter when he first received his fief. There have indeed been verified prognostications based on this, yet others reject the explanation. Why?

How many schools of thought concerning the heavens have there been since antiquity? Some commentators hold that only the spherical-heaven theory approaches the truth, while others maintain that the ancients’ intent never lay in this at all. Why? May we hear all these explanations? Changes in the five planets and the constellations have corresponding effects in misfortune and good fortune; it is certainly perverse to consider them unworthy of fear. Yet why are there also cases in which celestial changes occur without corresponding effects, or in which changes ought to occur but the heavens instead maintain their regular course? At present, a sage rules above, yet celestial portents and terrestrial anomalies in prefectures and counties throughout the realm repeatedly appear in memorials to the throne. [The final character 將 is unclear here: ?] …

translation_en: …within the capital region, spring droughts and autumn downpours impair both cultivation and harvest. Could this be what the ancients meant by Heaven’s benevolent concern, seeking thereby to warn and stir us to action? You candidates have long attended to the relationship between Heaven and humanity. Beyond elucidating celestial phenomena and their correspondences, if you have any means of dispelling anomalies and averting calamities, we hope you will not begrudge a word of counsel.

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
夫仁者己欲立而立人己欲達而達人
王正宗
同考試官給事中黄批講立達處善狀
仁者之心蓋究心於理學者
同考試官檢討郭批塲中作此題者多
以推己及人為言甚失聖人本旨是篇見理
精到語意渾成可以式矣
===
同考試官編修陸批論語義才着言語
便錯此作理明而詞盡錄之以示天下之尚
彌文者
同考試官編修嚴批刋落繁詞而理致
精到論語義似此作者絕少
同考試官侍讀崔批盡畧浮艶之詞深
得聖人之旨
考試官學士顧批文字明淨結亦有意
味錄之

王正宗。
同考試官給事中黄批：「講立達處，善狀仁者之心，蓋究心於理學者。」

translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“The benevolent person, wishing to establish himself, establishes others; wishing to attain success himself, enables others to attain success.”

Wang Zhengzong

Associate Examiner Huang, Supervising Secretary, comments: “The discussion of establishing oneself and attaining success aptly portrays the heart of the benevolent person. The author is evidently someone who has devoted himself to the learning of principle.”

Associate Examiner Guo, Examining Editor, comments: “Many candidates who addressed this topic in the examination spoke of extending consideration from oneself to others, greatly missing the sage’s original intent. This essay’s understanding of principle is precise and thorough; its language and meaning form a seamless whole. It may serve as a model.”

Associate Examiner Lu, Compiler, comments: “In elucidating the meaning of the Analects, the moment one becomes attached to verbal expression, one goes astray. In this composition, principle is clear and the wording fully conveys it. It is included to instruct those throughout the realm who prize excessive literary ornament.”

Associate Examiner Yan, Compiler, comments: “Superfluous wording has been cut away, while the exposition of principle is precise and thorough. Compositions elucidating the meaning of the Analects that are comparable to this are exceedingly rare.”

Associate Examiner Cui, Reader-in-waiting, comments: “It dispenses entirely with superficial, ornate wording and profoundly grasps the sage’s intent.”

Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “The writing is clear and clean, and the conclusion, too, has depth of meaning. Include it.”

考試官大學□劉批心裏真切方能如此作
良是
聖人指言仁者之心正以救賢者之識夫仁也
夫以己及人仁者之心也於此觀之則仁可識
矣而何高遠之求哉昔子貢以博施濟衆為仁
而聖人教之如此且仁之為道雖大而其本不
出於吾心所謂仁者豈必其施之博而濟之衆

translation_en:
Examiner Liu, Grand Secretary [?], comments: Only someone with genuine conviction in his heart could write in this way. Very true.

The Sage pointed out the heart of the benevolent precisely to correct the worthy man's understanding of benevolence. To extend one's concern from oneself to others is the heart of the benevolent. Viewed in this light, benevolence can be understood; why seek it in what is lofty and remote? Formerly, Zigong took bestowing benefits widely and bringing relief to the multitude to constitute benevolence, and the Sage instructed him in this way. Although benevolence as a Way is vast, its root lies nowhere outside our own hearts. Must those called benevolent necessarily bestow benefits widely and bring relief to the multitude? They need only possess this heart.

Thus, to live in one's age and stand firmly established—is this not something everyone desires? When the benevolent desire to establish themselves, the thought of establishing others arises along with it. Seeing those in the world who have fallen and are weak, they seek ways to support and nurture them, so that they too may establish themselves. For their concern of universal love flows freely between others and themselves: they regard others as they regard themselves. To make one's way in the world and advance freely in all endeavors—is this not also something everyone desires? When the benevolent desire to advance themselves, the thought of advancing others already wells up irresistibly. Seeing those in the world who are benighted and obstructed, they seek ways to guide, assist, and enlighten them, so that they too may advance themselves. For their utterly impartial hearts are not hindered by the separation between bodily forms: they bring others to fulfillment as they bring themselves to fulfillment. Ah! In establishing themselves, they do not establish themselves alone, but must wish to stand established together with others; in advancing themselves, they do not advance themselves alone, but must wish, together with others, to…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
俱達仁者之心如此聖人指以為子貢告豈非
欲其識仁之體而知所從事哉大抵學有次序
道有本體知其序而後可進識其體而後可入
此聖門之教也子貢有為仁之志而以博施濟
衆求之失之遠矣故聖人抑之使反求諸己而
下文又以能近取譬示以進為之方夫識其體
而由其方以入焉則仁可得而博濟之功亦於
是始矣此學之序也孟子亦曰强恕而行求仁
莫近焉讀者其合而觀之
敬大臣則不眩體羣臣則士之報禮重子
庶民則百姓勸來百工則財用足柔遠人
則四方歸之懷諸侯則天下畏之
李紹賢

則一類推之說或問詳矣此作發揮明白豈

俱達。仁者之心如此，聖人指以為子貢告，豈非欲其識仁之體而知所從事哉？大抵學有次序，道有本體，知其序而後可進，識其體而後可入，此聖門之教也。子貢有為仁之志，而以博施濟衆求之，失之遠矣。故聖人抑之，使反求諸己，而下文又以能近取譬示以進為之方。夫識其體，而由其方以入焉，則仁可得，而博濟之功亦於是始矣。此學之序也。孟子亦曰：「强恕而行，求仁莫近焉。」讀者其合而觀之。

敬大臣則不眩，體羣臣則士之報禮重，子庶民則百姓勸，來百工則財用足，柔遠人則四方歸之，懷諸侯則天下畏之。

李紹賢

同考試官主事王批：「九經事不同而理則一，類推之說，《或問》詳矣。此作發揮明白，豈亦留心治道而識其本者耶？」

同考試官都給事中俞批：「詞明意足，有布帛菽粟氣味，豈文之經常者耶？錄之。」
translation_en:
…attain fulfillment together. Such is the heart of the benevolent person. In pointing this out to Zigong, was the Sage not seeking to make him recognize the essential nature of benevolence and understand where to direct his efforts? In general, learning has a sequence, and the Way has an essential substance. Only after understanding that sequence can one advance; only after recognizing that substance can one enter. Such is the teaching of the Sage’s school. Zigong aspired to practice benevolence, yet sought it through bestowing benefits widely and bringing relief to the multitude: he had strayed far from the proper approach. Thus the Sage restrained him, making him turn back and seek it within himself. In the passage that follows, he further showed him how to advance in practice through “being able to draw an analogy from what is close at hand.” Once one recognizes its essential nature and enters by this method, benevolence can be attained, and the achievement of bringing relief widely also begins here. This is the sequence of learning. Mencius likewise said: “Strive to act with sympathetic understanding; in seeking benevolence, nothing comes closer than this.” Readers should consider these passages together.

“When one honors the great ministers, one is not bewildered; when one puts oneself in the position of the assembled ministers, the service they render in return is substantial; when one treats the common people as one’s children, the people are encouraged to exert themselves; when one attracts the various artisans, financial resources and supplies are sufficient; when one treats people from afar kindly, people from all quarters turn to one; when one cherishes the feudal lords, all under Heaven stand in awe of one.”

Li Shaoxian

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Secretary: “The nine guiding principles differ in their practical concerns, yet their underlying principle is one. The explanation of extending them by analogy is set out fully in Further Questions (Huowen). This composition expounds the matter clearly. Might its author also be someone who has devoted attention to the Way of governance and understands its foundation?”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Chief Supervising Secretary: “The wording is clear and the meaning fully expressed. It has the flavor of cloth and silk, beans and grain—the essentials of everyday life. Might this be writing that embodies enduring standards? Selected for inclusion.”

考試官大學士靳批得朱子意
聖人列常道之效有得於尊賢之所推者有得
===
於親親之所推者蓋政舉而效隨之此常道之
所以善也聖人以是告時君其開導之意深矣
中庸論道之費隱明以孔子告哀公問政之言
如此且脩身為九經之本而尊賢親親次之既
各有其效矣而尊賢親親之所推者又何如耶
是故朝廷之上有大臣焉有以敬之則禮遇周
至而聰明有寄信任專一而裁決不迷衆言不
為之淆惑也萬幾不為之叢脞也何有於眩乎
有羣臣焉有以體之則志意所孚而圖報之心

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Jin, Examining Editor, comments: “The nine guiding principles are the essentials of government, and their ordering is distinctly articulated and free of confusion. This composition expounds them in substantial, well-rounded prose, fully expressing their meaning and thoroughly reaching their underlying principles. Only someone who has long cultivated and nourished himself could accomplish this. It is selected to serve as a model.”
Associate Examiner Liu, Senior Compiler, comments: “On this topic, Zhu Xi’s commentary and his Questions and Answers illuminate one another, but comprehending them as a coherent whole is difficult. Compositions like this are very rare.”
Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “Detailed and ample, lucid and orderly. Its discussion of how results are achieved is especially concrete and sound. The author must be a man who understands government.”
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “It captures Master Zhu’s meaning.”
When the sage enumerated the effects of the constant Way, some arose from extending the principle of honoring the worthy, and others from extending the principle of affection for one’s kin. Once measures of government are put into practice, their effects follow: this is what makes the constant Way good. The sage used these teachings to instruct the ruler of his time; profound indeed was his intention to enlighten and guide him.
In discussing the Way’s wide reach and hidden subtlety, the Doctrine of the Mean elucidates them through these words of Confucius in response to Duke Ai’s question about government. Now, cultivating oneself is the foundation of the nine guiding principles, followed by honoring the worthy and showing affection for one’s kin. Each already has its own effects; what, then, of the further effects arising from extending the principles of honoring the worthy and showing affection for one’s kin? Thus, at court there are great ministers. If the ruler treats them with respect, the courtesies accorded them will be comprehensive, and his powers of perception and understanding will have someone on whom to rely. His trust in them will be undivided, and his judgments will not go astray. The multitude of voices will not confuse him, nor will the myriad affairs of state become tangled and disordered. How could he suffer bewilderment? There are also the assembled officials. If the ruler treats them with sympathetic consideration, his intentions will win their confidence, and their desire to repay him …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
益切感激所在而徇身之念自輕官守必脩其
職也言責必盡其忠也報禮何重乎效之得於
尊賢之所推者盖如此由是達之於國有庶民
焉有百工焉庶民而有以子之則羣心愛戴不
令而行趨事赴工之恐後不啻子弟之於父兄
也百姓無弗勸矣百工而有以來之則通工易
事農末相資軍需國用之不乏不啻水火之於
日用也財用無弗足矣又由是達之天下有遠
人焉有諸侯焉遠人而有以柔之則賔旅之往
===
來有資而愚良之志願各遂人皆悅出其途矣
四方有不歸乎諸侯而有以懷之則德之所施
者博而威之所制者廣莫敢有貳於我矣天下
有不畏乎效之得於親親之所推者又如此揆
厥所原何莫而非脩身為之本歟嗟夫此所謂
文武之政也豈哀公所能與哉而孔子告之諄
切如此何也聖人愛君之深所以引之于道者
不忍謂吾君為不能焉遽已也使哀公果能幡
然改悟魯其不為東周乎雖然孔子是言萬世

punctuated: 益切，感激所在，而徇身之念自輕。官守必脩其職也，言責必盡其忠也，報禮何重乎！效之得於尊賢之所推者，盖如此。由是達之於國，有庶民焉，有百工焉。庶民而有以子之，則羣心愛戴，不令而行，趨事赴工之恐後，不啻子弟之於父兄也，百姓無弗勸矣。百工而有以來之，則通工易事，農末相資，軍需國用之不乏，不啻水火之於日用也，財用無弗足矣。又由是達之天下，有遠人焉，有諸侯焉。遠人而有以柔之，則賔旅之往來有資，而愚良之志願各遂，人皆悅出其途矣，四方有不歸乎？諸侯而有以懷之，則德之所施者博，而威之所制者廣，莫敢有貳於我矣，天下有不畏乎？效之得於親親之所推者，又如此。揆厥所原，何莫而非脩身為之本歟？嗟夫！此所謂文武之政也，豈哀公所能與哉？而孔子告之諄切如此，何也？聖人愛君之深，所以引之于道者，不忍謂吾君為不能焉，遽已也。使哀公果能幡然改悟，魯其不為東周乎？雖然，孔子是言，萬世
translation_en:
…grows still more earnest. Moved by gratitude, they readily think little of sacrificing their lives. Those charged with official duties will certainly fulfill them; those responsible for remonstrance will certainly offer their utmost loyalty. How substantial their repayment of the ruler’s courtesy! Such are the results obtained by extending the principle of honoring the worthy.

Extending this to the state, there are the common people and the various artisans. If the common people are treated as one’s children, all will love and support the ruler and act without awaiting commands. In their eagerness to undertake tasks and hasten to labor, fearing to fall behind, they will be no less devoted than sons and younger brothers toward fathers and elder brothers. None of the people will fail to exert themselves. If artisans are encouraged to come, their skills will circulate and their services be exchanged, while agriculture and the subsidiary occupations will sustain one another. Military supplies and the state’s requirements will be as readily available as water and fire for daily use. Financial resources will be entirely sufficient.

Extending this further to all under Heaven, there are people from afar and the feudal lords. If people from afar are treated with kindness, visiting travelers will have the means to come and go, and the wishes of the foolish and the good alike [?] will be fulfilled. Everyone will gladly travel along the ruler’s roads. Will any of the four quarters fail to turn to him? If the feudal lords are cherished, his virtue will reach far and his authority will exercise broad control. None will dare harbor divided allegiance toward him. Will any under Heaven fail to hold him in awe? Such, too, are the results obtained by extending the principle of affection for one’s kin. Examining their source, which of these does not have self-cultivation as its foundation?

Alas! This is what is called the government of Kings Wen and Wu. How could Duke Ai have been equal to it? Yet why did Confucius instruct him with such earnest insistence? So deeply did the sage care for his ruler that, in seeking to guide him toward the Way, he could not bear to say, “My ruler is incapable,” and abruptly give up. Had Duke Ai truly awakened and reformed, would Lu not have become an Eastern Zhou? Nevertheless, these words of Confucius, for ten thousand generations…

殆不多見
考試官學士顧批能以通章要旨融會
成文要是不苟作者
考試官大學士靳批説仁政保民處意足
惟仁政成於國中則王業成於天下夫舉一國
之民而皆遂其養則仁政成矣王業其有不成
乎昔孟子論興王在於保民故詳言制民常産
之法而舉其成功謂夫待帛而暖待肉而飽老
===
者之所願未易遂也今也常産立而蠶桑畜養
之有制則杼軸其盈而五十者咸得以衣帛孕
字日蕃而七十者咸得以食肉非惟一人為然
而舉國之老者皆有以老之矣無食則飢無衣
則寒黎民之所患未易免也今也常産立而耕
耘收穫之以時則食雖不肉而亦可以無飢衣
雖不帛而亦可以無寒非惟一民為然而舉國
之幼者皆有以幼之矣庠序之教由是而立孝
第之風由是而行仁政之成也如此則保民之

惟仁政成於國中，則王業成於天下。夫舉一國之民而皆遂其養，則仁政成矣，王業其有不成乎？昔孟子論興王在於保民，故詳言制民常産之法，而舉其成功，謂夫待帛而暖、待肉而飽，老者之所願未易遂也。今也常産立，而蠶桑畜養之有制，則杼軸其盈，而五十者咸得以衣帛；孕字日蕃，而七十者咸得以食肉。非惟一人為然，而舉國之老者皆有以老之矣。無食則飢，無衣則寒，黎民之所患未易免也。今也常産立，而耕耘收穫之以時，則食雖不肉，而亦可以無飢；衣雖不帛，而亦可以無寒。非惟一民為然，而舉國之幼者皆有以幼之矣。庠序之教由是而立，孝第之風由是而行。仁政之成也如此，則保民之

…those capable of composing an essay like this one, probing deeply into the chapter’s meaning and giving it full expression in their writing, are probably seldom seen.

Examiner Academician Gu comments: He integrates the essential meaning of the entire chapter into a coherent essay. Clearly, this is no careless writer.

Examiner Grand Secretary Jin comments: The discussion of benevolent government and protecting the people fully develops its meaning.

When benevolent government is accomplished within a state, the work of true kingship is accomplished throughout All-under-Heaven. If all the people of a state obtain adequate sustenance, benevolent government is accomplished. How, then, could the work of true kingship fail to be accomplished? In the past, Mengzi argued that the rise of a true king depended upon protecting the people. He therefore explained in detail how to establish a stable livelihood for the people and described the successful results. Those who need silk to keep warm and meat to be well nourished—the aged—cannot easily have their wishes fulfilled. Now, however, stable livelihoods are established, and silkworm raising, mulberry cultivation, and livestock rearing are properly regulated. The looms yield abundantly, and all those aged fifty can wear silk; livestock breed and multiply daily, and all those aged seventy can eat meat. This is so not merely for one person: there are means to care fittingly for all the aged throughout the state.

Without food there is hunger; without clothing there is cold. These afflictions of the common people are not easily avoided. Now, however, stable livelihoods are established, and plowing, weeding, and harvesting take place in their proper seasons. Thus, although their food includes no meat, they can nevertheless avoid hunger; although their clothes are not silk, they can nevertheless avoid cold. This is so not merely for one subject: there are means to nurture all the young throughout the state. Instruction in the local schools is thereby established, and the practice of filial devotion and respect for elder brothers thereby spreads. When benevolent government is accomplished in this way, then the work of protecting the people…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
功大矣而有不王者哉吾見老者既老則天下
之老莫不有盍歸之願幼者既幼則四方之氓
莫不有受廛之心甲兵不必試也土地可闢秦
楚可朝九圍之廣將於我乎式矣孰敢有不臣
者乎權謀不必用也中國可蒞四夷可撫一統
之命將於我乎凝矣孰敢有自外者乎謂之曰
未之有也信乎王業之必成矣為人君者可不
推是心以行仁政哉抑斯言也孟子嘗以告梁
君矣梁無所遇而復舉以告齊王豈他無奇策
===
之可陳乎誠以衣食乃常生之道農桑實王政
之本禹謨之養民箕疇之食貨后稷公劉之稼
穡皆是意也舍乎此則儀秦孫吳所以毒吾民
而追時好者聖賢方深痛而力救之尚忍言哉先
儒謂孟子之書在乎明王道黜霸功觀於此尤信
易
剛過而中巽而說行利有攸往乃亨大過
之時大矣哉
倫以訓

剛過而中巽而說行利有攸往乃亨大過

punctuated:
功大矣，而有不王者哉？吾見老者既老，則天下之老莫不有盍歸之願；幼者既幼，則四方之氓莫不有受廛之心。甲兵不必試也，土地可闢，秦楚可朝，九圍之廣將於我乎式矣，孰敢有不臣者乎？權謀不必用也，中國可蒞，四夷可撫，一統之命將於我乎凝矣，孰敢有自外者乎？謂之曰「未之有也」，信乎王業之必成矣！為人君者可不推是心以行仁政哉？抑斯言也，孟子嘗以告梁君矣，梁無所遇，而復舉以告齊王，豈他無奇策之可陳乎？誠以衣食乃常生之道，農桑實王政之本。禹謨之養民，箕疇之食貨，后稷公劉之稼穡，皆是意也。舍乎此，則儀秦孫吳所以毒吾民而追時好者，聖賢方深痛而力救之，尚忍言哉？先儒謂孟子之書在乎明王道、黜霸功，觀於此尤信。
易
剛過而中，巽而說行，利有攸往，乃亨。大過之時大矣哉！
倫以訓
translation_en:
…the achievement is great: could anyone accomplish this and yet fail to become a true king? I see that, once the elderly are properly cared for, all the elderly under Heaven will wish to say, “Why not go to him?” Once the young are properly nurtured, the people of every quarter will wish to receive a homestead in his realm. Without putting arms to the test, territory can be expanded and Qin and Chu brought to court in homage. The vast nine domains will follow our example; who would dare refuse to become our subject? Without resorting to stratagems, the central states can be governed and the peoples of the four outer regions brought to peace. The mandate to unite all will become firmly vested in us; who would dare remain outside our rule? To say, “There has never been such a case,” surely affirms that the kingly enterprise must succeed! Can a ruler fail to extend this heart of compassion and practice benevolent government?
Yet Mengzi had already addressed these words to the ruler of Liang. Finding no receptive response in Liang, he offered them again to the king of Qi. Was it because he had no other remarkable policies to present? Truly, clothing and food are the means of sustaining ordinary life, and farming and sericulture are the foundations of kingly government. The nurturing of the people in the Counsels of Yu, food and goods in Jizi’s categories of the Great Plan, and the agricultural labors of Hou Ji and Gong Liu all embody this intention. Abandon this, and one turns to the methods of Zhang Yi, Su Qin, Sun Wu, and Wu Qi, which injure our people while catering to the tastes of the age. Sages and worthies grieve deeply over this and strive to remedy it; could they bear even to advocate such methods? Earlier Confucian scholars said that the purpose of the book Mengzi is to elucidate the kingly Way and reject the achievements of hegemons. This passage makes that especially clear.
Book of Changes
“The firm exceeds, yet occupies the center; yielding and joyous in action, it is favorable to have somewhere to go, and thus there is success. Great indeed is the significance of the time of Great Exceeding!”
Lun Yixun

Associate Examiner Wen, Director, comments: “The language is refined and concise; this essay presents the meaning of the Book of Changes just as it should. Its concern with handling excess and guarding against overfullness extends beyond what is explicitly stated. Might the writer also have given thought to worldly affairs?”

Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler, comments: “The discussion of the time draws together the ideas of firmness retaining centrality, yielding, and joy. Its meaning is subtly conveyed: the more one reads, the more rewarding it becomes.”

Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler, comments: “The ideas in this topic on Great Exceeding (Daguo) are closely interconnected. This essay integrates them into a coherent composition, with a continuous thread and pivotal connections. The intention of remedying excess is also naturally present. It cannot be compared with mere elaboration.”

Associate Examiner Teng, Librarian, comments: “You articulate distinctly the intention of remedying excess and comprehending the time. Might you yourself also be someone who greatly exceeds others?”

Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “This is precisely the meaning of the Book of Changes. The discussion of ‘great indeed!’ makes the reader alert and reflective.”

Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “To compose an exposition of a classic that bears upon the condition of the world: this merits being called skillful study of the Book of Changes.”

In his commentary on the Judgment of Great Exceeding, the Sage points out that its capacities permit action, while expressing wonder at how difficult it is to act in its time. For when a time reaches excessive fullness, it may seem to warrant little concern, yet action is actually difficult. Because its capacities offer a means of remedy, the Sage marvels at the greatness of its time. His purport is subtle indeed. Moreover, the fundamental meaning of the hexagram Great Exceeding lies in an excess of yang. Excess means losing centrality, and such a condition cannot endure. In the words King Wen appended to the hexagram, there is…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
所謂利有攸往亨者何歟盖以卦體言之四陽
雖失之過而二五皆得其中剛過而中則不恃
其聰明而權度能審不任其果决而時措適宜
是固有立事之本矣以卦德言之巽之德爲巽
而兌之德爲說內巽外說則思慮深微於理无
不順施為寬裕於衆无不宜是又有制事之用
矣如是則利有往焉以興天下之事功道可常
通而窮極非所患也宜有行焉以修天下之政
理治可常保而平陂非所憂也尚何所往之有
===
不亨哉然自大過之時而觀之盈成之久勢或
有趨於偏者不以剛中拯之則識不早而力不
易矣盖天下難處之事也是非有過人之才而
能濟乎泰寧之餘釁或有萌於漸者不以巽說
治之則弊未去而患已生矣盖安危倚伏之機
也是又豈尋常之才所能與乎故聖人嘆之曰
大矣哉以見才不常逢時所當戒未可以細故
視之也雖然時之既盛上下相安於无事而忽
心生焉亦孰知才之為急而求其人以圖之夫

punctuated:
所謂「利有攸往，亨」者，何歟？盖以卦體言之，四陽雖失之過，而二五皆得其中。剛過而中，則不恃其聰明，而權度能審；不任其果决，而時措適宜。是固有立事之本矣。以卦德言之，巽之德爲巽，而兌之德爲說。內巽外說，則思慮深微，於理无不順；施為寬裕，於衆无不宜。是又有制事之用矣。如是，則利有往焉，以興天下之事功，道可常通，而窮極非所患也；宜有行焉，以修天下之政理，治可常保，而平陂非所憂也。尚何所往之有不亨哉？
然自大過之時而觀之，盈成之久，勢或有趨於偏者，不以剛中拯之，則識不早而力不易矣。盖天下難處之事也，是非有過人之才而能濟乎？泰寧之餘，釁或有萌於漸者，不以巽說治之，則弊未去而患已生矣。盖安危倚伏之機也，是又豈尋常之才所能與乎？故聖人嘆之曰：「大矣哉！」以見才不常逢，時所當戒，未可以細故視之也。
雖然，時之既盛，上下相安於无事，而忽心生焉。亦孰知才之為急，而求其人以圖之？夫
translation_en:
…what is meant by the words, “It is beneficial to have somewhere to go; success”? Considering the hexagram’s structure, although its four yang lines err on the side of excess, the second and fifth both occupy the central positions. Firmness that is excessive yet centered means that one does not rely on one’s cleverness, but carefully weighs and judges; one does not give free rein to one’s decisiveness, but acts appropriately for the time. This indeed provides the foundation for accomplishing affairs. Considering the hexagram’s attributes, Xun has the attribute of yielding, while Dui has that of joy. Yielding within and joyful without, one’s deliberations are profound and subtle, wholly in accord with principle; one’s actions are generous and unhurried, wholly suited to the people. This further provides the practical means of managing affairs. Thus it is beneficial to go forward and advance the undertakings and achievements of the realm: the Way can remain unobstructed, and exhaustion need cause no anxiety. It is fitting to act and improve the realm’s governance: good order can be maintained, and changes from level ground to slopes—from stability to decline—need cause no concern. Wherever one goes, how could there be anything but success?
Yet viewed in terms of the time of Great Excess, after fullness and accomplishment have long prevailed, circumstances may begin to incline toward imbalance. Unless one rescues the situation through firmness held to the center, recognition will come too late and effective exertion will be difficult [?]. These are affairs in the realm that are hard to manage. Could anyone remedy them without surpassing talent? In the aftermath of peace and tranquility, seeds of trouble may gradually emerge. Unless one addresses them through yielding and joy, new calamities will arise before existing abuses have been removed. This is the critical juncture at which security and danger depend upon and lie concealed within one another. How could ordinary talent be equal to it? Hence the sage exclaims, “Great indeed!” This shows that such talent is not often encountered and that the times call for vigilance: these matters cannot be regarded as trifles.
Nevertheless, once an age has attained prosperity, those above and below grow comfortable with the absence of trouble, and carelessness arises. Who then recognizes the urgent need for talent and seeks out the right people to address the situation? Now, …

translation_en:
…Talent is not always to be found; even when it exists, if the world does not employ it, it cannot accomplish the work of remedying the needs of the age. Affairs throughout the realm thus reach a point where some can no longer be attended to in time. Truly, it is difficult for the right times and the right people to coincide. Even sages such as Yao and Shun worried that they could not obtain suitable men: was this not the reason? Can those living in a time of Great Exceeding (Daguo) fail to consider this?
“Great Power (Dazhuang): perseverance is beneficial. What is great is correct.”
Zheng Zibi
Associate Examiner Wen, Director, comments: “Many have written on the two words ‘great’ and ‘correct,’ but this essay develops its argument from the hexagram itself. Its reasoning is clear and its language fluent. Its author, too, has a profound understanding of the Book of Changes.”
Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler, comments: “It depicts the bearing of the gentleman, standing firm and commanding respect.”
Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler, comments: “In the examination hall, most attempts to explain the two words ‘great’ and ‘correct’ are strained. This essay alone depicts the bearing of yang firmness, luminous and penetrating between Heaven and Earth. Without realizing it, one feels one's faintheartedness stirred into resolve.”
Associate Examiner Teng, Librarian of the Heir Apparent, comments: “Explanations of the passage on ‘great’ and ‘correct’ abound, but most are stale and tiresome. We record this precise and incisive essay to serve as a model for future students.”
Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “This is writing worthy of Great Power.”
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “It captures the purport.”

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
原陽盛之宜正以陽道之本正此彖傳之旨也
蓋陽道在天下未有不正者也然則大壯之所
以利貞非有取於此哉昔伏羲畫卦合震乾而
名之曰大壯文王既係以利貞之辭矣吾夫子
彖傳舉而釋之蓋謂陽剛盛長之候正陽道大
行之時然必利於貞者何哉誠以易之定分陽
為大而陰為小陰陽之理大者正而小者邪大
壯之卦二陰在外而漸消四陽在內而過盛初
陽也二亦陽也陽之性純不為陰柔之所雜則
===
凡拔茅而升者皆夬夬中行之君子隨之小子
不敢干其類也三陽也四亦陽也陽之質粹不
為柔邪之所牽則凡盍簪而聚者皆乾乾自强
之君子否之匪人不容厠其間也吾見同心多
而協力衆運之於云為者何莫非天德之流行
發乎邇而見乎遠成之於事功者何往非天德
之運用或體仁以長人或嘉會以合禮蕩蕩乎
平平以躋斯世於文明格天偉績信非瑣瑣者
之可得經營也或利物以和義或貞固以幹事

punctuated:
原陽盛之宜正，以陽道之本正，此彖傳之旨也。

蓋陽道在天下，未有不正者也。然則大壯之所以利貞，非有取於此哉？昔伏羲畫卦，合震乾而名之曰大壯，文王既係以利貞之辭矣。吾夫子彖傳舉而釋之，蓋謂陽剛盛長之候，正陽道大行之時。然必利於貞者，何哉？誠以易之定分，陽為大而陰為小；陰陽之理，大者正而小者邪。大壯之卦，二陰在外而漸消，四陽在內而過盛。初陽也，二亦陽也，陽之性純，不為陰柔之所雜，則凡拔茅而升者，皆夬夬中行之君子，隨之小子不敢干其類也。三陽也，四亦陽也，陽之質粹，不為柔邪之所牽，則凡盍簪而聚者，皆乾乾自强之君子，否之匪人不容厠其間也。吾見同心多而協力衆，運之於云為者，何莫非天德之流行？發乎邇而見乎遠，成之於事功者，何往非天德之運用？或體仁以長人，或嘉會以合禮，蕩蕩乎平平，以躋斯世於文明，格天偉績，信非瑣瑣者之可得經營也。或利物以和義，或貞固以幹事
translation_en:
To trace why flourishing yang ought to be correct to the inherent correctness of the way of yang: this is the purport of the Commentary on the Judgment.

Nowhere under Heaven is the way of yang other than correct. Is this not, then, the basis for the statement that in Great Strength, constancy is beneficial? Long ago, when Fuxi drew the hexagrams, he combined Zhen and Qian and named the resulting hexagram Great Strength. King Wen then appended the words, “Constancy is beneficial.” Our Master Confucius took up these words and explained them in the Commentary on the Judgment. His meaning was that the season when firm yang flourishes and grows is precisely the time when the way of yang prevails widely. Yet why must its benefit depend upon constancy? Truly, according to the fixed distinctions of the Book of Changes, yang is the great and yin the small; in the principles governing yin and yang, the great is correct and the small deviant. In the hexagram Great Strength, the two yin lines occupy the outer positions and gradually diminish, while the four yang lines occupy the inner positions and flourish beyond the midpoint.

The first line is yang, and the second is also yang. The nature of yang is pure, unmixed with yielding yin. Thus all those who rise together, like uprooted thatch whose roots are intertwined, are gentlemen who act resolutely and walk the central course; the “little boy” of Following dares not intrude among their kind. The third line is yang, and the fourth is also yang. The substance of yang is pure, undrawn by yielding perversity. Thus all those who gather together, like companions coming together at a summons, are gentlemen who tirelessly strengthen themselves; the “unworthy men” of Obstruction are not allowed to mingle among them.

I see many united in purpose and multitudes joining their strength. When they put this into words and deeds, what is not the flowing forth of Heaven’s virtue? It issues from what is near and becomes manifest afar: wherever it achieves practical accomplishments, what is not the operation of Heaven’s virtue? Some embody benevolence and thereby lead others; some bring excellence together and thereby accord with ritual propriety. Broad and impartial, they raise this age to cultured enlightenment. Their mighty achievements, reaching Heaven itself, are assuredly beyond the capacity of petty men to undertake. Some benefit things and thereby bring rightness into harmony; some remain constant and firm and thereby take charge of affairs …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
无反无側于以囿斯民於平康盖世竒功亦豈
戔戔者之所能樹立也大者之正如此以之處
壮則自无不利矣占之利貞其有取於此也夫
雖然正大之義豈特人事有之在天地亦有然
者盖无不覆載天地之大而專直翕闢之機未
嘗踰時此則正也人或狹隘自私始與天地有
不相似而往无所之矣况大壮之時而欲利乎
然則當何如必非禮勿履而後可
成性存存道義之門
===
汪佃

詳明非衆作可及

自有區别處合異析同脉絡不紊如此作者

translation_en:
…Without deviation or partiality, thereby bringing the people into peace and well-being: how could petty men establish extraordinary achievements that surpass their age? Such is the correctness of the great. With this, when occupying a position of strength, nothing will be disadvantageous. The divination statement, “Favorable to be correct and firm,” surely draws upon this! Yet does the meaning of correctness and greatness apply only to human affairs? It is also so in Heaven and Earth. Their greatness consists in leaving nothing uncovered or unsupported; yet the workings of their concentrated directness, closing, and opening never depart from the proper timing. This is their correctness. When people become narrow-minded and selfish, they cease to resemble Heaven and Earth and have nowhere to proceed. How much less could they expect advantage at a time of Great Strength? What, then, should they do? Only by refusing to tread where ritual propriety forbids can they succeed.

“Continually preserving one's fully developed nature: the gateway to the Way and righteousness.”

Wang Dian

Associate Examiner Wen, Director, comments: “Writing on human nature and principle is difficult to elucidate. This composition develops its argument from knowing ritual propriety; it is closely reasoned and penetrating. No one who had not devoted effort to this could have expressed it.”

Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler, comments: “The language and tenor are substantial and vigorous, while the principles are also explained fully and clearly. Ordinary compositions cannot match it.”

Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler, comments: “The Way, righteousness, and human nature are inseparable, yet they also have their distinctions. Bringing together what differs and analyzing what is shared, the argument keeps its threads in order. Writers like this are rarely found.”

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官洗馬滕批性及道義發揮了
了可嘉
考試官學士顧批易之精蘊此作盡之
考試官大學士靳批講得存存意出
一理具於心者不息萬理出於心者无窮夫性
具於心一理而已誠能存而不息則道義之出
寧有窮乎大傳論聖人崇德廣業之事如此今
夫成性者渾然至善无少虧欠天之所以與我
而我所具於心之理也人皆有之而存焉者寡
===
況能存存而不息耶惟聖人也知崇如天而極
其高明禮卑如地而極其篤實是以天之所賦
於我者造詣深而體驗至既已存矣而尤存而
不息盖其一心之中天理渾全瞬息動靜无一
時之間斷也我之所得於天者知之明而守之
固存亦至矣而又存而不已盖其一心之內天
命流行造次顛沛无一息之雜擾也理之具于
心者其存存如此則性之在我者不異於天矣
由是大本固而達道行全體立而妙用出率之

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Teng, Librarian, comments: “The exposition of human nature, the Way, and righteousness is lucid and commendable.”
Associate Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “This composition fully conveys the profound essence of the Book of Changes.”
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “It brings out the meaning of continually preserving.”
The one principle inherent in the mind never ceases; the myriad principles issuing from the mind are inexhaustible. Human nature, as inherent in the mind, is simply one principle. If one can truly preserve it without ceasing, how could there be any limit to the issuing forth of the Way and righteousness? Such is the Great Commentary’s account of how the sage exalts virtue and broadens his achievements. Now, one’s fully constituted nature is an undivided whole of utmost goodness, without the slightest deficiency. It is what Heaven bestows upon us, the principle inherent in our minds. Everyone possesses it, but few preserve it; how much less can they continually preserve it without ceasing? Only the sage can do so. His knowledge is exalted like Heaven, attaining the utmost loftiness and illumination; his ritual propriety is humble like Earth, attaining the utmost solidity and substance. Thus, concerning what Heaven has endowed in him, his attainment is profound and his experiential understanding complete. Having already preserved it, he preserves it still further, without ceasing. For within his single mind, Heaven’s principle is whole and complete: from moment to moment, in activity and stillness, there is never any interruption. What he has received from Heaven he understands clearly and holds firmly. His preservation of it has reached its utmost, yet he continues to preserve it without stopping. For within his single mind, Heaven’s mandate flows forth; even in haste or adversity, there is not a moment of admixture or disturbance. When the principle inherent in the mind is continually preserved in this way, the nature within oneself does not differ from Heaven. Thus the great foundation is secure and the universally applicable Way proceeds; the entire substance is established and its wondrous functioning emerges. Following it …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
於日用之間則无反无側而道斯名焉質之古
今而皆同也質之四海而皆合也雖曰千變萬
化孰非吾心一理之發越乎夫道出於心而无
窮是性為道之門矣形之於應酬之際則无過
不及而義斯名焉處常而不失其經也處變而
不失其權也雖曰殊途百慮孰非吾心一理之
裁制乎夫義出于心而各當是性為義之門矣
吁一理常存而眾理出正猶天地設位而變化
行也聖人崇德廣業至於如此此易之所以為
===
至也歟抑論之夫子之言性與天道於此盡矣
其曰德業曰知禮曰成性曰道義若紛然不一
矣然德得於心者也業見於事者也知所知也
禮所行也性為道義之體而道又義之體也其
實皆本之天地具于易書而備于聖人此易與
天地聖人所以常相為流通也噫非達天德者
其孰能辨之

於日用之間，則无反无側，而道斯名焉。質之古今而皆同也，質之四海而皆合也。雖曰千變萬化，孰非吾心一理之發越乎？夫道出於心而无窮，是性為道之門矣。形之於應酬之際，則无過不及，而義斯名焉。處常而不失其經也，處變而不失其權也。雖曰殊途百慮，孰非吾心一理之裁制乎？夫義出于心而各當，是性為義之門矣。吁！一理常存而眾理出，正猶天地設位而變化行也。聖人崇德廣業至於如此，此易之所以為至也歟！抑論之，夫子之言性與天道，於此盡矣。其曰德業，曰知禮，曰成性，曰道義，若紛然不一矣。然德，得於心者也；業，見於事者也；知，所知也；禮，所行也；性為道義之體，而道又義之體也。其實皆本之天地，具于易書，而備于聖人。此易與天地聖人所以常相為流通也。噫！非達天德者，其孰能辨之？

書
元首明哉！股肱良哉！庶事康哉！
translation_en:
…in daily life, there is neither deviation nor partiality, and this is called the Way. Tested against antiquity and the present, it is everywhere the same; tested throughout the four seas, it everywhere accords. Though its transformations number in the thousands and tens of thousands, which is not an unfolding of the single principle within my heart? The Way issues from the heart without limit: thus human nature is the gateway to the Way. Manifested in dealings with others, there is neither excess nor deficiency, and this is called righteousness. In ordinary circumstances, it does not depart from the constant norm; in changing circumstances, it does not fail in judicious adaptation. Though paths diverge and deliberations are manifold, which is not a determination made by the single principle within my heart? Righteousness issues from the heart and is fitting in each instance: thus human nature is the gateway to righteousness.

Ah! The single principle constantly abides, and the many principles issue forth, just as heaven and earth take their positions and transformations proceed. The sage exalts his virtue and broadens his undertakings to this extent: is this not why the Book of Changes is supreme? To discuss it further, the Master's teaching about human nature and the Way of Heaven is fully expressed here. His references to virtue and undertakings, knowledge and ritual propriety, the fulfillment of one's nature, and the Way and righteousness may seem numerous and disparate. Yet virtue is what is attained in the heart; undertakings are what become manifest in affairs; knowledge is what one knows; ritual propriety is what one practices. Human nature is the substance of the Way and righteousness, while the Way is also the substance of righteousness. In truth, all are rooted in heaven and earth, contained in the Book of Changes, and fully embodied in the sage. This is why the Book of Changes, heaven and earth, and the sage are continually in mutual communion. Alas! Who but one who comprehends Heaven's virtue could discern this?

Shen Hongdao

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Secretary: Refined, elegant, harmonious, and balanced, this conveys the atmosphere of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers of that age. The closing few phrases are sincere, generous, and deeply solicitous; their meaning exceeds what words can express. Ah! With someone like you, one may indeed discuss the proper relationship between ruler and minister.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Chief Supervising Secretary: The language resembles the tones of ceremonial music, with loyalty and affection lodged within it. Here we see once again the atmosphere of Shun’s court.

Comment by Associate Examiner Jin, Examining Editor: Gao Yao lodged his loyalty and affection in his answering song; this essay expresses it fully. Its conclusion brings out the principle that ruler and ministers form one body, something absent from the other papers. Include it in the record.

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler: To expound within the words of a song the intention of holding the ruler to demanding standards is difficult. This writer is surely skilled in portraying it.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Academician: The prose has a dignified ease and captures the meaning of the answering song at Shun’s court.

Comment by Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary: It succeeds in expressing Gao Yao’s intention.

The great minister sang in response, declaring that when the ruler is sagely, his ministers are worthy and government is well conducted. His expectations of the emperor were of the highest order. In singing his response on this basis, was the great minister not holding the emperor to the highest expectations? …he then continued the song, as if to say: The ruler occupies an exalted position and governs those below, just as the head stands above the ministers who are his limbs. If the one who serves as the head truly harbors spiritual understanding within, attending only to the overarching principles, and oversees all with penetrating wisdom, disdaining scrutiny of administrative details, then in initiating undertakings he will lead appropriately, without encroaching from above upon his officials’ duties. In assessing achievements, he will demote and promote with perfect fitness, so that those below cannot conceal the true circumstances. Like Heaven surveying the world, he leaves no quarter unillumined; like the sun shining upon the earth, he reaches every place below. How enlightened the head is!

Thus those who serve as the emperor’s legs and arms reverently receive his gracious commands and labor in his service morning and night. They purify their hearts and devote all their strength to assisting him in matters great and small. Of those who advance the emperor’s undertakings, who is not benevolent and worthy? They take ever greater delight in helping their ruler initiate affairs. Of those who perform Heaven’s work on its behalf, who is not talented and capable? They grow ever more tireless in assisting their ruler in assessing accomplishments. How excellent the limbs are!

Thus, in matters whose overall direction rests with the ruler and whose execution is charged to his ministers, every task is accomplished, and achievements already consolidated become still firmer. All affairs are fully set in motion, and accomplishments already extensive become still broader. Given guiding principles and orderly arrangements, they proceed without confusion, with no fear of neglect or decay. Possessing established institutions and rules, they display a splendid order, with no danger of collapse. How well ordered all affairs are!

From this we know that ministers do not become excellent of themselves: only through the ruler’s enlightenment do they become excellent. Affairs do not become well ordered of themselves: only through the ruler’s enlightenment do they become well ordered. In continuing the song in this way, Gao Yao subtly reveals, beyond the words of his singing and sighing, his hope that the emperor’s enlightenment will preserve good government. title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
曰股肱于以見明良一體休戚相關所以敕天
圖治者心不可以不同而亦不容于不同也帝
德之明卓冠千古亦于此乎見之有虞之治所
以不可及也後世此義不明上下不交而君臣
道隔甚至有以土芥犬馬視其臣者治不古若
又何怪哉
予弗克俾厥后惟堯舜其心愧恥若撻于
市一夫不獲則曰時予之辜佑我烈祖格
于皇天
===
