punctuated:
曰股肱，于以見明良一體，休戚相關，所以敕天圖治者，心不可以不同，而亦不容于不同也。帝德之明，卓冠千古，亦于此乎見之。有虞之治所以不可及也。後世此義不明，上下不交，而君臣道隔，甚至有以土芥犬馬視其臣者。治不古若，又何怪哉？
予弗克俾厥后惟堯舜，其心愧恥，若撻于市。一夫不獲，則曰：「時予之辜。」佑我烈祖，格于皇天。
同考試官主事王批：知伊尹之志，又知傅說之學，則其所志所學可知矣。
同考試官都給事中俞批：伊尹自任處，摹寫曲盡，殆嘗志其所志者歟？
同考試官檢討金批：道尹之志，而使高宗望說之意躍然，亦可謂善言者。
同考試官編修劉批：古人立志建功，鋪叙明盡；且自任處，語意諄切，殆若尹自言者。
translation_en:
…calls them “thighs and arms.” This shows that the enlightened ruler and his worthy ministers form one body, sharing prosperity and adversity. In reverently heeding Heaven and seeking good government, their hearts must be united; indeed, they cannot be otherwise. The brilliance of the emperor’s virtue, surpassing all ages, is also evident here. This is why the government of Youyu [Shun] could not be equaled. In later ages this principle was not understood: those above and below ceased to communicate, and ruler and ministers became estranged. Some rulers even regarded their ministers as dirt and weeds, dogs and horses. What wonder, then, that their government fell short of antiquity?
“If I cannot make my sovereign a Yao or a Shun”—his heart felt shame and disgrace, as though he were being flogged in the marketplace. If even one man failed to find his proper place, he would say, “This is my fault.” He aided our illustrious ancestor, whose virtue reached August Heaven.
Associate Examiner Wang, a Secretary, comments: He understands Yi Yin’s aspirations and also Fu Yue’s learning; from this we can discern his own aspirations and learning.
Associate Examiner Yu, a Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: His portrayal of Yi Yin’s assumption of responsibility captures every nuance. Might he himself have aspired to what Yi Yin aspired to?
Associate Examiner Jin, an Examining Editor, comments: In describing Yi Yin’s aspirations, he also brings vividly to life what Gaozong hoped for from Fu Yue. He may indeed be called skilled in expression.
Associate Examiner Liu, a Compiler, comments: He sets out clearly and fully how the men of antiquity established their aspirations and accomplished great deeds. Moreover, in the passage on assuming responsibility, his language and meaning are earnest and deeply felt, almost as though Yi Yin himself were speaking.

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
考試官學士顧批文字平正可錄
考試官大學士靳批詞簡意足
賢王於先臣述其自任之重著其相業之隆夫
伊尹以天下為已任可謂重矣則其輔君格天
之功豈偶然哉宜高宗述之以告傅說也謂夫
輔君作聖此我之所望於爾也我先正盖有行
之者矣曷不以伊尹觀之乎其言有曰致吾君
為堯舜我之素志也今既居其職矣乃或君德
雖成而擬諸堯焉尚有歉於大哉之聖君道雖
===
立而擬諸舜焉尚有忝於君哉之稱則不惟負
吾之志而於吾職亦奚稱耶內省於心愧耻之
甚始若撻之於市焉盖君不堯舜不已也陶吾
民於唐虞我之素志也今已當其任矣而或四
海雖安猶有一夫之失所萬民雖化猶有一夫
之弗若是不惟非吾所志而於吾任不有負乎
靜言思之誰執其咎實我尹躬之辜焉盖民不
唐虞不已也夫伊尹自任之重如此故能輔我
烈祖懋昭大德于以盡燮猷之責克布昭聖武于

伊尹以天下為己任可謂重矣則其輔君格天

輔君作聖此我之所望於爾也我先正蓋有行
之者矣曷不以伊尹觀之乎其言有曰致吾君
為堯舜我之素志也今既居其職矣乃或君德
雖成而擬諸堯焉尚有歉於大哉之聖君道雖
===
立而擬諸舜焉尚有忝於君哉之稱則不惟負
吾之志而於吾職亦奚稱耶內省於心愧恥之
甚始若撻之於市焉蓋君不堯舜不已也陶吾
民於唐虞我之素志也今已當其任矣而或四
海雖安猶有一夫之失所萬民雖化猶有一夫
之弗若是不惟非吾所志而於吾任不有負乎
靜言思之誰執其咎實我尹躬之辜焉蓋民不
唐虞不已也夫伊尹自任之重如此故能輔我
烈祖懋昭大德于以盡綏猷之責布昭聖武于
punctuated:
考試官學士顧批：文字平正，可錄。
考試官大學士靳批：詞簡意足。
賢王於先臣，述其自任之重，著其相業之隆。夫伊尹以天下為已任，可謂重矣，則其輔君格天之功，豈偶然哉？宜高宗述之以告傅說也。謂夫輔君作聖，此我之所望於爾也。我先正盖有行之者矣，曷不以伊尹觀之乎？其言有曰：「致吾君為堯舜，我之素志也。今既居其職矣，乃或君德雖成，而擬諸堯焉，尚有歉於大哉之聖；君道雖立，而擬諸舜焉，尚有忝於君哉之稱，則不惟負吾之志，而於吾職亦奚稱耶？內省於心，愧耻之甚，始若撻之於市焉。盖君不堯舜不已也。陶吾民於唐虞，我之素志也。今已當其任矣，而或四海雖安，猶有一夫之失所；萬民雖化，猶有一夫之弗若，是不惟非吾所志，而於吾任不有負乎？靜言思之，誰執其咎？實我尹躬之辜焉。盖民不唐虞不已也。」夫伊尹自任之重如此，故能輔我烈祖，懋昭大德，于以盡燮猷之責，克布昭聖武，于
translation_en:
Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “The writing is balanced and correct, worthy of inclusion.”
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “Concise in wording and complete in meaning.”
The worthy king recounted the weighty responsibility his predecessor’s minister had taken upon himself and made manifest the greatness of his achievements as chief minister. Yi Yin took responsibility for all under Heaven upon himself—a weighty burden indeed. Could his achievement in assisting his ruler and reaching Heaven have been accidental? It was fitting that Gaozong should recount this to Fu Yue. His meaning was: Helping the ruler become a sage is what I expect of you. Among my former upright ministers there was indeed one who accomplished this. Why not consider Yi Yin?
He said: “To make my ruler a Yao or a Shun has always been my aspiration. Now that I occupy this office, suppose that, although my ruler’s virtue is established, when compared with Yao he still falls short of the sageliness praised as ‘How great!’; or that, although his way as ruler is established, when compared with Shun he remains unworthy of the acclaim ‘What a ruler!’ Then I would not merely have betrayed my aspiration: how could I be equal to my office? Examining my heart, I would feel such profound shame that it would be as though I were being flogged in the marketplace. Thus I will not rest until my ruler becomes a Yao or a Shun.
“To mould my people into the people of Tang and Yu has always been my aspiration. Now that I have undertaken this responsibility, suppose that, although the Four Seas are at peace, even one person still lacks a secure place; or that, although the myriad people have been transformed, even one person still fails to follow what is right. This would not merely fall short of my aspiration: would I not also have failed my charge? Reflecting quietly upon this, who should bear the blame? The fault would truly belong to me, Yin, personally. Thus I will not rest until the people become like those of Tang and Yu.”
Such was the weight of the responsibility Yi Yin took upon himself. Hence he was able to assist our illustrious ancestor, diligently making his great virtue manifest and thereby fulfilling his responsibility to harmonize the counsels of government; he was able to spread abroad his sage martial prowess, thereby …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
以建輯寧之功積累之乆其至純之治充塞無
間始與皇天之覆幬同一揆矣充積之盛其至
大之化磅礴無疆始與皇天之廣大無二致矣
盖至於是則君為堯舜之君民為唐虞之民其
志乃遂而其言克踐相業之隆所以不可尚歟
高宗以是告傅說其期望之意至矣抑觀傅說
之為相也爰立之後從諫則聖之對憲天聰明
之說皆輔君作聖之事也其後高宗中興卒為
有商之令主而說之功業亦無讓於尹焉是亦
===
君臣遭遇之盛也然說何以能若此哉觀其言
曰惟學遜志務時敏厥脩乃來萬世之言學者
實自茲始此又輔君作聖者之本也後之願學
伊傅者尚於此求之
身其康彊子孫其逢吉
同考試官主事王 批 九疇本一理貫通
大同之福非建極之君不能致也此作得之
同考試官都給事中俞 批 大同獲福理

蓋至於是則君爲堯舜之君民爲唐虞之民其

之爲相也爰立之後從諫則聖之對憲天聰明
之說皆輔君作聖之事也其後高宗中興卒爲
有商之令主而說之功業亦無讓於尹焉是亦

曰惟學遜志務時敏厥脩乃來萬世之言學者
實自茲始此又輔君作聖者之本也後之願學
伊傅者尚於此求之
===
身其康彊子孫其逢吉
同考試官主事王　批　九疇本一理貫通
同考試官都給事中俞　批　大同獲福理
〔大同之福非建極之君不能致也此作得之〕
punctuated:
以建輯寧之功。積累之乆，其至純之治充塞無間，始與皇天之覆幬同一揆矣；充積之盛，其至大之化磅礴無疆，始與皇天之廣大無二致矣。盖至於是，則君為堯舜之君，民為唐虞之民，其志乃遂，而其言克踐，相業之隆所以不可尚歟！高宗以是告傅說，其期望之意至矣。抑觀傅說之為相也，爰立之後，「從諫則聖」之對、「憲天聰明」之說，皆輔君作聖之事也。其後高宗中興，卒為有商之令主，而說之功業亦無讓於尹焉，是亦君臣遭遇之盛也。然說何以能若此哉？觀其言曰：「惟學遜志，務時敏，厥脩乃來。」萬世之言學者，實自茲始。此又輔君作聖者之本也。後之願學伊傅者，尚於此求之。
身其康彊，子孫其逢吉。
同考試官主事王批：九疇本一理貫通，大同之福，非建極之君不能致也。此作得之。
同考試官都給事中俞批：大同獲福，理
translation_en:
…thereby achieving the work of bringing concord and peace. Through long accumulation, his utterly pure governance permeated everything without a gap, finally becoming one in principle with August Heaven’s sheltering canopy. Through the fullness of this accumulation, his supremely great transforming influence spread boundlessly, finally becoming indistinguishable from August Heaven’s vastness. At this point, the ruler became a ruler like Yao and Shun, and the people became a people like those of Tang and Yu. His aspirations were thus fulfilled and his words put into practice. Was this not why his achievements as minister could not be surpassed? In telling Fu Yue this, Gaozong expressed the utmost expectations of him.
Consider, moreover, Fu Yue’s service as minister. After his appointment, his reply that “Following remonstrance makes one a sage” and his counsel to “Model your hearing and sight on Heaven” were both means of helping his ruler become a sage. Later, Gaozong brought about a restoration and ultimately became an excellent ruler of the Shang, while Yue’s achievements were in no way inferior to those of Yi Yin. This, too, was a splendid meeting of ruler and minister. Yet how could Yue accomplish this? Consider his words: “In learning, make your will humble and strive to be diligent at every moment; then your cultivation will advance.” Discourse on learning for all subsequent ages truly began here. This, moreover, is the foundation for helping a ruler become a sage. May those in later times who wish to emulate Yi Yin and Fu Yue seek it here.
“His person will be healthy and strong; his descendants will meet with good fortune.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Secretary: The Nine Categories are fundamentally connected by a single principle. The blessings of great concord can be brought about only by a ruler who establishes the supreme standard. This composition grasps that point.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yu, Chief Supervising Secretary: Obtaining blessings through great concord—the principle…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
正如此而詞又足以發之是可録也
同考試官撿討金批稽疑大同獲吉處
作者冗雜可厭醞藉整潔無踰此篇
同考試官編修劉批文字平正末復歸
重皇極所見良是録之
考試官學士顧批篇末歸重在建極良是
考試官大學士靳批箕疇之義似是如此
膺莫大之福垂無疆之慶此稽疑大同之所致
也盖福係於天不可以倖致尚矣然則膺大福
===
而垂之無疆稽疑之所得豈無自哉昔箕子演
疇以告武王及此意謂人君有疑必稽之人神
而後决誠使謀焉而大同則夫定天下之業而
享其福當何如耶近而吾身莫難於康疆也夫
惟稽疑而動無不吉吾知無憂於心自然無累
於身怡神於萬幾就叙之時樂天於百志惟熙
之日以承大祀則對越之餘何者非純嘏之錫
以行天討則戡定之暇何者非嘉靖之休高拱
穆清壽富康寧之益增也端居大寶威福玉食

punctuated:
正如此，而詞又足以發之，是可録也。
同考試官撿討金批：稽疑大同獲吉處，作者冗雜可厭，醞藉整潔，無踰此篇。
同考試官編修劉批：文字平正，末復歸重皇極，所見良是，録之。
考試官學士顧批：篇末歸重在建極，良是。
考試官大學士靳批：箕疇之義，似是如此。
膺莫大之福，垂無疆之慶，此稽疑大同之所致也。盖福係於天，不可以倖致，尚矣。然則膺大福而垂之無疆，稽疑之所得，豈無自哉？昔箕子演疇以告武王，及此，意謂人君有疑，必稽之人神而後决。誠使謀焉而大同，則夫定天下之業而享其福，當何如耶？近而吾身，莫難於康疆也。夫惟稽疑而動無不吉，吾知無憂於心，自然無累於身。怡神於萬幾就叙之時，樂天於百志惟熙之日。以承大祀，則對越之餘，何者非純嘏之錫？以行天討，則戡定之暇，何者非嘉靖之休？高拱穆清，壽富康寧之益增也；端居大寶，威福玉食
translation_en:
…the principle is precisely so, and the wording also suffices to bring it out. This deserves inclusion.
Associate Examiner Jin, Hanlin Compiler, comments: On the passage concerning the resolution of doubts, complete agreement, and the attainment of good fortune, writers are tiresomely prolix and confused. For restrained richness and orderly clarity, none surpasses this essay.
Associate Examiner Liu, Hanlin Editor, comments: The writing is balanced and sound. At the end it returns to emphasizing the August Ultimate. This understanding is indeed correct. Include it.
Examiner Gu, Hanlin Academician, comments: The essay’s conclusion places its emphasis on establishing the Ultimate. This is indeed correct.
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: The meaning of Jizi’s categories seems to be just this.
To receive the greatest blessings and transmit boundless felicity: this is what resolving doubts and attaining complete agreement bring about. That blessings depend upon Heaven and cannot be obtained by mere luck has long been understood. Yet if one receives great blessings and transmits them without limit, can these gains from resolving doubts be without a source? Long ago, Jizi expounded the categories to instruct King Wu. On reaching this point, his meaning was that, whenever a ruler has doubts, he must consult both men and spirits before deciding. If his deliberations truly achieve complete agreement, what must it be like to establish dominion over all under Heaven and enjoy its blessings?
Close at hand, for one’s own person, nothing is harder to secure than health and strength. Only when doubts are resolved and every action proves auspicious can I know that, with no anxiety in the heart, the body will naturally be free of burdens. The spirit is content when the myriad affairs of government fall into order; one rejoices in Heaven when the hundred purposes all prosper. When conducting the great sacrifices, after reverently attending upon the spirits, what is not a gift of abundant blessing? When carrying out Heaven’s punishments, in the respite after pacification, what is not the bounty of excellent and tranquil rule? Sitting with hands folded in solemn purity, one enjoys ever greater longevity, wealth, health, and peace. Dwelling composedly upon the imperial throne, wielding punishment and reward and enjoying precious food…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
之無替也身其有不康彊者乎遠而子孫尤難
於逢吉也夫惟稽疑而往無不利吾知考祥于
前自可垂裕於後襲鴻圖者得以享崇高于大
有承燕翼者得以介繁祉于無窮或祀典之脩
歟則受釐神明猶眷命之景福或戎事之舉歟
則肅清海宇猶神武之餘威繼身而子迪吉如
一日也繼子而孫迓衡如一世也子孫有不逢
吉者乎稽疑大同之所致如此欲建極者其可
輕忽也哉抑論稽疑固九疇之一事而大同獲
===
福則非建極之聖人莫之能與也蓋天人一道
聖人之猷為無一不本於人情而出於至理其
默契天心也久矣是以一卜筮之間不惟人弗
能違而天亦不能違之所謂建諸天地而不悖
質諸鬼神而無疑者豈徒取必於扐揲鑽灼之
間哉後世無聖人之心而惟聽於神以求所謂
吉不亦謬乎

之無替也。身其有不康彊者乎？遠而子孫，尤難於逢吉也。夫惟稽疑而往無不利，吾知考祥于前，自可垂裕於後。襲鴻圖者，得以享崇高于大有；承燕翼者，得以介繁祉于無窮。或祀典之脩歟，則受釐神明，猶眷命之景福；或戎事之舉歟，則肅清海宇，猶神武之餘威。繼身而子，迪吉如一日也；繼子而孫，迓衡如一世也。子孫有不逢吉者乎？稽疑大同之所致如此，欲建極者，其可輕忽也哉？抑論稽疑，固九疇之一事，而大同獲福，則非建極之聖人莫之能與也。蓋天人一道，聖人之猷為，無一不本於人情而出於至理，其默契天心也久矣。是以一卜筮之間，不惟人弗能違，而天亦不能違之。所謂建諸天地而不悖，質諸鬼神而無疑者，豈徒取必於扐揲鑽灼之間哉？後世無聖人之心，而惟聽於神以求所謂吉，不亦謬乎？

詩

彤弓弨兮，受言藏之。我有嘉賓，中心貺之，
translation_en:
…will remain undiminished. How could the ruler himself fail to enjoy health and strength? Looking farther ahead to his descendants, securing good fortune is especially difficult. Yet if he resolves doubts through consultation and finds advantage in every undertaking, I know that by examining auspicious signs beforehand he can leave abundant blessings to those who follow. Those who inherit his grand enterprise will enjoy exalted standing amid great abundance; those who receive his provisions for posterity will obtain manifold blessings without end. When they maintain the sacrificial observances, the blessings they receive from the spirits will still be the great felicity of Heaven’s favor and mandate. When they undertake military action and bring peace throughout the realm, this will still be the lingering authority of his divine martial prowess. Sons succeeding him will follow the path of good fortune as though it were still the same day; grandsons succeeding those sons will welcome peace as though it were still the same age. How could his descendants fail to encounter good fortune? Such are the results of resolving doubts and achieving complete agreement. Can anyone wishing to establish the supreme standard treat this lightly?

Now, resolving doubts is indeed one matter among the Nine Categories, but attaining blessings through complete agreement is something in which only the sage who establishes the supreme standard can participate. Heaven and humanity share a single Way. Every plan and action of the sage is grounded in human feelings and proceeds from ultimate principle; he has long been in tacit accord with Heaven’s mind. Thus, when divination is performed with tortoise shells or milfoil stalks, not only can human beings not go against him, but Heaven itself cannot go against him either. This is what is meant by establishing something before Heaven and Earth without contradiction, and submitting it to the spirits without doubt. Could it merely mean seeking certainty through sorting and counting stalks or drilling and scorching shells? Those of later ages lack the sage’s mind yet listen only to the spirits in pursuit of what they call good fortune. Is this not mistaken?

Book of Odes

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
天子燕有功諸侯而錫以弓矢之樂歌蓋於其
勸飲侑食之時而道達主人之意以為是弨然
之彤弓本弓人之所獻我其受之不敢以輕視
也必櫜而藏諸王府焉受而藏之不敢以他用
也將待夫有功而行賞焉慎重之心固已非一
日之積矣今我嘉賓敵王所愾而獻其戎功蓋
封疆之屏翰也念茲戎功而賞以大物實有國
之彝典也則彤弓之貺不由我之中心乎夫藏
之如此其重與之如此其誠則舉而頒之禮烏
===
可以弗稱耶於是焉夙戒夫矇瞍之官而鐘鼓
為之既設晨集於治朝之下而饗禮為之遂行
考我鐘焉酌大斗以相酬所以將之者此彤弓
也而報燕之禮大明於一日之間矣曾何有於
遲留乎伐我鼓焉進大烹以致養所以侑之者
此彤弓也而征伐之權盡畀於一朝之頃矣又
何有於顧惜乎吁周王之賞功可謂曲盡其道
矣大抵賞罰朝廷之大柄人主所以鼓舞一世
也有功不賞固不可以為治賞不以功則人將

天子燕有功諸侯而錫以弓矢之樂歌，蓋於其勸飲侑食之時，而道達主人之意，以為是弨然之彤弓，本弓人之所獻，我其受之，不敢以輕視也，必櫜而藏諸王府焉；受而藏之，不敢以他用也，將待夫有功而行賞焉。慎重之心，固已非一日之積矣。今我嘉賓，敵王所愾而獻其戎功，蓋封疆之屏翰也。念茲戎功而賞以大物，實有國之彝典也，則彤弓之貺，不由我之中心乎？夫藏之如此其重，與之如此其誠，則舉而頒之，禮烏可以弗稱耶？於是焉，夙戒夫矇瞍之官，而鐘鼓為之既設；晨集於治朝之下，而饗禮為之遂行。考我鐘焉，酌大斗以相酬，所以將之者，此彤弓也，而報燕之禮，大明於一日之間矣，曾何有於遲留乎？伐我鼓焉，進大烹以致養，所以侑之者，此彤弓也，而征伐之權，盡畀於一朝之頃矣，又何有於顧惜乎？吁！周王之賞功，可謂曲盡其道矣。
大抵賞罰，朝廷之大柄，人主所以鼓舞一世也。有功不賞，固不可以為治；賞不以功，則人將
translation_en:
…the ceremonial song for the Son of Heaven’s feasting of meritorious feudal lords and bestowal upon them of bows and arrows. As the guests were urged to drink and eat, it conveyed the host’s intentions: “This unstrung red bow was originally presented by the bow maker. When I received it, I dared not treat it lightly, but had it put in a case and stored in the royal treasury. Having received and stored it, I dared not put it to any other use, but kept it until there should be merit to reward. This careful regard has surely been cultivated over more than a single day. Now my honored guest has fought those against whom the king is angered and presented his military achievements: he is indeed a bulwark of our frontiers. To recognize these military achievements by awarding a great treasure is an established rule of the state. Does the gift of the red bow, then, not issue from my inmost heart?” Since it was stored with such care and given with such sincerity, how could the ritual of its presentation fail to match them? Accordingly, the blind musicians were instructed beforehand, and bells and drums were set out. The company assembled in the morning at the court for government business, and the ceremonial feast proceeded. “Strike my bells!” Wine was poured into great drinking vessels for the exchange of toasts, and this red bow accompanied the hospitality. Thus the ritual of feasting to requite service was fully displayed within a single day. What delay could there be? “Beat my drums!” A sumptuous meal was served to nourish the guest, and this red bow accompanied the offering. Thus authority to undertake punitive campaigns was fully conferred within a single morning. What reluctance to part with it could there be? Ah! In rewarding merit, the king of Zhou may be said to have fulfilled the proper way in every detail.
In general, rewards and punishments are the court’s great instruments of authority, by which the ruler spurs the people of his age to action. If merit goes unrewarded, good government is certainly impossible; if rewards are not based on merit, then people will…

…regard it lightly, and it will likewise be insufficient to encourage them. The regional lords of Zhou rendered meritorious service against the peoples of the four quarters, and the Son of Heaven bestowed vermilion bows upon them. This is why the Sage included this poem in his compilation, making it part of a classic for all ages. What, then, of those who regarded the contents of the state treasuries as their own private property and bestowed weapons upon court favorites? Alas! This is why later ages were ill governed.

“Majestic was King Wen; ah, unceasingly radiant, he abode in reverence.”

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
考試官大學士靳批善體貼
詩人指言聖德之實而深致其咏嘆之詞焉夫
聖人之德盛矣而實不外乎一敬也詩人之咏
歌可謂言有盡而意無窮者歟昔周公述文王
之德以戒成王上章極言其神明之昭著聲聞
之不已矣此乃指其實焉而先為咏歌之詞以
為穆穆乎我文王也德全天賦而聲色為之不
形其深則如淵焉蘊奧不可得而窺也理本生
知而聰明為之不作其遠則如天焉限量不可
===
得而窮也雖欲言之將何以為言哉於是又從
而嗟嘆之以為我文王之德誠難以形容約而
言之亦惟其能敬而已彼嚴於顯而肆於獨居
非所以為敬也文王則大廷敬焉深宮敬焉而
嚴肅之意常存緝而續之引其緒於無窮殆如
元氣之運乎四時也而何有於間乎謹於大而
忽於細微非所以為敬也文王則大事敬焉小
事敬焉而謹畏之心如一熈而明之極其光於
有融殆如日月之行乎兩間也而何有於息乎

之德以戒成王上章極言其神明之昭著聲聞
之不已矣此乃揩其實焉而先爲咏歌之詞以
爲穆穆乎我文王也德全天賦而聲色爲之不
形其深則如淵焉蘊奥不可得而窺也理本生
知而聰明爲之不作其遠則如天焉限量不可
===
得而窮也雖欲言之將何以爲言哉於是又從
而嗟嘆之以爲我文王之德誠難以形容約而
言之亦惟其能敬而已彼嚴於顯而肆於獨居
非所以爲敬也文王則大廷敬焉深宮敬焉而
嚴肅之意常存緝而續之引其緒於無窮殆如
元氣之運乎四時也而何有於間乎謹於大而
忽於細微非所以爲敬也文王則大事敬焉小
事敬焉而謹畏之心如一熙而明之極其光於
有融殆如日月之行乎兩間也而何有於息乎
punctuated:
考試官大學士靳批：善體貼。

詩人指言聖德之實，而深致其咏嘆之詞焉。夫聖人之德盛矣，而實不外乎一敬也。詩人之咏歌，可謂言有盡而意無窮者歟！昔周公述文王之德以戒成王，上章極言其神明之昭著、聲聞之不已矣。此乃指其實焉，而先為咏歌之詞，以為穆穆乎我文王也！德全天賦，而聲色為之不形，其深則如淵焉，蘊奧不可得而窺也；理本生知，而聰明為之不作，其遠則如天焉，限量不可得而窮也。雖欲言之，將何以為言哉？於是又從而嗟嘆之，以為我文王之德誠難以形容，約而言之，亦惟其能敬而已。彼嚴於顯而肆於獨居，非所以為敬也。文王則大廷敬焉，深宮敬焉，而嚴肅之意常存，緝而續之，引其緒於無窮，殆如元氣之運乎四時也，而何有於間乎？謹於大而忽於細微，非所以為敬也。文王則大事敬焉，小事敬焉，而謹畏之心如一，熈而明之，極其光於有融，殆如日月之行乎兩間也，而何有於息乎？
translation_en:
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: An excellent, sympathetic grasp of the meaning.

The poet points directly to the substance of sagely virtue and gives profound expression to his praise and admiration. The sage’s virtue is indeed abundant, yet in substance it amounts to nothing beyond reverent attentiveness. May we not say that the poet’s song has an end in words but no end in meaning? Long ago, the Duke of Zhou recounted King Wen’s virtue to admonish King Cheng. The preceding stanza spoke fully of the manifest radiance of his spiritual intelligence and the unceasing spread of his renown. Here the poet points to their substance, first singing in praise: “How solemn and majestic is our King Wen!” His virtue fulfilled his Heaven-endowed nature, without outward display in voice or countenance. Its depth was like an abyss whose hidden mysteries could not be fathomed. His knowledge of principle was innate, and he made no display of his intelligence. Its reach was like Heaven, whose bounds could not be exhausted. Even if one wished to speak of it, what words could one use?

The poet therefore goes on to sigh in admiration, saying that our King Wen’s virtue is truly difficult to describe. Put briefly, it consists simply in his capacity for reverent attentiveness. To be strict when in public but unrestrained when alone is not reverent attentiveness. King Wen was reverently attentive in the great court and in the palace’s secluded chambers alike; his solemn disposition was always present. Sustaining and continuing it, he extended its thread without end, much as primordial vital energy moves through the four seasons. How could there be any interruption? To be careful in great matters but neglect minute details is not reverent attentiveness. King Wen was reverently attentive in great affairs and small affairs alike; his cautious, watchful heart remained constant. Making this attentiveness bright and manifest, he brought its light to full radiance, much as the sun and moon travel between Heaven and Earth. How could there be any cessation?

Such was King Wen’s reverence: continually sustained and made luminous, without cease. Was this not why his virtue flourished and Heaven’s Mandate came to rest upon him? The Duke of Zhou’s admonition to King Cheng on this basis may be called concise yet comprehensive. Ah! Ruling all under Heaven is a great undertaking; decline and rise are matters of great consequence. From King Wen’s receipt of the Mandate, Zhou endured for eight hundred years before giving way to Qin. The length of its rule was unparalleled in ancient or later times. Yet if we trace the source of this achievement, it was reverence alone. Earlier Confucian scholars said that the Duke of Zhou, in teaching the king how to cultivate his virtue and take King Wen as his model, had no need to seek elsewhere. In my humble view, however, how could this apply only to King Cheng? It is surely a mirror and standard for rulers of every age.
“He brought peace to the myriad states, with abundant harvests time and again. Heaven’s Mandate did not slacken. Majestic King Wu held possession of his lands [?], thereby bringing the four quarters into submission. He firmly established his royal house. Oh, how illustrious before Heaven!”
Tian Xiu

…He makes clear how King Wu served Heaven, dispelling [?] the many doubts. His concluding invocation of Qin and Sui is particularly insightful.
Associate Examiner Cui, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: This essay develops its argument from the greatness of the sage’s achievements and virtue. Upright, profound, and comprehensive, it flows expansively [?] and is worthy of recitation.

In bringing peace to the people, the sage has the means to win Heaven’s favor; in preserving good order, the sage has the means to serve Heaven. All the sage’s actions accord with Heaven. King Wu eliminated tyranny to bring peace to the people and employed the worthy to preserve good order. How could any of this fail to accord with Heaven? The ode “Martial” (Huan) was composed to portray King Wu’s achievements. Its meaning is this: in the last days of Shang, the calamities and disorders afflicting the people had reached their utmost, and the crimes of the solitary tyrant had filled their measure. Thus all hearts cried out together, and our martial might was displayed. At the first assembly at Mengjin, he brought peace to their men and women, and households rejoiced with one another. When he next arrayed his forces at Muye and seized that cruel oppressor, the myriad states attained tranquility. He raised loyal and worthy men from captivity to prominence, and all under Heaven gave him their allegiance. He distributed lavish gifts throughout the four seas, and the people of every surname submitted with joy. Previously, the Zhou homeland at Qi had suffered famine; now yin and yang were in harmony, wind and rain came in season, and abundant harvests responded. Nor was this response of abundant harvests confined to a single season. Thereafter, the granaries of every household were full, and wives and children were at peace: these blessings appeared repeatedly without end. An impulse here elicited a response there. In bringing peace to the people, did King Wu not thereby win Heaven’s favor? Yet Heaven’s dealings with Zhou were not limited to commanding it to attack Shang. 命用休者矣非徒應之以豐年也佑命之純有
申錫無疆者矣夫是以丕圖肇啓而神武之德
不怠而愈强多士恊心而四方之任咸有所付
屬列爵則惟五也分土則惟三也使以其所以
綏士女者而又寧我邦家明德之光昭乎其上
達焉建官則惟賢也位事則惟能也使以其所
以取兇殘者而奠安我京室至治之馨居然而

translation_en:
…renewing its charge with blessings. Nor did Heaven merely respond with abundant harvests: in the fullness of its protecting mandate, it repeatedly bestowed boundless blessings. Thus the great undertaking was inaugurated, and King Wu’s divinely martial virtue, never flagging, grew ever stronger. The many worthy men were united in purpose, and responsibilities throughout the realm were all entrusted to suitable hands. There were five ranks of nobility and three grades of territorial allotment. Those entrusted with them were to use the means by which they had brought peace to men and women to secure our states and households as well; the radiance of their illustrious virtue shone upward to Heaven. In establishing offices, only the worthy were chosen; in assigning duties, only the capable. They were to use the means by which they had overcome the cruel and violent to establish peace in our capital and royal house; the fragrance of consummate government rose manifestly to Heaven. What Heaven initiated, King Wu brought to completion. Was not his preservation of good government the means by which he served Heaven?

Now commentators identify this poem as the sixth chapter of the Great Martial Dance (Dawu), composed by the Duke of Zhou. The Duke of Zhou composed the Great Martial Dance to represent King Wu’s achievements. Yet he did not lavishly set forth the might of his killing and campaigning, but recounted only his preservation of good government and his bringing peace to the people, seemingly failing to live up to the work’s title. Why was this? The answer is: this is what the sages meant by martial prowess. To make killing and campaigning a display of might, treating the people as mere grass and straw and employing them accordingly—as happened in the final years of Qin and Sui—is what later ages meant by martial prowess. Alas! The term is the same, yet its meaning differs between antiquity and later times. This is something those choosing their methods of government ought to understand.

Spring and Autumn Annals
“Jizi returned.” First year of Duke Min.
Ouyang Chujin.

於任親如此。此義行，則用羇用親，誰復有内外之偏哉？此外至也，而曰「来歸」，喜之也。盖友之歸有足喜者：國勢可憂，而恃以無恐；衆望益切，而惠然肯来。干旌之覿，緇衣之宜，盖於是為快焉。孰不為之喜乎？衆以為喜，此《春秋》亦喜之也。然友固奔也，其越在他國，而禍難之不能支，顛沛之不能免，雖曰蒙耻自昔，斯亦君子之不幸爾，烏可以是累其德乎？經故沒其出奔，而為之諱耻如此。此義明，則納汚與善，誰能無忠厚之情哉？由是觀之，一筆削之間，而尊賢親親之道昭，羣情掩細故之意靡不畢見，謂非聖人能修之乎？夷攷友之在魯，戮姦以靖國，決策以定君，魯祀幾絕而復續，皆其力也。惜乎貪於受費，以啓强都之僭；安於賜氏，而成世卿之專。則靖魯者友也，而亂魯者誰歟？君子責備賢者，於友不能無憾焉。

…from appointment on grounds of kinship, in this manner. If this principle were practiced, then, whether employing outsiders or relatives, who would still show partiality toward those within or outside the family? At this arrival from abroad [?], the text says “came back,” expressing joy at his return. Indeed, You’s return gave sufficient cause for joy: the state’s situation was alarming, but with him to rely upon there was no fear; everyone’s expectations grew more urgent, and he graciously agreed to come. The sight of the banners summoning worthy men, and the fitting provision of black robes for a minister, now brought satisfaction. Who would not rejoice at this? Everyone regarded it as a cause for joy, and the Spring and Autumn Annals likewise rejoices in it.
Yet You had indeed fled. He had gone abroad to another state because he could not withstand the calamity or escape displacement. Though he had borne this disgrace from that time, it was merely the misfortune of a gentleman. How could it be allowed to tarnish his virtue? Thus the Classic omits his flight abroad and conceals his disgrace in this manner. If this principle were understood, then, in tolerating faults and approving goodness, who could fail to feel loyalty and generosity? Viewed thus, through what is recorded or omitted, the Way of honoring the worthy and cherishing one’s kin becomes manifest; the intention concerning common sentiments [?] and overlooking minor faults is fully revealed. Could one say that anyone other than a sage could have compiled it?
Examining impartially You’s conduct in Lu, he executed the treacherous to pacify the state and settled policy to secure the ruler. The ancestral sacrifices of Lu were nearly extinguished but were restored, all through his efforts. Regrettably, his eagerness to accept Fei opened the way to the usurpations of a powerful city, while his contentment with receiving a clan name established the monopoly of hereditary ministers. If it was You who pacified Lu, who was it who brought disorder upon Lu? A gentleman demands completeness of the worthy; he cannot be without regret concerning You.

A hegemonic lord who brings distant states into submission, but disregards sound advice and takes no heed of their troubles, certainly deserves blame. A state of divided allegiance that provokes the barbarians, disregards sound advice, and consequently suffers calamity also deserves blame. Is this not why the Spring and Autumn Annals blames them equally—Qi for failing Huang, and Zheng for bringing disaster upon itself at the hands of Chu?

…the worthy ruler of a small state to be oppressed by a powerful aggressor. “Allying with others and suffering harm” [?] furnished Chu with a pretext; relying on others without taking precautions, Huang ultimately met with disaster. Huang indeed deserves pity! At that time, Guan Zhong’s warning that Qi was distant and would not come to the rescue should have alerted Duke Huan. Had he heeded it and kept it in mind, standing in awe of the obligations conveyed in the written summons, how could Huang have come to this? Why did he disregard those words and thereby bring such calamity upon Huang? Although Huang suffered the misfortune, Huan had much to be ashamed of before his “Father Zhong.” When the Classic records the destruction of Huang as an “attack,” what can this mean but condemnation of Huan?
As for Zheng, from the middle period onward it had suffered under the commands of powerful Chu and wished to follow Jin to ease its burden. It therefore raised troops to invade Cai and captured Zixie. Cai was under Chu’s protection: now that Zheng had maltreated it, how could Chu forget? Before long, Chu dispatched an army under Zinang to punish the invasion of Cai. If another state musters troops because we have provoked the conflict, how can we escape still greater distress? Thus, facing destruction, they feared a catastrophe like a bursting dike; deliberations over whom to follow and whom to defy filled the court with uproar. All this merely left the people in misery and straitened circumstances, with nowhere to appeal. Supplies of jade and silk were exhausted in receiving the two neighboring powers, and soldiers and chariots were worn out by the rushing to and fro of the three campaigns. Zheng was indeed in peril! At the outset, Zichan’s concern that military success would bring disaster should have prompted Zheng to reflect. Had it trusted his words without doubt and made plans to preserve the state, how could Zheng have come to this? Why did it dismiss his words and thereby hasten such calamity at Chu’s hands? Although Chu acted without principle, Zheng had much to be ashamed of before young Qiao, that is, Zichan. When the Classic records Zheng’s military action as an “invasion,” what can this mean but condemnation of Zheng? Thus, it was not Chu that destroyed Huang, but Qi; it was not Chu that attacked Zheng, but Zheng itself. 之見違奚獨二子然哉昭烈君臣魚水相得何
伐吳之後猶惜孝直之不存唐太宗從諫如流
何魏徵若在有悔於征遼之後彼皆英主也而
猶若是則吾於齊鄭二君又何尤焉雖然鄭簡
無足怪矣桓公一則仲父二則仲父而終以違
諫失黃可慨也夫
叔孫得臣會晉人宋人陳人衛人鄭人伐

translation_en:
…regret afterward? In general, heeding counsel is not easy, and discerning distant consequences is harder still. Throughout antiquity and down to the present, have these two men alone had their loyal counsels disregarded? Emperor Zhaolie and his minister were as well matched as fish and water; why, then, after attacking Wu, did he still lament that Xiaozhi was no longer alive? Emperor Taizong of Tang accepted remonstrance as readily as water flows; why, then, after campaigning against Liao, did he express regret with the words, “If Wei Zheng were still alive”? Both were enlightened rulers, yet even they acted thus. What further blame, then, can I lay upon the two rulers of Qi and Zheng? Nevertheless, Duke Jian of Zheng offers little cause for surprise. But Duke Huan was forever saying “Father Zhong”—“Father Zhong” at every turn—and ultimately lost Huang by disregarding his remonstrance. How lamentable!
“Shusun Dechen joined men of Jin, Song, Chen, Wei, and Zheng in attacking Shen. Shen collapsed.” “Yang Chufu of Jin led an army to attack Chu in order to rescue Jiang.” Both entries are from the third year of Duke Wen.
Ye Yingcong.
Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Director: “Military affairs are not something scholars versed in sacrificial vessels ordinarily discuss. You alone have brought them out through the meaning of the Classic, in full accord with military discipline. This is learning of practical use.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Compiler: “The meaning of the two comments in Hu’s Commentary is perfectly clear, yet many miss it. This composition grasps it clearly and precisely, and its language adequately expresses it. For this reason it has been selected for inclusion.”
Comment by Examiner Gu, Academician: “The composition has method and order; it merits inclusion.”
Comment by Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary: “It grasps the purport of arranging the wording and these events [?].”

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
春秋所書有示用師之道者有紀用兵之法者
夫兵戎重事也觀於伐沈救江之書而聖人愼
重之意可見矣且晉之伐沈以其服於楚也伐
國亦大矣何春秋無褒貶耶曰示用師之道也
師有權正道所寓焉權盡其變正守其常而莫
可易者也沈之即楚豈擇利從之耶將其情有
不獲已者晉能審權正而處之斯可矣顧乃求
細過於附庸泄遺怒於懷貳義舉弗聞而號召
何所驅人也然猶以討貳為名而勤此五國之
===
師以即夷致討而潰彼內携之衆其視怵私復
怨之兵不猶有間哉噫用兵者必知權而本之
以正也沈之伐其弗悖於此乎其盡悖於此乎
春秋詞無褒貶而用師之道於是見矣若晉之
救江以其困於楚也救兵亦善矣何春秋有譏
貶耶曰紀用兵之法也兵有竒正法所存焉正
奪其氣竒亂其謀而不可失者也楚之圍江豈
傾國赴之耶且其罪有不可赦者晉能用竒正
而乗之斯可矣顧乃秦不命之西師齊不用之

而乘之斯可矣顧乃㤗不命之西師齊不用之
punctuated:
春秋所書，有示用師之道者，有紀用兵之法者。夫兵戎，重事也。觀於伐沈、救江之書，而聖人愼重之意可見矣。且晉之伐沈，以其服於楚也。伐國亦大矣，何春秋無褒貶耶？曰：示用師之道也。師有權正，道所寓焉。權盡其變，正守其常，而莫可易者也。沈之即楚，豈擇利從之耶？將其情有不獲已者？晉能審權正而處之，斯可矣。顧乃求細過於附庸，泄遺怒於懷貳，義舉弗聞，而號召何所驅人也？然猶以討貳為名，而勤此五國之師；以即夷致討，而潰彼內携之衆。其視怵私復怨之兵，不猶有間哉？噫！用兵者必知權，而本之以正也。沈之伐，其弗悖於此乎？其盡悖於此乎？春秋詞無褒貶，而用師之道於是見矣。
若晉之救江，以其困於楚也。救兵亦善矣，何春秋有譏貶耶？曰：紀用兵之法也。兵有竒正，法所存焉。正奪其氣，竒亂其謀，而不可失者也。楚之圍江，豈傾國赴之耶？且其罪有不可赦者。晉能用竒正而乗之，斯可矣。顧乃秦不命之西師，齊不用之
translation_en:
Among the events recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals, some illustrate the proper way to employ armies, while others record the methods of conducting warfare. Warfare is a grave matter. In the records of the attack on Shen and the relief of Jiang, we can discern the sage’s cautious intent. Jin attacked Shen because Shen had submitted to Chu. Attacking a state is a momentous undertaking; why, then, do the Spring and Autumn Annals express neither praise nor blame? The answer is that they illustrate the proper way to employ armies. In employing armies there are expediency and adherence to what is right; therein lies the Way. Expediency accommodates every change, while adherence to what is right preserves the constant principles that cannot be altered. When Shen attached itself to Chu, was it choosing to follow its own advantage? Or were its circumstances such that it had no alternative? Had Jin weighed expediency against what was right and dealt with the matter accordingly, that would have sufficed. Instead, it sought petty faults in a dependent state and vented lingering anger upon one whose allegiance was divided. No righteous undertaking was heard of: on what grounds could its summons impel men to act? Nevertheless, it mobilized the armies of these five states in the name of punishing divided allegiance; it punished Shen for attaching itself to the barbarians and routed its internally divided forces. Compared with warfare prompted by private interests and the desire to avenge grievances, was there not still a distinction? Alas! Those who employ armies must understand expediency and ground it in what is right. Did the attack on Shen accord with this principle? Did it violate it entirely? The wording of the Spring and Autumn Annals offers neither praise nor blame, yet the proper way to employ armies is revealed here.
As for Jin’s relief of Jiang, this was undertaken because Jiang was hard pressed by Chu. Sending troops to its relief was surely good; why, then, do the Spring and Autumn Annals express criticism and blame? The answer is that they record the methods of conducting warfare. Warfare has unconventional and conventional operations; therein lie its methods. Conventional operations break the enemy’s morale; unconventional operations disrupt its plans. Neither can be neglected. When Chu besieged Jiang, did it commit the forces of its entire state? Moreover, its offense was unforgivable. text:
東略竒謀弗設而掎角無所成勢也況又大眾
不集而偏師失拒伍之全大惡不聲而逺攻斷
首尾之應其於恤患討罪之事胡能有濟哉噫
用兵者必由正而濟之以竒也江之救孰聚而
為正乎孰分而為竒乎春秋以以為譏而用兵
之法於是見矣合此而觀而聖人審事之宜待
人之恕恤患之大討賊之嚴豈不瞭然於書法
之間哉抑嘗因是而考晉襄之霸在位凡七年

translation_en:
…operations in the east. No unconventional stratagem was devised, and no mutually supporting disposition of forces was achieved. Moreover, the main army was not assembled, leaving the detached force without a complete fighting formation [?]; the enemy’s grave offenses were not publicly proclaimed, while the distant attack severed coordination between front and rear. How could this accomplish anything toward relieving distress and punishing wrongdoing? Ah! Those who employ troops must proceed by orthodox methods and supplement them with unconventional ones. In the relief of Jiang, which forces were concentrated to serve as the orthodox force? Which were detached to serve as the unconventional force? The Spring and Autumn Annals censures this, and the principles of warfare are thereby revealed. Considering these cases together, do we not see clearly in the manner of recording events the Sage’s fitness of judgment, his forbearance toward others, his great concern for those in distress, and his strictness in punishing wrongdoers?

I have also taken this occasion to examine the hegemony of Duke Xiang of Jin. He reigned for seven years, yet apart from his dealings with Qin and the Di, his involvement in the affairs of the regional lords was scant. In these two campaigns, he professed to be moving against Chu and proclaimed that he would rescue Jiang, as though he were confronting Chu as an enemy. Yet Shen collapsed, and Chu continued its unchecked aggression; Jiang was destroyed, and our prestige merely suffered. Having exhausted his strength in dealing with Qin, he had none left to discharge his duty of securing peace within and repelling threats from without. This is what the gentleman regrets.

Record of Rites
“The vessels used are of earthenware and gourd, to symbolize the natures of Heaven and Earth.”
Chen Huan

Writers either lapse into superficiality or struggle with obscurity. This essay is precise and accomplished in both expression and reasoning. Its author has evidently gained insight from studying the rites. It inspires respect! It inspires respect!”

祭器用物性之自然正以法造化之本然盖造
化之本然質而已矣郊祀之器用陶匏不有取
於是乎記郊特牲者申言以少為貴之義如此
且以天子之尊而行祀天之禮其器之陳於郊
兆者豈無金玉之貴以將吾之誠哉今則金玉
===
非所尚也而凡以薦以享者惟陶瓦之是供陶
也者凝土以為範煬火以為堅一自然之質也
亦豈無雕鏤之工以表吾之敬哉今則雕鏤非
所貴也而凡以挹以注者惟匏瓠之是取匏也
者得天以為氣資地以為形一自然之用也所
以然者其義何取哉誠以確然至健者天也其
知大始也但見其潜孚潜庸而妙神化於無為
天之性固質而已隤然至順者地也其作成物
也但見其默運默化而泯機緘於不露地之性

祭器用物性之自然，正以法造化之本然。盖造化之本然，質而已矣。郊祀之器用陶匏，不有取於是乎？記郊特牲者申言以少為貴之義如此。且以天子之尊，而行祀天之禮，其器之陳於郊兆者，豈無金玉之貴以將吾之誠哉？今則金玉非所尚也，而凡以薦以享者，惟陶瓦之是供。陶也者，凝土以為範，煬火以為堅，一自然之質也。亦豈無雕鏤之工以表吾之敬哉？今則雕鏤非所貴也，而凡以挹以注者，惟匏瓠之是取。匏也者，得天以為氣，資地以為形，一自然之用也。所以然者，其義何取哉？誠以確然至健者，天也。其知大始也，但見其潜孚潜庸，而妙神化於無為，天之性固質而已。隤然至順者，地也。其作成物也，但見其默運默化，而泯機緘於不露，地之性
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Wu, Examining Editor, comments: “The nature of Heaven and Earth is exceedingly difficult to express. This composition succeeds in elucidating it; its language is also concise and plain. It merits inclusion.”

Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “It accords very well with the meaning of the topic.”

Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “The composition itself also conveys an appreciation of simplicity.”

Sacrificial vessels employ the natural properties of materials precisely to emulate the inherent character of the creative workings of Heaven and Earth. That inherent character is simply unadorned simplicity. Is this not what the use of earthenware and gourds for the suburban sacrifice draws upon? Thus the author of ‘The Single Victim at the Suburban Sacrifice’ elaborates the principle that spareness is prized.

When one performs the rite of sacrificing to Heaven with all the dignity of the Son of Heaven, could precious vessels of gold and jade not be arrayed within the suburban sacrificial precinct to convey one’s sincerity? Yet here gold and jade are not esteemed: all vessels used to present offerings and make sacrifice are supplied solely in earthenware. Earthenware is earth consolidated into a mold and fired to make it hard: it embodies a wholly natural substance. Could the skill of carving and engraving not likewise express one’s reverence? Yet here carving and engraving are not prized: all vessels used for scooping and pouring are taken solely from gourds. A gourd receives its vital energy from Heaven and draws upon Earth for its form: it serves a wholly natural function.

Why is this so? What principle does it draw upon? Truly, that which is firm and supremely vigorous is Heaven. In its presiding over the great beginning, we see only its unseen trustworthiness and unseen operation, wondrously accomplishing spiritual transformation through nonaction. Heaven’s nature is indeed simply unadorned simplicity. That which is yielding and supremely compliant is Earth. In its bringing things to completion, we see only its silent movement and silent transformation, with the mechanisms of its workings effaced from view. Earth’s nature …

translation_en:
…is likewise simply unadorned. Thus, using earthenware in sacrifice is no mere simplification: it represents their nature, from which one dares not depart. Using gourds in sacrifice is no mere meagerness: it represents their nature, to which one dares not add. Such is the significance of using earthenware and gourds. Could the sages, then, have established the rites without purpose? Consider further: the achievements of Heaven and Earth are great, yet when we examine the rites of sacrifice that requite them, their ceremonial elaboration is less complete than that of other sacrifices. Why is this? All things under Heaven are produced by Heaven and Earth; no material object can adequately match the ritual honor due to them. Thus one sweeps the ground and offers sacrifice, using a calf as the victim and earthenware and gourds as vessels, solely to express sincerity and reverence. Certainly none but sages could have established this. Yet even with this teaching, later generations still performed the feng and shan sacrifices, thereby profaning Heaven. Alas!

“Thus those who understand the essential significance of rites and music can create them; those who recognize their outward forms can transmit them. Those who create are called sages; those who transmit are called enlightened.”

Wang Tingchen

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Supervising Secretary: “This topic seems easy but is actually difficult, because creation and transmission, sagehood and enlightenment, must not be discussed indiscriminately. Students speak loosely of them all together, greatly departing from the original purport. This composition traces matters from source to outcome and weighs them carefully. Profound in its reasoning and subtle in its expression, it merits inclusion.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Examining Editor: “He brings out almost the full meaning of the topic, and it comes from his own mind, without a single sentence borrowed from predecessors. Might he be one who has gained insight through reading the Book of Rites?”

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
考試官學士顧批論情文述作條理粲然
考試官大學士靳批發揮透徹豈亦有志於
禮樂者耶
人於禮樂有淺深故用不同而名亦異也盖禮
樂之作述其用不同而聖明之名亦異也所以
然者不以其所造有淺深哉且禮樂之道有情
有文其理趣之深奧而不可見者情也如合敬
同愛之類是已有人於此窮深極微妙契於器
數之表無遺漏焉則有以知其情矣若人也必
===
能以所獨得者而成之於制作緣義以起禮審
音以定樂曠古之制自我乎托始矣節奏之宣
著而可見者文也如制度聲容之類是已有人
於此探賾索隱博考於散逸之餘無疑貳焉則
有以識其文矣若人也必能以其所未備者而
形之於論著修補其殘闕叙正其次第百王之
法於我乎成終矣夫無所因而成者難為功也
故夫任創立之責者必其聰明睿知獨得於天
博達貫通高出於物造踐形合德之境入窮神

translation_en:
Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “In discussing the inner substance and outward forms, and the transmission and creation, the argument is lucidly ordered.”
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “The exposition is penetrating and thorough. Might the author also be someone devoted to rites and music?”
People attain different depths of understanding in rites and music; hence their functions differ, as do the designations they receive. Creating and transmitting rites and music differ in their functions, and the designations ‘sage’ and ‘enlightened’ likewise differ. Is this not because their attainments vary in depth? The Way of rites and music has both inner substance and outward forms. Its profound significance, which cannot be seen, is its inner substance: such things as bringing people together in reverence and uniting them in love. If someone plumbs its depths and reaches its subtlest aspects, attaining a wondrous accord with what lies beyond ritual implements and numerical prescriptions, leaving nothing unexplored, then he has the means to understand its inner substance. Such a person can assuredly embody his unique understanding in the creation of institutions, establishing rites in accordance with righteousness and determining music through discerning sounds. Institutions without precedent in antiquity thus take their origin from him. The manifest and visible articulation of rhythm and measure constitutes its outward forms: such things as institutions and regulations, sounds and ceremonial deportment. If someone probes the mysteries and seeks out what is hidden, extensively examining what remains after dispersal and loss, leaving no uncertainty, then he has the means to recognize its outward forms. Such a person can assuredly give expression in expositions and writings to what has yet to be fully set forth, repairing deficiencies and restoring the proper sequence. The standards of the hundred kings thus reach completion through him.
To accomplish something without a precedent to follow is difficult. Therefore, one who bears responsibility for establishing something anew must possess keen perception and sagacious understanding uniquely bestowed by Heaven, with extensive comprehension and integrated mastery that raise him far above ordinary things. He must reach the realm of fully realizing his bodily form and according with virtue, and enter into the fathoming of the spiritual…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
知化之地者然後能之也不謂之聖乎謂之聖
則明可兼矣有所承而為者易為力也故夫當
紹述之任者但其博洽之識得之於問學融會
之見得之於思惟知極於反情和志之後明發
於比類成行之餘者亦可能之也不謂之明乎
謂之明則聖可幾矣夫禮樂之述作有繋於人
如此道豈虚行乎哉雖然天下不可一日無禮
樂則亦不可一日無聖賢自周以後作者不可
得見矣雖述者或難其人焉此禮樂所以不興
===
而參天地賛化育之功泯矣是何怪乎世治之
日下也噫禮樂之興廢豈細故歟
故君使其臣得志則慎慮而從之

translation_en:
…the realm of understanding transformation: only such a person can accomplish this. Would we not call him a sage? If we call him a sage, discernment is included as well. Where there is an inherited foundation on which to work, the task is easier. Thus, those charged with continuing and transmitting the tradition can also accomplish it, provided that their comprehensive knowledge comes from inquiry and learning, their integrated understanding from reflection, their knowledge reaches its culmination through returning to their true feelings and harmonizing their intentions, and their discernment emerges through comparing analogous cases and perfecting their conduct. Would we not call them discerning? If we call them discerning, then sagehood is within their reach. The transmission and creation of rites and music depend upon people in this way: how could the Way operate of itself, without human agency? Yet if the world cannot go a single day without rites and music, neither can it go a single day without sages and worthies. Since the Zhou, no creators have been seen, and even suitable transmitters have sometimes been hard to find. This is why rites and music have failed to flourish, and why the achievement of standing alongside Heaven and Earth and assisting their transforming and nourishing work has vanished. What wonder, then, that the governance of the world declines day by day? Alas! Could the flourishing or abandonment of rites and music be a minor matter?
“Thus, when a ruler employs his minister, if the minister attains his aspirations, he considers carefully before complying.”
Wang Tingchen
Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Supervising Secretary: “Scholars can generally speak about the obligations of a minister in serving his ruler, but works that are precise, incisive, concise, and apt are seldom seen. This essay stands far apart from the others, as though its author had personally received instruction at the school of Confucius. Surely he is no ordinary scholar!”
Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Examining Editor: “The meaning of ‘considering carefully’ is explained thoroughly. From this we can predict how he will conduct himself when he attains his aspirations in the future. Could we select him merely for his literary skill?”

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
考試官學士顧批觀此作是必能慎慮者
考試官大學士靳批發明人臣處滿之道
殆盡
人臣受君之命不以有所遇而忽所事焉蓋臣
之事君以敬為本也使所事或隳於得志焉抑
何以盡其道哉表記引孔子之言如此謂夫人
臣之義處其位則當履其事其可苟焉而已哉
是故經理庶務君非臣無以承之也固必擇其
賢者而列之於朝廷戡定禍亂君非臣無以任
===
之也固必簡其材者而付之以軍旅人臣於斯
時也際胥慶之會而為所任使則經綸得以展
布平生之所深願者於是乎遂矣赴相遇之機
而為所委寄則材猷得以發舒窮居之所素尚
者於此乎得矣使得志而侈心或萌焉則前事
未成而近禍已伏矣其可乎哉故處朝廷也靖
共爾位而寅畏之心恒存圖事揆策必商其可
否之宜方物出謀必酌其利害之實位之崇卑
無擇也處軍旅也恪勤乃職而儆懼之念常在

translation_en:
Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: Judging from this composition, its author must be someone capable of careful deliberation.

Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: This almost exhaustively elucidates how a minister should conduct himself at the height of success.

A minister who receives his ruler’s command does not allow the favor he has met with to make him neglect his duties. For reverence is the foundation of a minister’s service to his ruler. If success should cause him to let his duties lapse, how could he fully fulfill the proper way of service? The chapter “Record of Exemplary Conduct” quotes Confucius’s words to this effect, meaning that a minister’s obligation is to discharge the duties of whatever position he occupies. How could he merely perform them perfunctorily?

Thus, in managing the many affairs of government, the ruler cannot have them carried out without ministers; he must therefore select worthy men and give them places at court. In suppressing calamity and disorder, the ruler cannot entrust the task to anyone without ministers; he must therefore select capable men and entrust them with military command. At such a time, when a minister encounters an occasion for mutual rejoicing and is employed in service, he can put his ability to order affairs into practice, and his lifelong, deeply cherished aspirations are fulfilled. When he meets the opportunity to find a ruler who appreciates him and receives his trust, his talents and plans can unfold, and what he has always prized while living in obscurity is now attained. But if, upon attaining success, an arrogant and extravagant disposition should arise, impending disaster will already lie hidden before the work before him is accomplished. How could this be acceptable?

Thus, when serving at court, he must diligently and reverently attend to his position, constantly maintaining a disposition of respectful awe. In planning affairs and weighing courses of action, he must consider whether they are appropriate; in assessing matters and offering proposals, he must weigh their actual benefits and harms, making no distinction between high and low office. When serving in the army, he must discharge his duties with diligence and respect, constantly maintaining vigilance and apprehension…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
運籌制勝惟欲其出於萬全料事應機惟恐其
貽夫後悔身之禍福不計也是則一日居乎其
位則一日不敢曠乎其官事君如此可謂能履
其事矣臣道其庶矣乎不特此耳下文又曰否
則熟慮而從之終事而退得志則畏命而不敢
恃不得志則畏義而無所尤非終事不敢退焉
必如此而後事君之義可全也莊子曰臣之於
君也命也義也無所逃於天地之間彼豈能見
於此夫

translation_en:
…In devising strategies to secure victory, he seeks only to ensure complete success; in assessing affairs and responding to circumstances, he fears only leaving cause for later regret. He gives no thought to his own fortune or misfortune. Thus, for every day that he occupies his position, he dares not neglect his official duties. Serving his ruler in this way, he may be said to fulfill his responsibilities and to come close to the proper way of a minister! Nor is this all. The text below further states: “Otherwise, deliberate carefully and follow through; complete the undertaking and withdraw.” When he achieves his aspirations, he reveres Heaven’s mandate and dares not presume upon his success; when he does not achieve them, he reveres righteousness and blames no one. Until the undertaking is complete, he dares not withdraw. Only in this way can the obligations of serving one’s ruler be fully discharged. Zhuangzi said: “For a minister in relation to his ruler, it is destiny and duty: there is no escape from it anywhere between Heaven and Earth.” Could he have understood this?

Second Session

Discourse

The Sages Follow but a Single Principle

Cui Tong

Comment by Associate Examiner Huang, Supervising Secretary: The argument is founded on the single word “sincerity.” Plain, substantial, pure, and correct, it naturally reveals the significance of principle. Print it to encourage those who do not esteem the Learning of Principle.

Comment by Associate Examiner Guo, Examining Editor: By founding its argument on “sincerity,” this essay encompasses almost the whole of moral principle. Moreover, its language and tone are elegant, vigorous, profound, and well integrated, naturally distinguishing it from works that indulge in superficial ornament. Reading it, one can discern the author’s character.

text:
同考試官編修　批　字字句句真切
同考試官編修嚴　批　本房竒作甚衆能
發明理□文暢而意足者此為稱
同考試官侍讀崔　批　論性理而能發揚
委曲佳作也
考試官學士顧　批　說理詳盡詞氣渾成
錄之以為尚雕麗者式
考試官大學士靳　批　論場無非能言之士
列此者取其質而當也
===
論曰凡生於兩間者不能無氣質之累也而聖
人所由無非一理而氣質不能累焉何哉亦曰
能全乎誠而已矣誠者真實无妄之謂天之道
也即所謂無極而太極者也人皆有之其初同
也而二五交錯氣質之性得以畧之而私欲生
焉於是漸失其初而同者異矣惟夫聖人氣質
清純渾然一理而誠無不至則精明應妙幾無
不燭德無不備此所以不思不勉而自然所由
皆一理也然則誠也者非聖人之所以為聖人

論曰：凡生於兩間者，不能無氣質之累也。而聖人所由，無非一理，而氣質不能累焉，何哉？亦曰能全乎誠而已矣。誠者，真實无妄之謂，天之道也，即所謂無極而太極者也。人皆有之，其初同也，而二五交錯，氣質之性得以畧之，而私欲生焉。於是漸失其初，而同者異矣。惟夫聖人氣質清純，渾然一理，而誠無不至，則精明應妙，幾無不燭，德無不備。此所以不思不勉，而自然所由皆一理也。然則誠也者，非聖人之所以為聖人
translation_en:
Comment by the Associate Examiner, a Compiler whose name is not supplied: Every word and every sentence is genuine and apt.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yan, Compiler: There are very many outstanding compositions in this examination section. For elucidating principle [illegible character], with fluent writing and fully developed meaning, this deserves praise.

Comment by Associate Examiner Cui, Reader-in-Waiting: This discusses human nature and principle while bringing out their subtleties in detail. It is an excellent composition.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Academician: Its explanation of principle is comprehensive, and its language and tenor form a seamless whole. It is included as a model for those who prize ornate elegance.

Comment by Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary: Those competing in the discourse examination are all skilled in expression. This piece is included for its substance and aptness.

The discourse reads: All who are born between Heaven and Earth inevitably bear the encumbrances of their material endowment. Yet the sage follows nothing but the single principle, and material endowment cannot encumber him. Why is this? Simply because he can fully realize sincerity. Sincerity means being real and true, without falsity; it is the Way of Heaven. It is precisely what is called “the Ultimateless and yet the Supreme Ultimate.” Everyone possesses it, and at the beginning all are alike. But as the two forces and the five phases intermingle, the nature arising from material endowment comes to override it [?], and selfish desires arise. Thus people gradually lose their original condition, and those who were alike become different. Only the sage has a clear and pure material endowment, wholly embodying the single principle, with sincerity perfected in every respect. His lucid intelligence responds with subtle mastery; no incipient movement escapes his illumination, and no virtue is lacking. This is why, without deliberation or exertion, all that he follows is naturally the single principle. Thus, is sincerity not what makes the sage a sage …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
者乎程子曰聖人所由惟一理愚以為聖人之
所以能然者一誠之外無他道也噫論聖人而
歸之誠可謂一言以蔽之矣曷不以天道觀之
乎今夫天之所以為天也大哉乾元萬物資始
陽之動也而實則誠之通也乾道變化各正性
命陰之靜也而實則誠之復也則天之為天其
道不外乎誠可知矣聖人與天合德者也而獨
不在於誠乎雖然誠非聖人天道之所獨有也
衆人失之君子脩之賢者存之而惟聖人則存
===
存不已與天一也是以一理之在聖人者不異
於在天氣稟不能為之拘物欲不能為之蔽凡
有所由無非一理體之為五常著之為百行達
之為禮樂刑政凡所以立人極而配天地者莫
非純粹至善之所為盖太極之全體一動一靜
無適非仁義中正之極不假脩為而然者也此
則所謂性焉安焉之聖人也非天下至誠其孰
能之哉自今觀之其寬裕溫柔而有容一理之
見於仁也發強剛毅而有執一理之見於義也

見於仁也發强剛毅而有執一理之見於義也
punctuated: 者乎？程子曰：「聖人所由惟一理。」愚以為聖人之所以能然者，一誠之外無他道也。噫！論聖人而歸之誠，可謂一言以蔽之矣。曷不以天道觀之乎？今夫天之所以為天也，「大哉乾元，萬物資始」，陽之動也，而實則誠之通也；「乾道變化，各正性命」，陰之靜也，而實則誠之復也。則天之為天，其道不外乎誠，可知矣。聖人與天合德者也，而獨不在於誠乎？雖然，誠非聖人天道之所獨有也。衆人失之，君子脩之，賢者存之，而惟聖人則存存不已，與天一也。是以一理之在聖人者，不異於在天，氣稟不能為之拘，物欲不能為之蔽。凡有所由，無非一理，體之為五常，著之為百行，達之為禮樂刑政。凡所以立人極而配天地者，莫非純粹至善之所為。盖太極之全體，一動一靜，無適非仁義中正之極，不假脩為而然者也。此則所謂性焉安焉之聖人也。非天下至誠，其孰能之哉？自今觀之，其寬裕溫柔而有容，一理之見於仁也；發強剛毅而有執，一理之見於義也。
translation_en:
…what makes a sage a sage? Master Cheng said: “What the sage follows is the single principle alone.” In my humble view, what enables the sage to be so is nothing other than sincerity: beyond this there is no other way. Ah! To discuss the sage and trace everything back to sincerity may indeed be called summing it up in a single phrase. Why not consider this through the Way of Heaven? As for what makes Heaven Heaven: “Great indeed is the primal power of Qian; the myriad things draw upon it for their beginning.” This is the movement of yang, and in truth it is the unfolding of sincerity. “The Way of Qian changes and transforms, and each thing receives its proper nature and allotted destiny.” This is the stillness of yin, and in truth it is the return of sincerity. Thus we can know that the Way by which Heaven is Heaven does not extend beyond sincerity. The sage unites his virtue with Heaven: could this alone fail to reside in sincerity?

Yet sincerity is not the exclusive possession of the sage or of the Way of Heaven. Ordinary people lose it; the gentleman cultivates it; the worthy preserve it. Only the sage preserves it without ceasing and is one with Heaven. Thus the single principle in the sage is no different from that in Heaven. His endowment of vital force cannot constrain it, and material desires cannot obscure it. Whatever he follows is nothing other than the single principle. Embodied, it constitutes the Five Constant Virtues; manifested, it constitutes the hundred forms of conduct; extended into practice, it constitutes rites, music, punishments, and government. Everything by which he establishes the supreme standard for humanity and matches Heaven and Earth proceeds from unalloyed, consummate goodness. For this is the complete substance of the Supreme Ultimate: in every movement and every stillness, there is nothing that is not the utmost realization of benevolence, righteousness, centrality, and correctness. It is so without recourse to deliberate cultivation. This is the sage who is said to possess these qualities by nature and to rest at ease in them. Who but one of the utmost sincerity under Heaven could achieve this?

Viewed in this light, his being generous, broad-minded, mild, gentle, and accommodating is the single principle manifested as benevolence; his being energetic, strong, firm, resolute, and steadfast is the single principle manifested as righteousness…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
齊莊中正而有敬一理之見於禮也文理密察
而有別一理之見於智也由一身而達之于家
于國于天下吾見本之端也則之善也禮法之
正也教化之脩也三綱之正而九疇之叙也百
姓之大和也萬物之咸若也樂作而天下之化
中也見焉而天下之皆敬也言焉而天下之皆
信也行焉而天下之皆悅也固也然孰非一理
所由之所致哉聖人胡為而能然也靈秀所鍾
在人獨異而聖人則又秀之秀者一心之中真
===
實无妄肫肫其仁淵淵其淵浩浩其天舉天下
之誠莫能加也不然則聖人亦人耳惡能從容
中道而與天地合德也哉予竊慨夫斯人之梏
於氣質而自異於聖人也剛柔雜揉美惡不齊
不啻倍蓰什伯千萬之相遠也其欲動情勝利
害相攻者不足言矣知脩焉者君子也君子之
於一理盖欲由之而未能者也就焉優焉者賢
者也賢者之於一理盖勉強由之而未純者也
是雖不囿於氣稟而亦超乎人人矣然視聖人

punctuated:
齊莊中正而有敬，一理之見於禮也；文理密察而有別，一理之見於智也。由一身而達之于家、于國、于天下，吾見本之端也，則之善也，禮法之正也，教化之脩也，三綱之正而九疇之叙也，百姓之大和也，萬物之咸若也。樂作而天下之化中也，見焉而天下之皆敬也，言焉而天下之皆信也，行焉而天下之皆悅也，固也。然孰非一理所由之所致哉？聖人胡為而能然也？靈秀所鍾，在人獨異，而聖人則又秀之秀者。一心之中，真實无妄，肫肫其仁，淵淵其淵，浩浩其天，舉天下之誠莫能加也。不然，則聖人亦人耳，惡能從容中道而與天地合德也哉？
予竊慨夫斯人之梏於氣質而自異於聖人也。剛柔雜揉，美惡不齊，不啻倍蓰什伯千萬之相遠也。其欲動情勝、利害相攻者，不足言矣。知脩焉者，君子也。君子之於一理，盖欲由之而未能者也。就焉優焉者，賢者也。賢者之於一理，盖勉強由之而未純者也。是雖不囿於氣稟，而亦超乎人人矣，然視聖人
translation_en:
…To be disciplined, dignified, centered, and upright, and thus reverent, is the manifestation of the one principle in ritual propriety; to be ordered, finely discerning, and thus capable of making distinctions, is its manifestation in wisdom. Extending from one's own person to the family, the state, and all under Heaven, it produces, as I see it, an upright foundation, good standards, correct rites and laws, cultivated moral instruction, the rectification of the Three Bonds, and the ordering of the Nine Categories. The common people enjoy great harmony, and all things accord with their proper order. When music is performed, all under Heaven are transformed and attain the mean; when the sage appears, all under Heaven revere him; when he speaks, all trust him; when he acts, all delight in him. This is indeed so. Yet which of these effects does not arise from following the one principle? How can the sage accomplish this? The concentrated spiritual and refined endowments of the cosmos distinguish human beings alone, and the sage is the finest among the fine. Within his single heart there is reality without falsity: earnest is his benevolence, deep his profundity, and vast his Heaven-like greatness. All the sincerity in the world cannot surpass his. Were it otherwise, the sage would merely be another person: how could he effortlessly accord with the Way and unite his virtue with that of Heaven and Earth?
I privately lament that people are fettered by their material dispositions and set themselves apart from the sage. Firmness and softness mingle in them, and their qualities differ in goodness and badness; the distances between them are not merely twofold or fivefold, tenfold or a hundredfold, but a thousandfold and ten thousandfold. Those whose desires are stirred and whose feelings prevail, within whom considerations of gain and harm contend, are not worth discussing. Those who know to cultivate themselves are gentlemen. In relation to the one principle, gentlemen wish to follow it but are not yet able to do so. Those who approach it and become at ease in it are the worthy. In relation to the one principle, the worthy follow it through effort but have not yet attained purity. Though these people are not confined by their endowment of material force and have risen above ordinary people, yet compared with the sage …

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官郎中聞批論欲觀士子才氣
學識塲中作者率多撫拾通書語排比成文
殊為可厭此篇議論滔滔出自胷次且筆力
雄健理致精深殆績學而有得者耶
同考試官編修尹批性理題目作者不
局於陳言即過為穿鑿此篇立論平正不失
濂洛意而文又足以發之錄之允當
同考試官編修劉批此作據理立論殆
千餘言且開闔抑揚自中矩度末復推本堯
===
舜相傳以盡一理蘊奧是可以擅塲矣
同考試官洗馬滕批近日士子作論類
多浮冗至理學題目則大為所窘晚得此卷

Associate Examiner Wen, Director, comments: A discourse is intended to reveal a candidate’s talent, spirit, learning, and understanding. Most writers in the examination hall merely gather phrases from the Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu) and arrange them in parallel constructions to form an essay. This is exceedingly tiresome. This essay’s arguments flow abundantly from the writer’s own mind; moreover, its brushwork is vigorous and its exposition of principle profound and precise. Surely this is someone who has accumulated learning and attained understanding?

Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler, comments: On topics concerning human nature and principle, writers either confine themselves to stale expressions or go too far in strained interpretations. This essay’s argument is balanced and sound, remaining faithful to the intent of the Lian and Luo traditions, while its prose adequately brings that intent to light. Its selection is entirely appropriate.

Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler, comments: This composition grounds its argument in principle and runs to over a thousand words. Its opening and closing movements, restraint and emphasis, all naturally accord with the proper standards. At the end it further traces the source to the transmission from Yao to Shun, fully exploring the profound mysteries of the single principle. It can indeed command the field.

Associate Examiner Teng, Librarian, comments: Recently, candidates’ discourses have mostly been superficial and prolix; when faced with topics concerning the learning of principle, they find themselves severely constrained. Coming upon this script late in the proceedings, I find its grasp of principle precise and incisive, and its language rich and ample. Reading it makes one leap with delight.

Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: Writing a discourse becomes difficult when it comes to human nature and principle. This essay ranges freely, with restraint and emphasis, without becoming cramped or constrained. Its author must be a man of accumulated learning.

Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: This composition takes as its main basis the explanation of establishing the human ultimate in the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate. This also accords with the original meaning, so I do not object to its repetition and select it for inclusion.

The discourse reads: There is nothing else by which the sage establishes the human ultimate; it is simply a matter of fully realizing the Supreme Ultimate…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
之理而已太極之理無乎不在其合也萬物之
統體也其分也萬物之各具也一理之外豈復
有他道哉而天下之動常病於不一者太極之
妙本無不一而不一者人也聖人亦人耳而人
極立焉是眾人不能全而聖人獨全之也然則
人極之立聖人豈有所待於其外哉何以言之
由太虚有天之名由氣化有道之名合虚與氣
有性之名故曰天命之謂性率性之謂道性即
理也理即太極之謂也太極不可二天之不可
===
二也而理可二乎哉不可二而二之者所謂人
為之也非天也非太極也何也太極具于冲漠
無朕之中而樞紐乎造化根柢乎品彙所謂上
天之載無聲無臭此理之本原也本原者一之
謂也一動一靜分陰分陽理之一者分而為二
而實未嘗二也五氣順布四時行焉理之一者
分而為五而實未嘗五也是故無極之真惟無
妄也二五之精惟不二也故能妙合而生人人
之生也舉太極二五之理而全之即其各具之

punctuated: 之理而已。太極之理無乎不在，其合也，萬物之統體也；其分也，萬物之各具也。一理之外，豈復有他道哉？而天下之動常病於不一者，太極之妙本無不一，而不一者，人也。聖人亦人耳，而人極立焉，是眾人不能全而聖人獨全之也。然則人極之立，聖人豈有所待於其外哉？何以言之？由太虚有天之名，由氣化有道之名，合虚與氣有性之名。故曰：「天命之謂性，率性之謂道。」性即理也，理即太極之謂也。太極不可二，天之不可二也，而理可二乎哉？不可二而二之者，所謂人為之也，非天也，非太極也。何也？太極具于冲漠無朕之中，而樞紐乎造化，根柢乎品彙。所謂「上天之載，無聲無臭」，此理之本原也。本原者，一之謂也。一動一靜，分陰分陽，理之一者分而為二，而實未嘗二也。五氣順布，四時行焉，理之一者分而為五，而實未嘗五也。是故無極之真，惟無妄也；二五之精，惟不二也。故能妙合而生人。人之生也，舉太極二五之理而全之，即其各具之
translation_en:
…the principle of the Supreme Ultimate, and nothing more. The principle of the Supreme Ultimate is present everywhere. Taken together, it is the unified substance of the myriad things; considered separately, it is what each of the myriad things possesses individually. Beyond this single principle, could there be any other Way? Yet the activities of the world constantly suffer from a lack of unity. The wondrous working of the Supreme Ultimate is fundamentally never without unity; it is human beings who lack unity. The sage, too, is merely human, yet in him the ultimate standard of humanity is established. This means that what ordinary people cannot preserve in its entirety, the sage alone preserves completely. In establishing the ultimate standard of humanity, then, how could the sage depend on anything outside himself? How can this be explained?
From the Great Vacuity comes the designation Heaven; from the transformations of vital force comes the designation the Way; from the conjunction of vacuity and vital force comes the designation human nature. Thus it is said: “What Heaven commands is called human nature; following that nature is called the Way.” Human nature is principle, and principle is what is meant by the Supreme Ultimate. The Supreme Ultimate cannot be two, just as Heaven cannot be two. How, then, could principle be two? To divide into two what cannot be two is what is called human contrivance: it is neither Heaven nor the Supreme Ultimate. Why is this?
The Supreme Ultimate is fully present amid utter emptiness and stillness, without any discernible trace; yet it is the pivot of creation and transformation and the root of all categories of beings. As the saying goes, “The workings of Heaven above have neither sound nor smell.” This is the original source of principle. By “original source” is meant unity. Through movement and stillness, yin and yang are differentiated: the single principle divides into two, yet in truth it has never become two. The five vital forces spread in due order, and the four seasons proceed: the single principle divides into five, yet in truth it has never become five. Thus the reality of the Ultimateless consists simply in being without falsity; the essences of the two modes and five phases consist simply in being undivided. Hence they can wondrously unite and give birth to human beings. At birth, human beings possess in its entirety the principle of the Supreme Ultimate, the two modes, and the five phases. Within what each individually possesses…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
中而有統體之妙理惡有不一者哉此則聖人
所由之本然也惜乎人之生不能皆聖人也何
也有理斯有氣有氣斯有形天下之一者惟理
而已二氣五行之運已不能無偏駁而又梏之
以耳目口鼻四肢之形則夫氣質之稟其為吾
累也多矣夫理之一者未嘗分而氣稟有以為
吾之累於是乎有偏於剛者矣於是乎有偏於
柔者矣於是乎有剛而惡柔而惡者矣於是乎
有剛柔之善而弗中者矣性之感也而善惡分
===
物之感也而萬事出其始一而其既也倍蓰十
伯千萬而至於不可窮矣是豈理之本然而人
之所共由者當如是哉聖人之生得夫至秀而
至靈者其氣之清明質之純粹既未嘗有所拘
而物欲又不能為吾蔽故其心涵太虛一理之
體也身備萬善一理之用也體用一原顯微無
間一理之流行不息也其行之也中其處之也
正其發之也仁其裁之也義所存所發不同而
其理一也其倫君臣父子兄弟夫婦朋友其行

中，而有統體之妙，理惡有不一者哉？此則聖人所由之本然也。惜乎人之生不能皆聖人也！何也？有理斯有氣，有氣斯有形。天下之一者，惟理而已。二氣五行之運，已不能無偏駁，而又梏之以耳目口鼻四肢之形，則夫氣質之稟，其為吾累也多矣！夫理之一者未嘗分，而氣稟有以為吾之累，於是乎有偏於剛者矣，於是乎有偏於柔者矣，於是乎有剛而惡、柔而惡者矣，於是乎有剛柔之善而弗中者矣。性之感也而善惡分，物之感也而萬事出。其始一，而其既也倍蓰十伯千萬，而至於不可窮矣。是豈理之本然，而人之所共由者當如是哉？

聖人之生，得夫至秀而至靈者，其氣之清明、質之純粹，既未嘗有所拘，而物欲又不能為吾蔽，故其心涵太虛，一理之體也；身備萬善，一理之用也；體用一原，顯微無間，一理之流行不息也。其行之也中，其處之也正，其發之也仁，其裁之也義。所存所發不同，而其理一也。其倫君臣、父子、兄弟、夫婦、朋友，其行
translation_en:
…within what each individually possesses lies the wondrous unity of the whole: how could principle fail to be one? This, then, is the original condition that the sage follows. Alas, human beings cannot all be sages from birth! Why is this? Where there is principle, there is material force (qi); where there is material force, there is form. What is one throughout the world is principle alone. The workings of the two forces of yin and yang and the Five Phases already cannot be free of partiality and admixture. Further confined by the bodily forms of ears, eyes, mouth, nose, and limbs, we are greatly encumbered by our endowment of material force and physical constitution. Principle in its unity has never been divided, yet our endowment of material force can encumber us. Thus there are those who incline excessively toward firmness, those who incline excessively toward yielding, those whose firmness is evil and those whose yielding is evil, and those whose firmness or yielding is good yet fails to attain due measure. When the nature is stirred, good and evil diverge; when external things act upon us, the myriad affairs arise. At the beginning there is unity, but subsequently there is multiplication—twofold, fivefold, tenfold, a hundredfold [?], a thousandfold, ten thousandfold—until the variations are inexhaustible. Could this be the original condition of principle? Should what all people alike follow be like this?

At birth, the sage receives what is most refined and most spiritually perceptive. With his material force clear and luminous and his constitution pure, he has never been subject to their constraints; nor can desires for external things obscure him. Thus his mind embraces the Great Void: this is the substance of the one principle. His person embodies every goodness: this is the functioning of the one principle. Substance and functioning have one source, and between the manifest and the subtle there is no separation: this is the ceaseless circulation of the one principle. In carrying things out, he attains due measure; in dealing with them, he is correct; in expressing himself, he is benevolent; in making judgments, he is righteous. What he preserves within and what he expresses outwardly differ, yet their principle is one. His human relationships are those of ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife, and friend and friend; his conduct…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
孝友睦婣任恤其文易詩書禮樂春秋其教文
行忠信其政工虞教養其功化位育參贊其用
不同而理亦一也是其所存主而發用也猶陰
陽動靜而五氣布四時行也聖人則亦天而已
矣夫豈於性分之外別有所加哉是故賢者此
理愚者亦此理古人此理今人亦此理而由之
云者獨歸于聖人愚所以深為夫人慨也雖然
聖人亦為夫人者慨之也于是乎有人極之立
焉主靜云者又人極之所以立也不專一則不
===
能直遂不翕聚則不能發散夫天亦靜而已矣
太極先體而應用民生因情以鑿性故聖人主
靜以立體而所謂中正仁義之德無一不本於
是焉定其所未定齊其所未齊而天下之人一
矣何也靜可以制動一可以統萬也然又豈聖
人強彼之所無分我之所有以予之哉一理之
由天下所共至是始各得其分焉耳天下各得
其分而聖人亦不得而踰焉聖人所由之理豈
有二哉是故惟精惟一允執厥中堯舜之所由

punctuated:
孝友睦婣任恤，其文《易》《詩》《書》《禮》《樂》《春秋》，其教文行忠信，其政工虞教養，其功化位育參贊。其用不同，而理亦一也。是其所存主而發用也，猶陰陽動靜而五氣布、四時行也。聖人則亦天而已矣，夫豈於性分之外別有所加哉？是故賢者此理，愚者亦此理；古人此理，今人亦此理。而由之云者，獨歸于聖人，愚所以深為夫人慨也。雖然，聖人亦為夫人者慨之也。于是乎有人極之立焉。主靜云者，又人極之所以立也。
不專一則不能直遂，不翕聚則不能發散。夫天亦靜而已矣。太極先體而應用，民生因情以鑿性，故聖人主靜以立體，而所謂中正仁義之德，無一不本於是焉。定其所未定，齊其所未齊，而天下之人一矣。何也？靜可以制動，一可以統萬也。然又豈聖人強彼之所無，分我之所有以予之哉？一理之由，天下所共，至是始各得其分焉耳。天下各得其分，而聖人亦不得而踰焉。聖人所由之理，豈有二哉？是故惟精惟一，允執厥中，堯舜之所由
translation_en:
…filial devotion, brotherly affection, harmony among kin, amity through marriage, trustworthiness, and relief of those in need. His cultural writings are the Changes, Odes, Documents, Rites, Music, and Spring and Autumn Annals; his teachings concern cultural learning, conduct, loyalty, and trustworthiness; his government concerns crafts, management of natural resources, education, and sustenance; his achievements consist in transforming people, bringing heaven and earth into their proper places and nurturing all things, and assisting the work of cosmic transformation. These functions differ, yet their principle is likewise one. What he preserves and takes as his guiding principle, and then brings into operation, is like yin and yang in movement and stillness, through which the five vital energies spread and the four seasons proceed. The sage is simply Heaven itself. How could he have anything added beyond his endowed nature? Thus the worthy possess this principle, and so do the foolish; the ancients possessed it, and so do people today. Yet following it is attributed to the sage alone: this is why I, in my ignorance, grieve deeply for people. Nevertheless, the sage also grieves for them. Hence the ultimate standard for humanity is established. What is called giving primacy to stillness is, moreover, the means by which this standard is established.
Without concentration upon unity, there can be no direct advance; without gathering inward, there can be no outward diffusion. Heaven, too, is simply stillness. The Supreme Ultimate gives priority to substance and responds through function; people, in living, injure their nature through their feelings. Therefore the sage gives primacy to stillness in order to establish substance, and none of the virtues called centrality, correctness, humaneness, and righteousness fails to be rooted in this. He settles what is not yet settled and brings into alignment what is not yet aligned, so that all people under Heaven become one. Why is this? Stillness can govern movement, and unity can command the myriad. Yet how could the sage force upon others something they do not possess, dividing what he himself possesses to give it to them? Following the one principle is common to all under Heaven; only at this point does each fully realize his own allotted share. When all under Heaven realize their allotted shares, even the sage cannot exceed his. Could there be two principles that the sage follows? Thus, “Be discerning, be single-minded, and truly hold fast to the mean”: what Yao and Shun followed …

…the Han dynasty [?]?

Associate Examiner Jin 金, an Examining Editor, comments: “Its adherence to classical standards amid ornate parallel prose is commendable.”

Associate Examiner Liu, a Compiler, comments: “It does not pursue flowery embellishment. In reading it, one clearly perceives the intention of a Confucian minister to use the occasion to offer loyal counsel.”

Examiner Gu, an Academician, comments: “Though written in ornate parallel prose, it has a substantial and dignified spirit. It may serve as a model.”

Examiner Jin 靳, a Grand Secretary, comments: “This is one instance of our sagely founder’s honoring letters and diligently pursuing learning. Loyal devotion should be conveyed within the praise of his virtue; this composition achieves that.”

On an unspecified month and day in the third year of Hongwu [1370], your servants Song Lian and others, Academicians of the Hanlin Academy, humbly observed that the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi) had been inscribed on the walls of the two side galleries of the inner hall. We respectfully present this memorial of congratulation.

We humbly consider: as your sagely learning is daily renewed, you apprehend upon your embroidered throne the subtle meaning of the books; as your imperial residence is opened by Heaven, the vermilion writing makes resplendent the admonitory inscriptions at doors and windows. Only a true king can find a teacher for himself; none but a great sage could undertake such a work. Thus you elucidate the Canon of Shun: how could this be called mere ornamental elaboration? Your servants Lian and the others, truly joyful and truly delighted, bow our heads to the ground, again and again.

We respectfully reflect that this work, the Extended Meaning, truly elucidates the Great…
