學之道。雖三綱八目悉祖舊文，而奧旨微詞更無餘蘊。觀其所分四要，庶幾作宋一經。首撮聖賢性命道德之言，旁采古今治亂安危之迹。凡儒先之講明，悉加檃括；于邪正之情狀，尤極形容。蘊于心，則天德之純；達於治，則王道之大。淵源遠矣，信東魯教人之準繩；事理燦然，尤南面臨民之龜鑑。慨惟真氏志在格君，獻曝之忱于中徒切，納約之效沒世無聞。遭逢雖厄于當時，顯晦亦關乎氣數。豈意百年之素願，受知千載之明時！
茲盖伏遇皇帝陛下，聰明睿知，文武聖神。再造寰區，與天地而同大；長舒臨照，合日月以為明。修乾坤既墜之綱常，復帝王已淪之土宇。功高千古，德冠羣倫。竊窺撥亂反正之鴻模，已協聖經
translation_en:
…the Way of the Great Learning. Although its Three Guiding Principles and Eight Steps all derive from the original text, it leaves none of that text’s profound meanings and subtle expressions unexplored. Considering the four essentials into which it is divided, it might almost constitute a classic of the Song dynasty. It first gathers the sages’ and worthies’ pronouncements on human nature, destiny, the Way, and virtue, and draws broadly upon instances of order and disorder, security and peril, past and present. It distills all that earlier Confucian scholars elucidated, and describes with particular thoroughness the dispositions and manifestations of perversity and uprightness. Stored within the heart, these teachings constitute the purity of Heaven’s virtue; expressed in government, they constitute the grandeur of the kingly Way. Their sources reach far back: truly they provide the standard by which the master of eastern Lu taught others. Their principles shine clearly: above all, they offer a mirror for the ruler who faces south to govern his people. We reflect with regret that Master Zhen aspired to rectify his sovereign, yet his earnest wish to offer his humble insight—like a rustic offering the warmth of the sun—remained merely fervent within him; throughout his life, no successful effect of his sincere, unadorned counsel was heard of. Though his circumstances were constrained in his own time, recognition and obscurity also depend upon the cycles of fortune. Who could have imagined that his long-cherished wish, after a hundred years, would find recognition in an enlightened age such as comes once in a thousand years!
Now we have humbly had the fortune to encounter Your Majesty the Emperor, perceptive, wise, discerning, accomplished in civil and martial affairs, sagely and inspired. You have created the realm anew, matching Heaven and Earth in greatness; your enduring illumination joins the sun and moon in brilliance. You have restored the cardinal relationships and constant moral principles that had fallen into decay between Heaven and Earth, and recovered the territories of emperors and kings that had been lost. Your achievements surpass those of all antiquity; your virtue excels that of all others. We humbly discern that your grand design for quelling disorder and restoring proper rule already accords with the sages’ classics…

translation_en:
…the essential purport of the commentaries of the worthies. This indeed is Heaven-given; how could it be achieved by human effort alone? Recently, an insight was incidentally presented and fortunately received Your Majesty’s gracious acceptance. You took up the book to read it, penetrating its subtlest meanings, and declared that cultivation pursued along these lines should continue without interruption. On the day the inner hall was completed, You established a practice unprecedented among former rulers, specially commanding Your close ministers to inscribe the text in large characters on the corridor walls. Its radiance shines like the Milky Way, before which even Shun’s painted colors pale; with divine presences ascending and descending, it solemnly recalls the constant contemplation enjoined by the inscription on Tang’s washbasin. It never leaves the place where You rise early and remain diligent late into the night, and constantly meets Your gaze in intervals of leisure from holding court. Entering the eyes, it admonishes the heart, everywhere providing the assistance of cutting and polishing in self-cultivation. Taking present circumstances as the measure and weighing ancient precedents, You constantly devise ways for the people to cherish the worthy and rejoice in their benefits. Your government is already without fault, and Your learning yields further gains.
Looking reverently upon this communion between sage and worthy, how does it differ from ruler and minister journeying together? The undertaking has never been heard of before; their accord in the Way arises from within. Abiding where one should abide, You thus attain the blessing of resting in the highest good; renewing Yourself again and again, You further extend the transforming influence that renews the people. Surveying former ages, we find them all inferior. The profuse splendor of Renshou Palace indulged an extravagant heart in useless things; how did the magnificence of Weiyang Palace help make the virtue of frugality manifest? Moreover, this comes just after the dynastic tripods have been established, at the very beginning of the undertaking to build at Luo. Here one sees that August Heaven’s favor and mandate are assuredly no accident, and that the inauguration of peace for ten thousand generations has a genuine foundation. We, Your servants, unworthily holding offices in the Hanlin Academy, have personally encountered…

…the splendor of the civil and military achievements and virtues of our Sagely Founder: he can recount their particulars distinctly, and may indeed be called well versed in historical precedents.

Associate Examiner Yin, Compiler, comments: “The vast scope of our Sagely Founder’s achievements and virtues is not easily described. This composition manages to set them forth and expound them at length—an accomplishment indeed difficult to achieve. Moreover, his work in the preceding two sessions was exceptionally refined and outstanding. Who could say it is unfitting to rank him first in the empire?”

Associate Examiner Liu, Compiler, comments: “Reading examination scripts these past several days has been like sifting sand for gold. Late in the process we obtained this script, which all pronounced exquisite and beyond price. Furthermore, the five policy essays display learning, discernment, and ability in statecraft. Regrettably, we cannot print them all, but this one gives some sense of the whole.”

Associate Examiner Teng, Librarian, comments: “Few candidates can recount and reverently embrace our Imperial Founder’s achievements and virtues as this author does. Moreover, his work in all three sessions is comprehensive, learned, and elegant. How could he be unworthy of a recommendation for high rank?”

Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: “In expounding the splendor of the Sagely Founder’s achievements and virtues, he may be said to grasp what is most significant. His writing is expansive and learned, commensurate with its subject. Might he be one who has accumulated learning and awaits his opportunity [?]? His expositions on the Classics and his memorial are also excellent. Regrettably, we cannot print them all.”

Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: “This script is outstanding in all three sessions. This particular policy essay is especially accomplished in extolling the splendor of our Sagely Founder’s perfect civil and military virtues. No one could replace you as the first choice in the Metropolitan Examination.”

In ruling all under Heaven, emperors and kings possess sagely civil virtue and divine martial prowess. What is meant by sagely civil virtue? It is ordering Heaven and Earth. title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
聖祖文武之全德則上與帝王同而功尤過焉
豈漢唐諸君所能及哉嗚呼盛矣請敢陳
之人君為治非文無以成大化非武無以
戒不虞故書稱堯曰乃武乃文盖帝王之
全德莫之尚也至于有周文王曰文以丕
顯之謨也然觀詩有遏密之詠書有戡黎
之言則穆穆之文豈不足於武乎武王曰
武以丕承之烈也然觀訪洪範于箕子受
丹書於太公則桓桓之武豈不足於文乎
===
二聖人之於堯盖異世而同符也自是而
後則不然矣彼唐文宗之優柔不斷武宗
之崇尚清虛其各以文武見稱固不必論
也而漢文帝之禮樂未遑武帝之海內虛
耗亦豈其盡美者哉若唐之太宗身兼將
相功德俱隆固一代帝王之冠冕也然遼
左黷兵豈盡順天應人之舉閨門慚德豈
有純一不已之誠進之於周亦碔砆之於
美玉耳豈其倫哉此文武之全德所以必

之宗尚清虛其各以文武見稱固不必論

punctuated:
聖祖文武之全德，則上與帝王同，而功尤過焉，豈漢唐諸君所能及哉？嗚呼，盛矣！請敢陳之。

人君為治，非文無以成大化，非武無以戒不虞。故《書》稱堯曰：「乃武乃文。」盖帝王之全德，莫之尚也。至于有周，文王曰文，以丕顯之謨也。然觀《詩》有遏密之詠，《書》有戡黎之言，則穆穆之文，豈不足於武乎？武王曰武，以丕承之烈也。然觀訪《洪範》于箕子，受《丹書》於太公，則桓桓之武，豈不足於文乎？二聖人之於堯，盖異世而同符也。

自是而後，則不然矣。彼唐文宗之優柔不斷，武宗之崇尚清虛，其各以文武見稱，固不必論也。而漢文帝之禮樂未遑，武帝之海內虛耗，亦豈其盡美者哉？若唐之太宗，身兼將相，功德俱隆，固一代帝王之冠冕也。然遼左黷兵，豈盡順天應人之舉？閨門慚德，豈有純一不已之誠？進之於周，亦碔砆之於美玉耳，豈其倫哉？此文武之全德所以必
translation_en:
…the complete civil and martial virtue of our Sagely Ancestor equals that of the ancient emperors and kings, while his achievements surpass theirs. How could the rulers of Han and Tang attain to it? Ah, how magnificent! Permit me to venture an account.

When a ruler governs, without civil virtue he cannot accomplish the great work of moral transformation; without martial virtue he cannot guard against unforeseen dangers. Thus the Book of Documents praises Yao, saying, “Both martial and civil.” Nothing surpasses this complete virtue of emperors and kings. Coming to the Zhou, King Wen was called “Civil” because of his greatly illustrious plans. Yet the Book of Odes sings of his silencing and stilling, and the Book of Documents speaks of his conquest of Li. Could his reverent civil virtue, then, have been deficient in martial virtue? King Wu was called “Martial” because of his glorious achievement in carrying forward his predecessor’s work. Yet he consulted Jizi about the Great Plan and received the Cinnabar Writing from Taigong. Could his majestic martial virtue, then, have been deficient in civil virtue? These two sages and Yao lived in different ages, yet their virtues corresponded like matching tallies.

After this, however, things were otherwise. Tang Wenzong was irresolute and indecisive, while Wuzong prized purity and emptiness. That they were respectively styled “Civil” and “Martial” scarcely merits discussion. Yet Han Wendi had no leisure for rites and music, and Wudi depleted the resources of the realm: how could either have attained perfection? As for Tang Taizong, he combined in his own person the capacities of general and chief minister, and both his achievements and his virtue were eminent. He was assuredly the foremost sovereign of his dynasty. Yet was his reckless warfare in Liaozuo entirely an undertaking that accorded with Heaven and answered the wishes of the people? With shameful failings in his conduct within the household, could he possess sincerity that was pure, undivided, and unceasing? Set beside the Zhou kings, he was merely a jade-like stone beside fine jade. How could he rank with them? This is why the complete possession of civil and martial virtue must…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
我
聖祖出而後於帝王無愧焉何者胡元之亂生
民以来所未有也夫以犬羊之桀亂華猾
夏入為中國之主變衣冠於左衽汚俎豆
于腥羶三綱盡淪九法俱斁天地於是乎
易位日月於是乎晦冥且遲遲於百年之
久老者日以逝少者日以長幾何不盡淪
於禽獸異類也哉惟我
聖祖大德受命驅其種類返其故域復我二帝
===
===
三王之境土明我天地開闢以来之彜倫
功德之盛亦生民以来所未有也
聖文神武之德雖曰難名而父老之所傳聞學
士先民之所叙載亦有可得而言者蓋弔
伐之師有征無戰一舉而江漢清再駕而
吳會平三征而閩越歸命四伐而荆湖率
從中原之師兵不血刃太平之績一怒而
成執事以為武略天授是固然矣而愚則
以為此神武之末事非其至也

於禽獸異類也哉惟我
聖祖大德受命驅其種類返其故域復我二帝

從中原之師兵不血刃太平之績一怒而
成執事以為武略天授是固然矣而愚則
以為此神武之事非其至也
punctuated:
我聖祖出而後於帝王無愧焉。何者？胡元之亂，生民以来所未有也。夫以犬羊之桀，亂華猾夏，入為中國之主，變衣冠於左衽，汚俎豆于腥羶，三綱盡淪，九法俱斁，天地於是乎易位，日月於是乎晦冥。且遲遲於百年之久，老者日以逝，少者日以長，幾何不盡淪於禽獸異類也哉！惟我聖祖大德受命，驅其種類，返其故域，復我二帝三王之境土，明我天地開闢以来之彜倫，功德之盛，亦生民以来所未有也。
聖文神武之德，雖曰難名，而父老之所傳聞、學士先民之所叙載，亦有可得而言者。蓋弔伐之師，有征無戰，一舉而江漢清，再駕而吳會平，三征而閩越歸命，四伐而荆湖率從。中原之師，兵不血刃，太平之績，一怒而成。執事以為武略天授，是固然矣，而愚則以為此神武之末事，非其至也。
translation_en:
…only when our Sagely Progenitor arose could he stand without shame among the emperors and kings. Why was this? The disorder wrought by the barbarian Yuan was unprecedented since humankind first came into being. Those brutes, like dogs and sheep, brought turmoil to Hua and disorder to Xia, entering to become masters of the Central Kingdom. They changed its caps and robes to garments fastening on the left and polluted its sacrificial vessels with rank, reeking flesh. The Three Bonds were utterly submerged, and the Nine Norms wholly corrupted. Heaven and earth thereby exchanged places; sun and moon thereby grew dark. Moreover, this dragged on for a full hundred years. Day by day the old passed away and the young grew up. How close were all to sinking into the condition of birds, beasts, and alien kinds! Our Sagely Progenitor alone, through his great virtue, received the Mandate, drove out their kind and returned them to their former territory, restored the lands of our Two Emperors and Three Kings, and made manifest the enduring human relationships established since heaven and earth first opened. The greatness of his achievements and virtue was likewise unprecedented since humankind first came into being.
Although the virtue of his sagely civil accomplishments and divine martial prowess is said to defy description, something can nevertheless be said from what the elders have handed down and what scholars and worthy predecessors have recorded. His army, bringing relief to the afflicted and punishment to the guilty, went forth to chastise and met no resistance in battle. With its first advance, Jianghan was cleared; with its second expedition, Wuhui was pacified; with its third campaign, Minyue submitted to his authority; with its fourth attack, Jinghu followed in allegiance. In the campaign in the Central Plain, the soldiers did not bloody their blades. The achievement of Great Peace was accomplished in a single outburst of wrath. You, sir, consider his military strategy Heaven-bestowed. That is certainly so; yet I, in my humble view, regard this as merely a peripheral manifestation of his divine martial prowess, not its highest expression.

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
萬幾之暇親洒宸翰體裁迥別援筆立成若
大祀文有我將之誠大誥三篇有夙愆之訓註
洪範而遠傳箕子之心定書傳而近糾蔡
沉之失醉學士歌虞廷明良之氣象也閱
江樓記周公相洛之謀猷也執事以為文
章出於天性是亦然矣而愚則以為此聖
文之餘緒非其大也蓋我
聖祖因元政之不綱憫生民之無主其舉義也
以救民為心其為治也以綱常為重取中
===
國之人民而冠裳之取三代之禮樂而損
益之禁兄弟之婚均父母之服合天地之
祀而金人祀天之陋習已除正神祇之號
而王公帝后之瀆禮盡革設官則六卿分
職無專任之患紀元則一定不易無數改
之煩禮儀有定式上下有章矣洪武有正
韻遠邇同文矣罷黜異論表章經籍嚴重
典以懲愚頑尊高年以彰有德乾坤為之
再造日月為之重光若此者所謂經天緯

以救民為心其為治也以綱常為重取中
===

益之禁兄弟之婚均父母之服合天地之
祀而金人祀天之陋習已除正神祇之號
而王公帝后之瀆禮盡革設官則六卿分
職無專任之患紀元則一定不易無數改
之煩禮儀有定式上下有章矣洪武有正
韻遠邇同文矣罷黜異論表章經籍嚴重
典以懲愚頑尊高年以彰有德乾坤為之
再造日月為之重光若此者所謂經天緯
punctuated:
萬幾之暇，親洒宸翰，體裁迥別，援筆立成。若大祀文，有《我將》之誠；《大誥》三篇，有夙愆之訓；註《洪範》，而遠傳箕子之心；定《書傳》，而近糾蔡沉之失。《醉學士歌》，虞廷明良之氣象也；《閱江樓記》，周公相洛之謀猷也。執事以為文章出於天性，是亦然矣，而愚則以為此聖文之餘緒，非其大也。
蓋我聖祖因元政之不綱，憫生民之無主，其舉義也，以救民為心；其為治也，以綱常為重。取中國之人民而冠裳之，取三代之禮樂而損益之。禁兄弟之婚，均父母之服；合天地之祀，而金人祀天之陋習已除；正神祇之號，而王公帝后之瀆禮盡革。設官則六卿分職，無專任之患；紀元則一定不易，無數改之煩。禮儀有定式，上下有章矣；洪武有正韻，遠邇同文矣。罷黜異論，表章經籍；嚴重典以懲愚頑，尊高年以彰有德。乾坤為之再造，日月為之重光。若此者，所謂經天緯
translation_en:
In moments of leisure amid the myriad affairs of government, he personally wielded the imperial brush. His compositions were distinctive in form and style, completed as soon as he took up his brush. His text for the Great Sacrifice possessed the sincerity of the ode “I Bring My Offerings” (Wo jiang); the three parts of his Grand Pronouncements (Da gao) offered admonitions concerning past faults. In annotating the Great Plan (Hong fan), he transmitted the intent of Jizi from the distant past; in settling the Commentary on the Documents (Shu zhuan), he corrected the errors of the more recent Cai Chen. His Song of the Drunken Academician evoked the enlightened ruler and worthy ministers at the court of Shun; his Record of the River-Viewing Tower embodied the strategic foresight of the Duke of Zhou when he surveyed Luo. You, sir, consider his literary accomplishments to have sprung from his innate nature. This is indeed true, but I humbly regard these as merely incidental expressions of his sagely literary virtue, rather than its greatness.
Our Sagely Progenitor, seeing the disorder of Yuan government, pitied the people for having no true ruler. When he raised his righteous forces, his purpose was to save the people; when he governed, he placed foremost the cardinal relationships and constant moral principles. He clothed the people of the Central Kingdom in proper caps and robes, and adapted the rites and music of the Three Dynasties through judicious additions and omissions. He prohibited marriages involving brothers [?] and made mourning for fathers and mothers equal. He combined the sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, eliminating the crude practices of the Jin people's worship of Heaven. He rectified the titles of the gods and spirits, entirely abolishing the irreverent practice of styling them kings, dukes, emperors, and empresses. In establishing offices, he divided responsibilities among the Six Ministers, avoiding the danger of entrusting authority exclusively to one man. In naming his reign era, he fixed it once and left it unchanged, avoiding the trouble of repeated alterations. Ritual and ceremony had prescribed forms, giving superiors and inferiors established rules; the Hongwu reign had its Correct Rhymes, bringing distant and nearby regions into a shared written culture. He rejected heterodox doctrines and promoted the canonical writings. He enforced severe laws to punish the ignorant and recalcitrant, and honored the elderly to give recognition to virtue. translation_en:
…their people would not suffice to serve us. I fear that later generations, relying on the wealth and strength of China, will raise armies without cause and thereby harm human lives. Remember well: this must not be done.” This expresses a resolve to end warfare and carries forward the spirit of returning the horses and releasing the oxen. Master Dong said: “Yang always occupies the height of summer and takes producing, nurturing, and fostering growth as its work; yin always occupies the depth of winter and is relegated to an empty place where it is not employed.” This shows that Heaven relies on virtue, not punishment. Warfare is the gravest form of punishment. Was not the intention of our Sagely Progenitor the very intention of Heaven? If we reverently uphold it without fail, we can fulfill Heaven’s intention above and inspire sincerity among the common people below; even peace for ten thousand generations would be possible. The Book of Odes says: “Neither erring nor forgetting, follow the established rules.” I venture to offer this to the imperial throne.

則所以明夫執中之功必如是而後盡也
哲人旣頹異端並起于是子思推本聖賢
相傳之意質以平日所聞父師之言而中
庸作焉其言切其說詳非得已也若擇善

punctuated: 以「人心惟危，道心惟微，惟精惟一」之三言，則所以明夫執中之功必如是而後盡也。哲人旣頹，異端並起，于是子思推本聖賢相傳之意，質以平日所聞父師之言，而《中庸》作焉。其言切，其說詳，非得已也。若「擇善固執」、「君子時中」之言，盖即精一執中之謂。即其言，可以知其傳之有在矣。一書之中，至德至誠之道，其言高矣，然皆自誠而明之事，而自明而誠者，入德之方，則未有詳於「尊德性，道問學」之一章。《章句》謂尊德性所以存心而極道體之大，道問學所以致知而盡道體之細，又以其下八者為存心致知之屬。盖必如是，則大小相資，首尾相應，德脩道凝，而動罔非中矣。此作聖之極功，雖至聖至誠，亦由是至焉。盖求之千載之前，則存心云者，即所以惟一之功；致知云者，即所以惟精之功也。其於三聖人之言，實有據矣。求之千載之下，則程子所謂

…with the three statements, “The human mind is precarious; the mind of the Way is subtle; be discerning and single-minded.” These clarify that the work of holding fast to the Mean can be fully accomplished only in this way. Once the sage had passed away and heterodox teachings arose together, Zisi traced back the meaning transmitted among the sages and worthies and verified it against the words he had regularly heard from his father and teachers. Thus he composed the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong). His words were pointed and his explanations detailed: he could not do otherwise. Statements such as “choose what is good and hold firmly to it” and “the gentleman accords with the Mean as circumstances require” refer precisely to being discerning and single-minded and holding fast to the Mean. From these words we can recognize that this transmission had a firm foundation.
Throughout the book, its discussion of the way of consummate virtue and consummate sincerity is lofty. Yet these are all matters of proceeding from sincerity to understanding. As for proceeding from understanding to sincerity—the method of entering into virtue—nowhere is this explained more fully than in the chapter on “honoring one’s virtuous nature and pursuing inquiry and learning.” The Commentary in Chapters and Sentences (Zhangju) says that honoring one’s virtuous nature is the means of preserving the mind and fully realizing the vastness of the substance of the Way, while pursuing inquiry and learning is the means of extending knowledge and exhausting the subtleties of the substance of the Way. It further classifies the eight items that follow under preserving the mind and extending knowledge. Only in this way can the great and the small support one another and beginning and end correspond, so that virtue is cultivated, the Way is firmly established, and every action accords with the Mean. This is the consummate work of becoming a sage. Even consummate sageliness and sincerity are attained by this means.
Looking back a thousand years, what is called preserving the mind is precisely the work of being single-minded, and what is called extending knowledge is precisely the work of being discerning. 之而為典學之訓周公得之而為禮樂之

translation_en:
…“In nurturing oneself, one must employ reverence” refers precisely to this honoring of one’s moral nature; “Advancement in learning lies in extending knowledge” refers precisely to this pursuit of inquiry and study. How could their meanings differ? Viewed in this way, the thousand sages share one mind, and through all ages there is one principle: their standard is the same. Tang attained this learning and accomplished deeds that reached Heaven; Wu attained it and ruled with his robes hanging loose and his hands folded. Here we can find evidence of fully developed talent manifested in rulers. Yi Yin attained it and assisted his ruler with undivided virtue; Fu Yue attained it and offered instruction on steadfast learning; the Duke of Zhou attained it and brought about transformation through rites and music; the Duke of Shao attained it and delivered an admonition on reverence for virtue. Here we can find evidence of fully developed talent manifested in ministers. Is this not the basis for my humble claim that, when the learning of the sages is made clear, fully developed talent emerges?

Master Zhu also said that after Mengzi died, the learning of the sages ceased to be transmitted. This too is an unalterable judgment. For a thousand desolate years after the Qin burning of the books, no age lacked classical scholars and men of letters; yet they lived as if drunk and died as if dreaming, with no real insight into the Way. Let us set aside for now Xunzi’s doctrine that human nature is evil and Yang Xiong’s praise of the Xin dynasty. Master Dong was a Confucian of pure learning in the Han dynasty, and he advanced the teaching that one should rectify one’s mind in order to rectify the court. This seems to accord with the sages’ learning. Yet to speak of rectifying the mind without speaking of making reverence one’s guiding principle is not Zisi’s learning of honoring one’s moral nature. Master Han was a great Confucian of the Tang dynasty, and he was also able to address the Great Learning’s discussion of making one’s intentions sincere. This seems to accord with the sages’ learning. Yet to speak of making one’s intentions sincere without addressing the investigation of things is not Zisi’s learning of extending knowledge. Thus, what they…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
得終未離乎言語文字之間而謂其於□
學有傳可乎若夫孔明三代之遺才靜以
成學學以廣才之二言盖其所自得者然
靜不可以言存心之功則其大本固已異
矣又其讀書獨觀大旨則所以致其知者
亦何以悉事理之詳耶故其天資之美足
為王佐之才而取劉璋寫刑書則未免為
王道之累此固亦血氣用事與聖人之所
為異矣出處正大事業光明雖曰庶幾禮
===
樂而比之博厚配地高明配天功用所極
直與天地同流者又惡可並論也哉愚所
謂聖學晦而全才無聞焉於此又可見矣
此孔氏真傳所以斷斷乎必有待於程子
而後續也若乃朱子之於程子盖猶禹之
於舜舜之於堯其授受之的固也章句存
心致知之云實本程子涵養進學之論非
朱子一人之私言也顧其道雖同而其時
則異矣偽學之禁既啓于王淮太極之論

punctuated:
得終未離乎言語文字之間，而謂其於□學有傳，可乎？若夫孔明，三代之遺才，靜以成學、學以廣才之二言，盖其所自得者。然靜不可以言存心之功，則其大本固已異矣。又其讀書獨觀大旨，則所以致其知者，亦何以悉事理之詳耶？故其天資之美，足為王佐之才，而取劉璋、寫刑書，則未免為王道之累。此固亦血氣用事，與聖人之所為異矣。出處正大，事業光明，雖曰庶幾禮樂，而比之博厚配地、高明配天、功用所極直與天地同流者，又惡可並論也哉？愚所謂聖學晦而全才無聞焉，於此又可見矣。此孔氏真傳所以斷斷乎必有待於程子而後續也。
若乃朱子之於程子，盖猶禹之於舜，舜之於堯，其授受之的固也。《章句》存心致知之云，實本程子涵養進學之論，非朱子一人之私言也。顧其道雖同，而其時則異矣。偽學之禁既啓于王淮，太極之論
translation_en:
…what they attained ultimately remained within the realm of words and writing. Can one therefore say that they transmitted the learning of □ [?]? As for Kongming, a talent surviving from the Three Dynasties, his two statements, “Through stillness, bring learning to fruition” and “Through learning, broaden one’s abilities,” surely expressed insights he had attained for himself. Yet stillness cannot adequately describe the work of preserving the mind; thus his fundamental basis was already different. Moreover, in reading he looked only to the broad purport. How, then, could his means of extending knowledge encompass the details of the principles governing affairs? His excellent natural endowments qualified him to assist a true king, yet his seizure of Liu Zhang’s territory and his writing of a penal code inevitably compromised the Kingly Way. Here, too, he acted under the sway of his physical impulses, differing from the conduct of the sages. His decisions to serve or withdraw were upright and honorable, and his achievements bright and clear. Although these might be said to approach the ideals of ritual and music, how could he be placed on a par with one whose breadth and depth match Earth, whose loftiness and brilliance match Heaven, and whose efficacy ultimately flows together with Heaven and Earth? Here again we can see what I humbly meant in saying that the learning of the sages had become obscure and fully accomplished talents were no longer heard of. This is why the true transmission of Confucius assuredly had to await Master Cheng before it could be continued.
As for Master Zhu’s relationship to Master Cheng, it was like Yu’s to Shun and Shun’s to Yao: the authenticity of their transmission was secure. The statements in the Commentary in Chapters and Sentences concerning preserving the mind and extending knowledge were indeed based on Master Cheng’s discussion of nurturing one’s moral nature and advancing in learning; they were not merely Master Zhu’s personal opinions. Yet although their Way was the same, their times differed. The prohibition of “spurious learning” had already begun with Wang Huai, and the discussion of the Supreme Ultimate…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
復疑于陸氏伊洛一脉不絕如綫其憂深
慮遠以為世道計者又豈能在子思下耶
其所以為章句為或問者正欲是學常明
于世耳聖賢繼往開來拳拳之盛心未可
以孔子罕言性命者例論也夫惟精惟一
而執中存心致知而時中其旨一也夫何
雙峯饒氏乃有疑於存心致知之言倡為
異說以誤後學且願為朱子之忠臣其亦
不思甚矣夫學至於朱子精矣粹矣使於
===
此猶有未融尚足以為朱子哉且饒氏之
論謂温故知新皆知之事不可以温故為
存心此一說也而不知吾心虛靈萬理畢
具良知良能何者非故况此心一放則昏
昧雜擾釋卷茫然以是為存心奚不可也
謂敦厚崇禮皆行之事不可以崇禮為致
知此又一說也不知三千三百之儀毫釐
之差千里之謬非辨析之精考索之當則
禮何以崇以是為致知亦奚不可也若饒

禮何以崇以是為致知亦奚不可也若饒
punctuated:
復疑于陸氏，伊洛一脉不絕如綫。其憂深慮遠，以為世道計者，又豈能在子思下耶？其所以為章句、為或問者，正欲是學常明于世耳。聖賢繼往開來拳拳之盛心，未可以孔子罕言性命者例論也。夫惟精惟一而執中，存心致知而時中，其旨一也。夫何雙峯饒氏乃有疑於存心致知之言，倡為異說以誤後學，且願為朱子之忠臣，其亦不思甚矣！夫學至於朱子，精矣，粹矣，使於此猶有未融，尚足以為朱子哉？

且饒氏之論，謂温故知新皆知之事，不可以温故為存心，此一說也。而不知吾心虛靈，萬理畢具，良知良能，何者非故？况此心一放，則昏昧雜擾，釋卷茫然，以是為存心，奚不可也？謂敦厚崇禮皆行之事，不可以崇禮為致知，此又一說也。不知三千三百之儀，毫釐之差，千里之謬，非辨析之精、考索之當，則禮何以崇？以是為致知，亦奚不可也？若饒
translation_en:
…was again called into question by Lu. The single thread of the tradition of Yi and Luo survived, tenuous as a strand of silk. In his profound concern and far-reaching deliberations for the moral order of the world, how could Zhu Xi have ranked below Zisi? His purpose in writing the Chapters and Sentences and the Questions and Answers was precisely to keep this learning ever clear in the world. The earnest devotion with which sages and worthies carried forward the past and opened the way for the future cannot be judged simply by the precedent of Confucius’s seldom speaking of human nature and Heaven’s decree. To be discerning and single-minded and thereby hold fast to the mean, and to preserve the mind and extend knowledge and thereby accord with the mean as circumstances require, have the same purport. Why, then, did Rao of Shuangfeng question the words about preserving the mind and extending knowledge, promoting divergent explanations that misled later students, while also aspiring to be Zhu Xi’s loyal minister? His failure to reflect was extreme indeed! With Zhu Xi, learning reached refinement and purity. If he had still failed to achieve full comprehension here, could he have deserved to be called Master Zhu?

Furthermore, Rao argues that reviewing the old and knowing the new both concern knowledge, and that reviewing the old therefore cannot be taken as preserving the mind. This is one of his claims. Yet he fails to understand that our mind is empty and numinously aware, fully endowed with all principles. Of its innate knowledge and innate capacities, which is not already there? Moreover, once this mind is let loose, it becomes benighted, confused, and disturbed; one puts down the book and is utterly at a loss. Why, then, should reviewing the old not be understood as preserving the mind? He says that deepening generosity and honoring ritual both concern practice, and that honoring ritual therefore cannot be taken as extending knowledge. This is another of his claims. He does not understand that, among the three thousand and three hundred ritual observances, a discrepancy of a hair’s breadth can lead to an error of a thousand li. Without precise discrimination and proper investigation, how can ritual be honored? Why, then, should this not also be understood as extending knowledge? As for Rao…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
氏者豈其徒知以章分句析為功而不知
以心領神契為得耶管窺蠡測舉一廢百
其亦不思甚矣嗣是諸儒蛙鳴蟬噪出口
入耳無足多論而獨其謂此章八者皆無
力行之事為朱子之小疵者則不可以不
辯蓋凡聖賢立言各有旨趣故有自下學
之功言者亦有自上達之妙言者不可拘
拘以一端論也若此章所言蓋專心學與
三聖人授受之意同非朱子之私言也今
===
夫精一之功無少間斷則動靜云為自無過
不及之差雖不言行而行在其中矣若以
朱子為疵則三聖人之說謬矣而亦可以
疵三聖人乎愚故曰惟精惟一而執中存
心致知而時中其言一也嗚呼安得起雙
峯諸子於九原而與之論哉至當歸一之
說朱子之章句固在學聖學者誠於此實
用其力而不已焉則能盡其性由是以盡
人物之性以成參贊之功如是而才不古

punctuated: 氏者，豈其徒知以章分句析為功，而不知以心領神契為得耶？管窺蠡測，舉一廢百，其亦不思甚矣！嗣是諸儒，蛙鳴蟬噪，出口入耳，無足多論。而獨其謂此章八者皆無力行之事，為朱子之小疵者，則不可以不辯。蓋凡聖賢立言，各有旨趣，故有自下學之功言者，亦有自上達之妙言者，不可拘拘以一端論也。若此章所言，蓋專心學，與三聖人授受之意同，非朱子之私言也。今夫精一之功，無少間斷，則動靜云為，自無過不及之差。雖不言行，而行在其中矣。若以朱子為疵，則三聖人之說謬矣，而亦可以疵三聖人乎？愚故曰：「惟精惟一而執中，存心致知而時中，其言一也。」嗚呼！安得起雙峯諸子於九原，而與之論哉！至當歸一之說，朱子之章句固在。學聖學者，誠於此實用其力而不已焉，則能盡其性，由是以盡人物之性，以成參贊之功。如是而才不古
translation_en:
…as for Master Rao, could it be that he knows only how to make a task of dividing chapters and analyzing sentences, but does not know that true attainment lies in apprehending their meaning in the heart and grasping it in spirit? Peering through a tube and measuring the sea with a ladle, he takes up one point and discards a hundred. His failure to reflect is extreme indeed! The scholars who followed him croaked like frogs and chirped like cicadas, their words passing from mouth to ear; they merit no lengthy discussion. Yet his assertion that none of the eight items in this chapter concerns putting learning vigorously into practice, and that this constitutes a minor flaw in Master Zhu, cannot go unanswered.

Whenever sages and worthies set forth their teachings, each pronouncement has its particular purport. Some speak from the perspective of the work of elementary learning; others speak from that of the subtleties of attaining higher understanding. One must not cling narrowly to a single aspect in judging them. What this chapter says is devoted specifically to the learning of the heart-mind. Its meaning accords with what the Three Sages transmitted to one another; it is no mere private pronouncement of Master Zhu. Now, if the work of refinement and singleness suffers not the slightest interruption, then in stillness and activity, speech and action, there will naturally be no error of excess or deficiency. Although practice is not explicitly mentioned, it is included within this. If one faults Master Zhu, then the teaching of the Three Sages must be erroneous too. But can one also fault the Three Sages?

Thus I humbly say: “To be refined and single-minded and thereby hold fast to the Mean, and to preserve the heart-mind and extend knowledge and thereby accord with the Mean as circumstances require, express the same teaching.” Alas! How might I raise Shuangfeng and the other masters from their graves and discuss this with them? As for the teaching that what is supremely fitting comes down to one principle, Master Zhu’s Commentary in Chapters and Sentences is certainly still available. If those who pursue the learning of the sages truly devote their efforts to this without ceasing, they will be able fully to realize their own nature. From this they can fully realize the natures of other people and things, and accomplish the work of participating in and assisting the transforming and nourishing powers of Heaven and Earth. If, having done this, their talents should fail to equal those of antiquity…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
若吾未之信也執事欲諸生極論以祛千
載之惑愚非其人也然一得之見言及之
亦不敢不言非好辯也誠慮聖學不明而
成才之方弗至也嗚呼是學明于一方則
一方之全才出矣是學明于一國則一國
之全才出矣是學明于天下則天下之全
才出矣夫天下之全才出而實本於聖學
之明然則君子奚容于無言哉
第三問
===
同考試官給事中黃批用人貴明安民

translation_en:
…would fall short of the ancients in talent—I cannot believe it. You, sir, wish the candidates to discuss this exhaustively, dispelling doubts that have persisted for a thousand years. I am not equal to that task. Yet, having gained this one insight, when the subject arises I dare not leave it unspoken. It is not that I delight in disputation: I truly fear that the learning of the sages may remain obscure and that the means of developing talent may not be fully realized. Alas! If this learning is made clear in one locality, people of fully developed talent will emerge there; if it is made clear in one state, such people will emerge throughout that state; if it is made clear throughout the realm, such people will emerge throughout the realm. The emergence of people of fully developed talent throughout the realm is, in truth, rooted in making the learning of the sages clear. How, then, can a gentleman remain silent?

Third Question

text:
君者以堯舜其所學可知矣
同考試官侍讀崔批策主仁智深達治
體而文復爾然
考試官學士顧批六經萬理皆具讀書
而不能處事者不善讀書者也觀知人安民
一策可以占子之他日矣
考試官大學士靳批書以道政事此策於

translation_en:
…for our ruler, he takes Yao and Shun as his models. From this one can discern the character of his learning.
Associate Examiner Cui, Reader-in-waiting, comments: This policy essay centers on benevolence and wisdom and shows a profound understanding of the essentials of government; its writing, moreover, is likewise so [?].
Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: The Six Classics contain all principles. Those who read books but cannot handle affairs have not read well. From this single policy essay on discerning people’s abilities and bringing peace to the people, one can foresee your future accomplishments.
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: The Documents expounds affairs of government. This policy essay treats the discerning of people’s abilities and the pacification of the people most appropriately. What its author has gained from the Classics seems far from shallow. We therefore publish it as a model for those who study the Classics but cannot manage the affairs of the world.
I have heard that the rule of Tang and Yu was the pinnacle of government, and that Yao and Shun were sages among sages. To govern without taking Yao and Shun as models is merely to muddle through. Can the government of Tang and Yu be restored? You gentlemen, examining candidates by policy questions at the spring Metropolitan Examination, have condescended to ask us students about the governance of discerning people’s abilities and bringing peace to the people. You lament the merely modest peace of the Western Han and long for the flourishing government of Tang and Yu. Furthermore, you wish us students to consult the Classics in answering. Thus you expect from us the genuine talent that understands the Classics and puts them to practical use. This is a most generous intention. I, in my ignorance, am not such a person; yet I dare not give up on myself. Allow me to answer by reference to the Documents of Yu. When Gao Yao set forth his counsels, he said: “It lies in discerning people’s abilities; it lies in bringing peace to the people.” He also said: “To discern people’s abilities is to be wise, and thus able to appoint people to office; to bring peace to the people is to be benevolent, so that the common people cherish him.” Now, to discern people’s abilities to the point of being able to appoint them to office cannot be accomplished without wisdom…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
也安民至於黎民懷之非仁不能也嗚呼
盡之矣雖然堯舜之所謂智非察察自用
之謂也惟不察察而以明目達聰為事故
後世知人者宜法焉堯舜之所謂仁非煦
煦姑息之謂也惟不煦煦而以博施濟衆
為功故後世安民者宜法焉今以唐虞之
治觀之堯日以舉舜為先舜舉則凡九官
十二牧之舉于舜者無弗當矣舜日以舉
禹臯陶為先禹臯陶舉則凡三德六德之舉
===
于禹臯陶者無弗當矣堯舜之智如此野
無遺賢庶績咸熙豈偶然哉當是之時典
樂有夔敷教有契風氣純固既與後世不
同造就長育又非後世可及人之才德兼
全又何怪哉才德二者之分在夏無聞其
見於書任官惟賢才左右惟其人商伊尹
之言也建官惟賢位事惟能周武成之誥
也豈至是始分乎然非才無以立事一於
任德而盡棄其才固不可非德無以善俗

punctuated:
也。安民至於黎民懷之，非仁不能也。嗚呼！盡之矣！雖然，堯舜之所謂智，非察察自用之謂也。惟不察察，而以明目達聰為事，故後世知人者宜法焉。堯舜之所謂仁，非煦煦姑息之謂也。惟不煦煦，而以博施濟衆為功，故後世安民者宜法焉。今以唐虞之治觀之，堯日以舉舜為先，舜舉，則凡九官十二牧之舉于舜者，無弗當矣。舜日以舉禹臯陶為先，禹臯陶舉，則凡三德六德之舉于禹臯陶者，無弗當矣。堯舜之智如此，野無遺賢，庶績咸熙，豈偶然哉？當是之時，典樂有夔，敷教有契，風氣純固，既與後世不同；造就長育，又非後世可及。人之才德兼全，又何怪哉？

才德二者之分，在夏無聞。其見於《書》，「任官惟賢才，左右惟其人」，商伊尹之言也；「建官惟賢，位事惟能」，周《武成》之誥也。豈至是始分乎？然非才無以立事，一於任德而盡棄其才，固不可；非德無以善俗，
translation_en:
…so it is. To bring peace to the people to the point that the common people cherish their ruler is impossible without benevolence. Ah! This says it all! Yet what Yao and Shun called wisdom did not mean scrutinizing every detail and relying solely on one’s own judgment. Precisely because they avoided such scrutiny and made it their task to broaden what they saw and heard, those in later ages who would discern worthy men should take them as their model. What Yao and Shun called benevolence did not mean petty kindness and indulgence. Precisely because they avoided such petty kindness and devoted their efforts to extending benefits widely and aiding the multitude, those in later ages who would bring peace to the people should take them as their model.

Consider the government of Tang and Yu. Yao daily gave priority to elevating Shun. Once Shun had been elevated, all those whom he appointed to the nine offices and the twelve regional governorships were appropriate choices. Shun daily gave priority to elevating Yu and Gao Yao. Once Yu and Gao Yao had been elevated, all those possessing three virtues or six virtues whom they appointed were appropriate choices. Such was the wisdom of Yao and Shun. No worthy man remained overlooked outside office, and every undertaking flourished. Could this have been accidental? At that time, Kui directed music, and Xie spread moral instruction. The prevailing customs were pure and steadfast, already unlike those of later ages; the cultivation and nurturing of men likewise surpassed anything later ages could achieve. Why, then, should it be surprising that men possessed both ability and virtue in full measure?

Of a distinction between ability and virtue, nothing is recorded under the Xia. As it appears in the Book of Documents, “In appointing officials, choose only the worthy and talented; for those at your side, choose suitable men”—these are the words of Yi Yin of the Shang. “In establishing offices, choose only the worthy; in assigning duties, choose only the capable”—this is the declaration in the Zhou chapter “Completion of the War.” Could the distinction have begun only then? Yet without ability, there is no means to accomplish affairs: it is certainly unacceptable to employ men solely for their virtue and entirely disregard their ability. Without virtue, there is no means to improve customs…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
一於用才而不知尊賢尤不可無已亦惟
求善用人之人而任之乎善用人之人盖
亦所謂智者之徒是也得是人而用之則
道自我行兼容噐使無不可矣後世稱知
人者吾得漢高焉蕭何當股肱之任張良
受心腹之託或賜劔履上殿或稱子房不
名所謂任賢勿貳者帝盖有之何首薦信
以成滅項之功晚又舉參以守畫一之法
良分王布越既成垓下之捷招致四皓又
===
有助於國本之定其所報効亦豈小哉帝
之任使如此彼平噲輩適足以充吾奔走
之役又何足為羣策之累乎不五載而成
炎漢之業帝之智雖非堯舜之比而實超
乎他人之上矣堯舜之安民也放勲之功
一本於如天之仁重華之績一本於好生
之德四凶退毒民者去矣八元舉愛民者
進矣敷典庸禮何者非化導之方五服五
刑何者非勸懲之具堯舜之仁如此四方

道自我行兼容器使無不可矣後世稱知

punctuated:
一於用才而不知尊賢，尤不可。無已，亦惟求善用人之人而任之乎？善用人之人，盖亦所謂智者之徒是也。得是人而用之，則道自我行，兼容噐使，無不可矣。後世稱知人者，吾得漢高焉。蕭何當股肱之任，張良受心腹之託，或賜劔履上殿，或稱子房不名，所謂任賢勿貳者，帝盖有之。何首薦信以成滅項之功，晚又舉參以守畫一之法。良分王布、越，既成垓下之捷，招致四皓，又有助於國本之定。其所報効，亦豈小哉！帝之任使如此，彼平、噲輩，適足以充吾奔走之役，又何足為羣策之累乎？不五載而成炎漢之業，帝之智雖非堯舜之比，而實超乎他人之上矣。
堯舜之安民也，放勲之功，一本於如天之仁；重華之績，一本於好生之德。四凶退，毒民者去矣；八元舉，愛民者進矣。敷典庸禮，何者非化導之方？五服五刑，何者非勸懲之具？堯舜之仁如此，四方
translation_en:
…To employ talent exclusively without knowing to honor the worthy is still less permissible. If one must pursue the matter further, should one not simply seek out and appoint someone skilled at employing others? Those skilled at employing others are surely among those called wise. Once such a person is found and employed, the Way can be put into practice through oneself; by accommodating people of diverse abilities and employing each according to his capacity, nothing will be beyond accomplishment.
Among men of later ages renowned for discerning others, I find Gaozu of Han. Xiao He shouldered the responsibilities of an indispensable minister, and Zhang Liang received the trust accorded an intimate confidant. The one was granted permission to ascend the palace hall wearing his sword and shoes; the other was addressed by his courtesy name, Zifang, rather than his personal name. The emperor indeed exemplified what is meant by “employing the worthy without wavering.” Xiao He first recommended Han Xin, thereby bringing about the destruction of Xiang Yu; later he recommended Cao Shen, thereby preserving the uniform laws. Zhang Liang arranged for territories to be apportioned and Ying Bu and Peng Yue to be made kings, thus securing victory at Gaixia. He also summoned the Four Hoary Elders, helping to secure the foundation of the state—the imperial succession. Could the service they rendered in return have been insignificant? Such was the emperor’s way of appointing and employing men. Men like Chen Ping and Fan Kuai were adequate to carry out his errands; how could they have encumbered the counsels of the assembled advisers? In fewer than five years he established the enterprise of the Han dynasty, associated with the virtue of Fire. Though the emperor’s wisdom could not compare with that of Yao and Shun, it far surpassed that of other men.
As for Yao and Shun’s bringing peace to the people, the achievements of Fangxun [Yao] were rooted entirely in benevolence as vast as Heaven; the accomplishments of Chonghua [Shun] were rooted entirely in the virtue of cherishing life. When the Four Villains were dismissed, those who harmed the people were removed; when the Eight Worthies were raised to office, those who loved the people were advanced. In promulgating the canonical norms and putting ritual into practice, what was not a means of transforming and guiding the people? Of the five grades of ceremonial dress and the five punishments, what was not an instrument of encouragement or correction? Such was the benevolence of Yao and Shun, and throughout the four quarters…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
風動萬國咸寧豈無自耶矧當是時阡陌
之制已出人人受田矣是以無甚貧甚富
之家成均之制已立在在有教矣是以有
不識不知之化又不特氣運之使然也後
世之君誠異於是田不井受而無幷者多
賦無常則而横斂者衆其農桑果什一之
法乎雖日增廣生員而所以教之者無術
雖日增葺學舍而所以訓之者無方其學
校果明倫之制乎借曰古法盡復然不得
===
真知愛民之人而任之則亦徒法云耳真
知愛民之人蓋亦所謂仁者之徒是也誠
得是人任之則法自我立雖不必一一復
古亦可也若夫愛養元元三代以後則未
有如漢之文帝者二十四年之間不曰賜
租則曰勸農不曰養老則曰賑貸深仁厚
澤其入於民者深矣所謂政在養民實無
愧焉帝之仁雖未可上比堯舜而四百年
靈長之祚終亦賴之惜乎賈生之請謙讓

世之君誠異於是田不井受而無幷者多
賦無常則而橫斂者衆其農桑累什一之
法乎雖日增廣生員而所以教之者無術
雖日增葺學舍而所以訓之者無方其學
校累明倫之制乎借曰古法盡復然不得
===
真知愛民之人而任之則亦徒法云耳真
知愛民之人蓋亦所謂仁者之徒是也誠
得是人任之則法自我立雖不必一一復
古亦可也若夫愛養元元三代以後則未
有如漢之文帝者二十四年之間不曰賜
租則曰勸農不曰養老則曰賑貧澤仁厚
澤其入於民者深矣所謂政在養民實無
愧焉帝之仁雖未可上比堯舜而四百年
靈長之祚終亦賴之惜乎賈生之請議譏
punctuated: 風動，萬國咸寧，豈無自耶？矧當是時，阡陌之制已出，人人受田矣，是以無甚貧甚富之家；成均之制已立，在在有教矣，是以有不識不知之化，又不特氣運之使然也。後世之君誠異於是，田不井受而無幷者多，賦無常則而横斂者衆，其農桑果什一之法乎？雖日增廣生員，而所以教之者無術；雖日增葺學舍，而所以訓之者無方，其學校果明倫之制乎？借曰古法盡復，然不得真知愛民之人而任之，則亦徒法云耳。真知愛民之人，蓋亦所謂仁者之徒是也。誠得是人任之，則法自我立，雖不必一一復古亦可也。若夫愛養元元，三代以後則未有如漢之文帝者。二十四年之間，不曰賜租則曰勸農，不曰養老則曰賑貸，深仁厚澤，其入於民者深矣。所謂政在養民，實無愧焉。帝之仁雖未可上比堯舜，而四百年靈長之祚終亦賴之。惜乎，賈生之請，謙讓
translation_en:
…were moved as by the wind, and all the myriad states were at peace. Could this have been without a cause? Moreover, at that time the system of field boundaries had already been instituted, and everyone received land; hence there were no households that were exceedingly poor or exceedingly rich. The Chengjun system of education had already been established, and instruction was available everywhere; hence people were transformed without conscious awareness or knowledge. Nor was this merely the working of the fortunes of the age.

The rulers of later ages were indeed different. Fields were not allotted under the well-field system, and many were without land or engrossed it [?]; taxation had no fixed rules, and arbitrary exactions were numerous. Did their arrangements for agriculture and sericulture really follow the rule of taking one tenth? Though they daily increased the number of government students, they had no method for teaching them; though they daily enlarged and repaired school buildings, they had no proper means of instructing their pupils. Did their schools really embody the system for illuminating human relationships? Even supposing that the ancient institutions were entirely restored, unless men who truly knew how to love the people were found and appointed, these would remain mere institutions. Those who truly know how to love the people are precisely those who belong to the company of the benevolent. If such men were indeed found and appointed, we could establish institutions ourselves; there would be no need to restore every ancient practice individually.

As for loving and nurturing the common people, since the Three Dynasties there has been no one like Emperor Wen of Han. Throughout his twenty-four years, his measures were either remitting land taxes or encouraging agriculture, either supporting the elderly or providing relief and loans. His profound benevolence and abundant beneficence reached deeply into the lives of the people. He truly deserved the description, “Government consists in nurturing the people.” Although the emperor’s benevolence could not yet rank with that of Yao and Shun, the dynasty’s enduring imperial fortune of four hundred years ultimately depended upon it. Regrettably, in response to Jia Sheng’s request, he modestly demurred…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
未遑漢治小康正坐于此禮樂謂非治道
所急豈通論哉故曰為治不法堯舜皆苟
而已此之謂也然則今日草茅末見求欲
于安民知人有萬一之助者又豈有他道
哉亦惟于仁智焉加之意而已必也以用
人之權盡責之于真能用人之人而當用
人之責者又必精鑒裁於一心稽察識于
眾論孰可在位孰可在職辨之審也孰宜
在內孰宜在外處之當也棄短取長不求
===
備于一人因才授職開自新于使過則大
賢既舉小才不遺今日之官人庶幾乎唐
虞之官人也擇真能安民之人授以安民
之任而當安民之任者又必以勞心撫字
為賢以申明教化為急薄賦稅輕徭役停
額外之徵而又嚴禁夫暴日入粟諸例則
富者不能巧免貧者不致重累又何患乎
貧富之不均重師儒脩學政敦明倫之義
而又痛革夫一時入監濫恩則廉恥之化

punctuated:
未遑。漢治小康，正坐于此。禮樂謂非治道所急，豈通論哉？故曰：「為治不法堯舜，皆苟而已。」此之謂也。然則今日草茅末見，求欲于安民知人有萬一之助者，又豈有他道哉？亦惟于仁智焉加之意而已。必也以用人之權，盡責之于真能用人之人，而當用人之責者，又必精鑒裁於一心，稽察識于眾論。孰可在位，孰可在職，辨之審也；孰宜在內，孰宜在外，處之當也。棄短取長，不求備于一人；因才授職，開自新于使過。則大賢既舉，小才不遺，今日之官人，庶幾乎唐虞之官人也。
擇真能安民之人，授以安民之任，而當安民之任者，又必以勞心撫字為賢，以申明教化為急。薄賦稅，輕徭役，停額外之徵，而又嚴禁夫暴日入粟諸例，則富者不能巧免，貧者不致重累，又何患乎貧富之不均？重師儒，脩學政，敦明倫之義，而又痛革夫一時入監濫恩，則廉恥之化
translation_en:
…there was no time for it. That Han government attained only modest order was precisely because of this. To say that rites and music are not urgent concerns of government—can this be a sound general judgment? Thus it is said: “To govern without taking Yao and Shun as models is merely to make do.” This is what that saying means.
Now, with the limited understanding of one living in obscurity, if I seek to contribute even the slightest assistance toward bringing peace to the people and discerning worthy men, could there be any other course? It is simply to devote attention to benevolence and wisdom. Authority over appointments must be entrusted, with full responsibility, to those truly capable of employing men. Those who bear this responsibility must refine their discernment and judgment within their own minds and test their assessments against the opinions of others. They must carefully distinguish who is fit to hold a position and who is fit to discharge particular duties; they must appropriately place those suited to service at court and those suited to service outside it. They must overlook shortcomings and draw on strengths, without demanding every excellence in a single person; assign duties according to ability, and allow those employed despite past faults an opportunity to reform themselves. Then the greatly worthy will be promoted, and those of lesser talent will not be overlooked. The appointment of officials today may thus approach that of the age of Tang and Yu.
Choose those truly capable of bringing peace to the people and entrust them with that responsibility. Those who bear it must regard devoted care for the people as a mark of worthiness, and the clarification and promotion of moral instruction as an urgent task. Reduce taxes, lighten labor services, and halt levies beyond the prescribed quotas; moreover, strictly prohibit the various provisions concerning “bao ri” and grain contributions [?]. Then the rich will be unable to evade their obligations by clever devices, and the poor will not suffer excessive burdens. What further concern need there be about unequal burdens upon rich and poor? Honor Confucian teachers, put the administration of schools in order, and strengthen the principle of making human relationships clear. Moreover, thoroughly abolish the indiscriminate favors granting admission to the Directorate of Education on an ad hoc basis. Then the moral influence that fosters integrity and a sense of shame…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
復敦奔競之風自息又何患乎薄惡之未
化行之以誠而虛文不事守之以信而一
定不移則民生可厚民德可正庶幾乎今
日之安民即唐虞之安民也彼西京區區
雜霸之治又惡足多乎抑茲二者固皆為
治之務而知人則尤安民之要所謂人主
之職在論一相相道得而萬國理矣此亦
唐虞論治之意也敢以是為
今日之堯舜獻
===

陳琛

復敦，奔競之風自息，又何患乎薄惡之未化？行之以誠，而虛文不事；守之以信，而一定不移，則民生可厚，民德可正。庶幾乎今日之安民，即唐虞之安民也。彼西京區區雜霸之治，又惡足多乎？抑茲二者，固皆為治之務，而知人則尤安民之要。所謂人主之職在論一相，相道得而萬國理矣。此亦唐虞論治之意也。敢以是為今日之堯舜獻。

translation_en:
…will again be strengthened, and the habit of scrambling for advancement will subside of itself. Why then worry that shallow and pernicious customs will remain unreformed? Carry these measures out sincerely, without pursuing empty formalities; uphold them faithfully, remaining steadfast once they are established. The people's livelihood can then be enriched and their moral character set right. Bringing peace to the people today may thus approach what was achieved under Tang and Yu. How could the paltry government of the Western Han, mingled with the methods of hegemons, merit much praise? Yet although these two tasks are both essential to governing, discerning men's abilities is especially crucial to bringing peace to the people. As the saying goes, the ruler's duty lies in selecting a single chief minister: when the proper way of chief ministership is attained, the myriad states are well governed. This, too, is the meaning of the discussions of government under Tang and Yu. I venture to offer these words to the Yao and Shun of our own day.

Fourth Question
Chen Chen 陳琛

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
乃堪經濟觀此策殆飽於問學者歟
同考試官洗馬滕批是策言宋事歷歷
若身處其地者足見用世之學
考試官學士顧批昔程伯子讀史至難
處事必掩卷深思求所以為之處者子之為
宋兩君謀豈亦有得於是者耶
考試官大學士靳批此策雖論宋一代事
而古今治道實不外此矧三場多自得之言
必一佳士也
===
人君之為天下也不可無渾厚之治體亦
不可無精明之治功莫不有治體也而惟
惇大乃成溫裕之俗莫不有治功也而惟
明作乃無弗成之績二者不偏則治體敦
而治功張矣然此非愚之言也周公相成
王之道也其繫泰之九二爻曰包荒用憑
河不遐遺朋亡夫以包荒之量濟之以憑
河之勇以不遐遺慮遠之智而又有朋亡
無我之公此中行之道亦惇大明作之意

人君之為天下也，不可無渾厚之治體，亦不可無精明之治功。莫不有治體也，而惟惇大乃成溫裕之俗；莫不有治功也，而惟明作乃無弗成之績。二者不偏，則治體敦而治功張矣。然此非愚之言也，周公相成王之道也。其繫泰之九二爻曰：「包荒，用憑河，不遐遺，朋亡。」夫以包荒之量，濟之以憑河之勇，以不遐遺慮遠之智，而又有朋亡無我之公，此中行之道，亦惇大明作之意
translation_en:
…only then can one be fit to order the world and aid its people. Judging by this policy essay, its author must surely be steeped in inquiry and learning!
Associate Examiner Teng, Librarian, comments: This policy essay discusses Song affairs so vividly and distinctly that its author seems to have been there himself. It amply demonstrates learning suited to practical service in the world.
Examiner Gu, Academician, comments: In former times, when the Elder Master Cheng read history and came upon matters difficult to handle, he would invariably close the book and reflect deeply, seeking a way to deal with them. In devising plans for the two Song rulers, have you perhaps gained something from this practice as well?
Examiner Jin, Grand Secretary, comments: Although this policy essay discusses the affairs of the Song dynasty alone, the principles of government, ancient and modern, truly extend no further than this. Moreover, the writings from all three sessions contain many insights of his own. He must surely be an outstanding scholar.
When a ruler governs the realm, he must possess a generous and substantial foundation for government, and also achieve perceptive and discerning practical governance. Every government has its underlying character, but only magnanimity can produce gentle and tolerant customs; every government undertakes practical work, but only enlightened action can yield accomplishments in which nothing remains unfulfilled. If neither aspect is neglected, the foundation of government will be solid and its achievements will flourish. Yet these are not the words of this foolish man: they are the principles by which the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng. The statement he attached to the second, yang line of the hexagram Tai (Peace) reads: “Embrace the uncultivated; cross the river on foot; neglect not the distant; let factional ties disappear.” Thus, the capacity to embrace the uncultivated is supplemented by the courage to cross the river on foot; together with the wisdom to consider distant concerns and neglect nothing far away, there is also the selfless impartiality of relinquishing factional ties. This is the way of proceeding in the mean, and likewise the meaning of magnanimity and enlightened action…

也然則為治之道豈復有加于此哉蓋竊
其似者固足以成治而得其偏者亦可以
有聞二者俱非乃入於亂耳姑以執事所
舉宋事陳之宋之立國之勢何如也太祖
以仁厚開基太宗以右文守業文教有餘
武事不競而建都失策尤異漢唐蓋北無
燕雲則門庭無鎖鑰之地西無寧夏則關
中無藩屏之隔形勢一失防守多岐于是
兵不得不勞財不得不費其立國規模弱
===
矣時至仁宗慈孝恭儉以寬厚待民以恩
禮待士以不殺為刑之威以不蓄為財之
富深仁厚德與漢文同所謂渾厚之治體
帝實有之然上下姑息綱紀漸隳吏治怠
惰邊警屢聞其勢之弱者未能有改而事
之弊者日增于前矣明作之功其可少哉
一時名賢亟將建議思欲變通以抹其敝
其道則然非得已也夫何夷簡吕公以二
十年執政最為帝所信任專且久矣乃惟

也。然則為治之道，豈復有加于此哉？蓋竊其似者，固足以成治；而得其偏者，亦可以有聞。二者俱非，乃入於亂耳。姑以執事所舉宋事陳之。宋之立國之勢何如也？太祖以仁厚開基，太宗以右文守業，文教有餘，武事不競，而建都失策，尤異漢唐。蓋北無燕雲，則門庭無鎖鑰之地；西無寧夏，則關中無藩屏之隔。形勢一失，防守多岐，于是兵不得不勞，財不得不費，其立國規模弱矣。
時至仁宗，慈孝恭儉，以寬厚待民，以恩禮待士，以不殺為刑之威，以不蓄為財之富。深仁厚德，與漢文同，所謂渾厚之治體，帝實有之。然上下姑息，綱紀漸隳，吏治怠惰，邊警屢聞。其勢之弱者未能有改，而事之弊者日增于前矣。明作之功，其可少哉？一時名賢，亟將建議，思欲變通，以抹其敝。其道則然，非得已也。夫何夷簡吕公，以二十年執政，最為帝所信任，專且久矣，乃惟
translation_en:
…indeed. What, then, could be added to this way of governing? Even those who merely approximate it can certainly achieve orderly government, while those who grasp only one side of it may still win renown. Only when both aspects are absent does government descend into disorder. Let me explain this through the affairs of the Song that you, sir, have raised. What was the strategic position upon which the Song founded its state? Taizu established its foundations through benevolence and generosity; Taizong preserved its achievements by honoring civil learning. Cultural instruction flourished, but military affairs languished, and the ill-advised choice of capital placed it in a position particularly different from that of the Han and Tang. Without Yan and Yun in the north, its gateway lacked the territory that could serve as lock and key; without Ningxia in the west, Guanzhong lacked a protective barrier. Once this strategic advantage was lost, defense had to be spread across many fronts. Thus the troops inevitably grew weary and resources inevitably had to be expended. The framework upon which the state was founded was weak.
When the reign of Renzong arrived, he was kind, filial, reverent, and frugal. He treated the people with generosity, and scholars with favor and courtesy. He made abstention from killing the source of his punishments’ authority, and abstention from hoarding the source of his fiscal abundance. In profound benevolence and ample virtue, he equaled Emperor Wen of the Han. The emperor truly possessed what is called a generous and substantial foundation of government. Yet those above and below indulged one another; the guiding principles and disciplines of government gradually deteriorated; officials grew negligent in their administration; and alarms from the frontier were repeatedly heard. The weakness of the state’s position remained unchanged, while abuses in its affairs increased daily beyond those of earlier times. Could the work of enlightened action possibly be dispensed with? The eminent worthies of the day urgently sought to submit proposals, hoping to adapt existing arrangements and thereby eliminate their defects. Their course was right: necessity compelled it. Why, then, did Lord Lü Yijian, who held governing office for twenty years and enjoyed the emperor’s greatest trust—exercising dominant authority over a long period—merely…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
用數固寵而不知為國任怨以柔佞易制
者為心腹以憂時建議者為好名陽排陰
沮事多報罷橫山之議既不能賛成于西
歳幣之遺又不免有增于北國勢益弱人
實為之謂之何哉借曰不用新進喜事乃
李文靖王文正之家法而中國之大險失
據漢唐之故地未復僅免女吳之耻而已
尋城下之盟此其時何時可宴然脩太平
之故事以誇張天下耶是又不獨吕公之
===
過而王李諸賢亦若有不可委其咎者豈
徒知治體之當敦而不知治功之不可不
振耶至於神宗之時盖又異矣其勢之承
于前者如故而弊之生于政者愈多語民
則財力困竭語軍則驕惰無功廟堂以簡
重為當然風俗以因循為得計是時宋興
已踰百年而夷狄之跳梁未已易窮則變
不大有所更張以捄之可乎帝之英明絕
人盖已素燭其然于是慨然興懷奮然圖

punctuated:
用數固寵，而不知為國任怨；以柔佞易制者為心腹，以憂時建議者為好名。陽排陰沮，事多報罷。橫山之議既不能賛成于西，歳幣之遺又不免有增于北。國勢益弱，人實為之，謂之何哉？借曰不用新進喜事，乃李文靖、王文正之家法，而中國之大險失據，漢唐之故地未復，僅免女吳之耻而已。尋城下之盟，此其時何時？可宴然脩太平之故事，以誇張天下耶？是又不獨吕公之過，而王、李諸賢亦若有不可委其咎者。豈徒知治體之當敦，而不知治功之不可不振耶？
至於神宗之時，盖又異矣。其勢之承于前者如故，而弊之生于政者愈多。語民，則財力困竭；語軍，則驕惰無功。廟堂以簡重為當然，風俗以因循為得計。是時宋興已踰百年，而夷狄之跳梁未已。《易》：「窮則變。」不大有所更張以捄之，可乎？帝之英明絕人，盖已素燭其然，于是慨然興懷，奮然圖
translation_en:
…used stratagems to secure imperial favor, without knowing how to incur resentment for the sake of the state. He made pliant flatterers who were easy to control his confidants, while treating those who worried about the times and offered proposals as seekers of fame. Through open opposition and covert obstruction, he caused many proposals to be rejected. He failed to support the Hengshan proposal in the west, while an increase in the annual tribute sent north proved unavoidable. The state grew ever weaker, and men themselves were responsible: what can one say of this? Granted that refusing to employ eager newcomers fond of stirring up affairs was the established practice of Li Wenjing and Wang Wenzheng, China had nevertheless lost possession of its great strategic defenses, and the former territories of the Han and Tang remained unrecovered. It had merely escaped the humiliation of “making Wu a woman” [?]. With a treaty concluded beneath the city walls renewed, what sort of times were these? Could one complacently revive the precedents of an age of peace to make a boastful display before the world? This was not Lord Lü’s fault alone; worthy men such as Wang and Li also seem unable to disclaim responsibility. Did they know only that the foundations of governance should be made solid, without knowing that its practical achievements must also be invigorated?
By the time of Shenzong, however, matters were different again. The circumstances inherited from earlier reigns remained unchanged, while abuses arising in government grew ever more numerous. As for the people, their wealth and strength were exhausted; as for the army, it was arrogant, indolent, and accomplished nothing. At court, restrained dignity was regarded as the proper course; in society, following established routines was considered sound policy. By then, more than a hundred years had passed since the rise of the Song, yet the incursions of the foreign peoples had not ceased. The Book of Changes says: “When things reach their limit, they change.” Could one remedy this without substantial reform? The emperor’s exceptional intelligence had long enabled him to perceive the situation clearly. Thus, deeply stirred, he resolutely began to plan…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
治誠欲上繼藝祖取燕之志以復中華一
統之盛此其心胡可非議而其為謀固亦
臧矣一時舊臣徒知守常不能通變為國
當事四顧無人於是王安石進矣夫以帝
大有為之志誠得同心同德之臣則勵精
之治將與漢宣中興同稱而又何治功之
不可振哉惜其最所信任之安石實以狷
狹執拗之資素有矯世變俗之志外示朴
野中藏巧機雖有吕誨先見而神宗方且
===
以聖人目之深謀密議宜無不聽較之申
公得君之專又有過焉於是外假周公泉
府之名陰用管商富强之術創立新法引
用羣邪曩時祖宗良法美意一掃無餘而
仁厚之治體亦虧矣盖不惟不能善治而
欲復如慶曆嘉祐之時亦不可得此則非
其更張之過實安石曲學以誤國而惠卿
之徒又有以誤安石也可勝嘆哉眉山蘇
子有感于心發為策問實欲警動當時意

野中藏巧獪雖有呂誨先見而神宗方且

子有感于心發爲策問實欲警動當時意
punctuated:
治，誠欲上繼藝祖取燕之志，以復中華一統之盛。此其心胡可非議？而其為謀固亦臧矣。一時舊臣徒知守常，不能通變，為國當事，四顧無人，於是王安石進矣。夫以帝大有為之志，誠得同心同德之臣，則勵精之治將與漢宣中興同稱，而又何治功之不可振哉？

惜其最所信任之安石，實以狷狹執拗之資，素有矯世變俗之志，外示朴野，中藏巧機。雖有吕誨先見，而神宗方且以聖人目之，深謀密議，宜無不聽。較之申公得君之專，又有過焉。於是外假周公泉府之名，陰用管商富强之術，創立新法，引用羣邪。曩時祖宗良法美意，一掃無餘，而仁厚之治體亦虧矣。盖不惟不能善治，而欲復如慶曆嘉祐之時，亦不可得。此則非其更張之過，實安石曲學以誤國，而惠卿之徒又有以誤安石也。可勝嘆哉！眉山蘇子有感于心，發為策問，實欲警動當時，意
translation_en:
…to bring about good government, sincerely wishing to carry forward the founding emperor’s ambition to recover Yan and thereby restore the splendor of a unified China. How could this intention be censured? His plan was indeed a worthy one. The veteran ministers of the day knew only how to preserve established practices and could not adapt to changing circumstances. Looking about for someone to undertake the affairs of state, he found no one; thus Wang Anshi advanced to power. With the emperor’s ambition to accomplish great things, had he truly obtained ministers who shared his mind and purpose, his energetic government would have been praised alongside the restoration under Emperor Xuan of Han. How, then, could practical achievements in government have failed to flourish?

Regrettably, Anshi, whom he trusted most, was narrow-minded and obstinate by disposition and had long harbored an ambition to reform the world and transform its customs. Outwardly he displayed rustic simplicity, while inwardly he concealed cunning designs. Although Lü Hui foresaw the danger, Emperor Shenzong was then regarding Anshi as a sage: whatever profound plans and confidential proposals he offered, the emperor could be expected to accept them all. His exclusive hold on his ruler’s confidence exceeded even that of Master Shen. Thus, outwardly borrowing the name of the Duke of Zhou’s Treasury Office (quanfu), he covertly employed the techniques of Guan Zhong and Shang Yang for enriching the state and strengthening its military. He established the New Policies and brought a host of wicked men into office. The fine laws and benevolent intentions of the imperial ancestors were swept away without a trace, and the humane and generous character of government was also impaired. Not only did he fail to govern well; even a return to conditions in the Qingli and Jiayou eras became impossible. This was not the fault of reform itself. Rather, Anshi misled the state through his distorted learning, while Huiqing and his associates in turn misled Anshi. How could one lament this enough! Master Su of Meishan, moved by these matters, expressed his feelings in a policy question, truly wishing to rouse and admonish his contemporaries. His intention…

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
亦善矣顧其論宋二帝似亦近之至於漢
之二君則其言有未然者盖文帝寛大長
者以德化民治體甚裕而不朝者賜以几
杖受賄者遺以金錢怠廢不舉之患正所
不免宣帝綜核名實技巧咸精治功可稱
而刻薄少恩良臣被戮漢家寛仁一脉剺
削殆盡則督責過甚之失又惡能無使非
丙魏作相任用得人則其去神宗亦五十
步百步之間爾先儒林氏謂文帝有惇大
===
之體宣帝有明作之功各得其一偏其言
當矣彼成王之治所以永有辭于後者又
豈二君之所能與哉夫眉山宋室名臣其
論必自有見而愚所深信而願學者則周
公之道之外皆非所聞也執事又欲諸生
為二宗一時執政諸君子審時度勢擬議
其善治之方以代為之處此非末學所敢
及也顧嘗歷攷史傳得其高賢論議盖有
先得我心之同然者矣請舉以就正可乎

其善治之方以代爲之處此非末學所敢
及也顧嘗歷攷史傳得其高賢論議蓋有
先得我心之同然者矣請舉以就正可乎
punctuated:
亦善矣。顧其論宋二帝，似亦近之；至於漢之二君，則其言有未然者。盖文帝寛大長者，以德化民，治體甚裕，而不朝者賜以几杖，受賄者遺以金錢，怠廢不舉之患，正所不免。宣帝綜核名實，技巧咸精，治功可稱，而刻薄少恩，良臣被戮，漢家寛仁一脉剺削殆盡，則督責過甚之失，又惡能無？使非丙魏作相，任用得人，則其去神宗，亦五十步百步之間爾。先儒林氏謂文帝有惇大之體，宣帝有明作之功，各得其一偏，其言當矣。彼成王之治，所以永有辭于後者，又豈二君之所能與哉？
夫眉山，宋室名臣，其論必自有見，而愚所深信而願學者，則周公之道之外，皆非所聞也。執事又欲諸生為二宗一時執政諸君子，審時度勢，擬議其善治之方，以代為之處，此非末學所敢及也。顧嘗歷攷史傳，得其高賢論議，盖有先得我心之同然者矣。請舉以就正，可乎？
translation_en:
…was also a good intention. Yet his discussion of the two Song emperors seems fairly close to the mark, whereas his remarks on the two Han rulers are not entirely sound. Emperor Wen was magnanimous and generous, transforming the people through virtue, and the character of his government was most lenient. Yet he bestowed armrests and staffs upon those who did not attend court, and gave money to those who accepted bribes. The danger of indolence, neglect, and failure to act was therefore precisely what he could not avoid. Emperor Xuan comprehensively checked actual performance against professed responsibilities and was thoroughly versed in the techniques of government; his achievements deserve praise. Yet he was harsh and ungenerous, and worthy ministers were executed. The Han dynasty’s tradition of leniency and benevolence was almost entirely whittled away. How, then, could he have avoided the fault of excessively exacting supervision? Had Bing and Wei not served as his chief ministers, and had he not appointed suitable men, his distance from Emperor Shenzong would have been merely that between retreating fifty paces and retreating a hundred. The earlier Confucian scholar Master Lin said that Emperor Wen possessed the substance of broad generosity, while Emperor Xuan achieved results through discerning action, each attaining only one aspect. His words are apt. How could either ruler compare with King Cheng, whose government has continued to win praise from later generations?
Master Su of Meishan was an eminent minister of the Song dynasty, and his arguments must have rested upon insights of his own. Yet as for what I, in my ignorance, deeply believe and wish to study, I acknowledge no teaching beyond the Way of the Duke of Zhou. You further ask us candidates to put ourselves in the place of the gentlemen who held power under the two Song emperors, assess the times and circumstances, and deliberate upon methods of good government, devising on their behalf how they should have dealt with affairs. This is beyond what a novice scholar such as I dares attempt. Nevertheless, I have examined the histories and biographies and encountered the arguments of their eminent and worthy men. Among these are views that anticipated what my own heart likewise recognizes as right. May I present them for your correction?

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
在仁宗時有若希文范公者經濟之畧成
於布衣忠義之氣振勵天下不擇利害以
為取舍凡有所為必盡其方所謂傑出之
才有宋一人而已平生奏議罔非對病之
藥石如曰均分田厚農桑減徭役阜民生
財之道具矣如曰明黜陟精貢舉革任子
進賢退不肖之法具矣其他嘉謀至論不
可枚舉而漸營洛陽以為都陜之計尤萬
世長策一時諸公所不及也使仁宗移所
===
以待夷簡者以待希文則精明之治功有
成敦裕之治體彌固先憂後樂之設施且
將逺出西京之上熙寧紛更太甚之禍亦
無自起矣然則相仁宗之道孰有過於希
文者哉在神宗時有若明道程子以揚休
山立之姿接聖賢不傳之道寛而有制和
而不流忠誠貫於金石孝弟通于神明賢
愚善惡咸得其心狡偽者獻其誠暴慢者
致其恭龍德正中蓋有不言而信者即其

在仁宗時，有若希文范公者，經濟之畧成於布衣，忠義之氣振勵天下，不擇利害以為取舍，凡有所為，必盡其方。所謂傑出之才，有宋一人而已。平生奏議，罔非對病之藥石。如曰均分田、厚農桑、減徭役、阜民，生財之道具矣；如曰明黜陟、精貢舉、革任子，進賢退不肖之法具矣。其他嘉謀至論，不可枚舉，而漸營洛陽以為都陜之計，尤萬世長策，一時諸公所不及也。使仁宗移所以待夷簡者以待希文，則精明之治功有成，敦裕之治體彌固，先憂後樂之設施，且將逺出西京之上，熙寧紛更太甚之禍亦無自起矣。然則相仁宗之道，孰有過於希文者哉？

In Renzong’s reign there was Lord Fan, styled Xiwen (Fan Zhongyan). His strategies for ordering the state and aiding the people took shape while he was still a commoner, and his spirit of loyalty and righteousness stirred the whole realm. He did not base his decisions on personal advantage or harm; whatever he undertook, he pursued every means of accomplishing it. Of those called outstanding talents, he alone deserved the name throughout the Song. The memorials he submitted over his lifetime were all remedies addressed to particular maladies. His proposals to distribute fields equitably, promote farming and sericulture, reduce labor service, and enrich the people provided a complete approach to producing wealth. His proposals to make demotions and promotions discerning, refine recruitment through examinations, and reform appointments of officials’ sons through hereditary privilege provided a complete method for advancing the worthy and dismissing the unworthy. His other excellent plans and profound arguments are too numerous to enumerate. His proposal to develop Luoyang gradually as part of a plan to establish the capital in Shan [?] was especially a lasting strategy for all ages, beyond anything the other gentlemen of his day could devise. Had Renzong accorded Xiwen the treatment he accorded Yijian (Lü Yijian), discerning government would have achieved its results, and the generous foundations of his rule would have become still firmer. Measures embodying the principle of being first to worry and last to enjoy would have far surpassed even those of the Western Han. The calamity of excessive and disruptive changes during the Xining reign period would then have had no occasion to arise. Who, then, could have surpassed Xiwen in serving Renzong as chief councilor?

In Shenzong’s reign there was Master Cheng, known as Mingdao (Cheng Hao). With his radiant excellence and mountain-like steadfastness, he took up the Way of the sages and worthies whose transmission had been interrupted. He was tolerant yet disciplined, harmonious yet never carried along by the crowd. His loyalty and sincerity penetrated metal and stone; his filial devotion and brotherly respect reached the spirits. He won the hearts of all, whether wise or foolish, good or evil. The cunning and deceitful offered him their sincerity; the violent and insolent showed him respect. title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
立朝論白如王霸誠偽之辨欲於其初審
之此則格心之論而十事之陳與正風俗
得賢才之疏規模次第亦孰及之信乎孟
子以後一人而已使神宗移所以待安石
者以待明道且將以光明正大之學為推
誠好治之輔雖周公之治可復也又豈特
鞭撻四夷復土宇如漢唐之盛而已哉然
則相神宗之道盖無過於明道者矣嗚呼
君子經世未嘗有不可為之時天矜下民
===
亦未嘗有無才之日惟其賢者不用用者
非賢此治日之所以長少也若謂人漸澆
漓成周之治不可復見則非愚之所敢知
也敷對至此不知狂斐之甚惟執事裁之
第五問
江暉
同考試官郎中陳 批 五策才氣逸宕沛
若懸河而天人一篇尤著知人之所不能知
非老於文學者不能是之取耳

第五問
江暉

同考試官郎中陳批：五策才氣逸宕，沛若懸河，而天人一篇尤著，知人之所不能知。非老於文學者，不能是之取耳。
translation_en:
…his arguments presented at court—for example, his distinction between the kingly and hegemonic ways, and between sincerity and falsity, which he wished to have carefully examined at the outset—were arguments for rectifying the ruler’s heart. As for his presentation of ten proposals and his memorials on correcting customs and securing worthy talent, who could match their scope and orderly arrangement? Truly, he was the one man since Mengzi! Had Shenzong treated Mingdao as he treated Anshi, he would have gained, through Mingdao’s learning, so luminous, upright, and great, an assistant in extending sincerity and pursuing good government. Even the government of the Duke of Zhou could have been restored. How could the achievement have been limited to subduing the peoples of the four quarters and recovering territory, as in the flourishing days of Han and Tang? Thus, in the way of serving Shenzong as chief councillor, surely none surpassed Mingdao.

Alas! For a gentleman who brings order to the world, there has never been a time when nothing could be accomplished. Heaven has compassion for the common people below, and there has likewise never been a day without men of talent. It is only because the worthy are not employed, while those employed are not worthy, that days of good government have always been so few. If it is claimed that people have gradually become shallow and insincere, and that the good government of the Zhou in its flourishing age can never be seen again, that is something I, in my ignorance, would not presume to accept. Having expounded my answer thus far, I have been unaware of how wildly presumptuous my words have become. I ask only that you, sir, judge them.

Fifth Question
Jiang Hui

The essay on Heaven and humanity is especially outstanding, revealing knowledge of what others cannot know. Only someone seasoned in literary learning could recognize its merit and select it.”

title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
同考試官修撰唐批通天地人曰儒觀
子是策豈予所謂其人耶他策亦詳整有議
論有考據取冠本房允愜輿論
考試官學士顧批曆象之學不知者類
以卜數視之識達天人兼該理器如此策者
非吾儒所當然耶他作俱優錄此以例之耳
考試官大學士靳批此卷五策出經入史
知古知今足見學識而天人一篇考據尤詳
故刻之
===
觀象緯而審禨祥者星官曆家之事也推
天以合人者也因禨祥而修德政者有天
下國家者之事也以人而合天者也天道
之災祥不忒人事之感應相形天人之際
其微矣哉執事春闈策諸生以星野之占
驗博之以當日之事而欲聞所以應天之
道愚知執事其不以數術望諸生也夫星
曆之術固非所知而國家修德應天之事
則嘗聞之矣星官之書自黃帝有之高陽

text:
氏以南正重司天北正黎司地而其職始
專唐虞而降世有其人而巫咸甘德石申
之書獨為星經之祖凡今十二辰野之相
配五星列宿干支方位之相屬六家星譜
之異同要皆其術之餘也星野之不相值
自昔疑之蓋古有其書而今亡之矣惟唐
僧一行雲漢山河之說君子有取焉其言
以為懸象在天其本在地星之與土以精
氣相屬而不係乎方隅其占測以山河為

也論占天之器者有三宣夜有名而無術

君子復有取焉其言以為古之人所以步

在乎辰次之周徑所以重曆數之意將以

非若乃述無稽之言於視聽之所不及則

translation_en:
…appointed Chong, the Director of the South, to oversee heaven, and Li, the Director of the North, to oversee earth; only then did these duties become specialized. From the times of Tang Yao and Yu Shun onward, every age had men versed in these matters, but the writings of Wu Xian, Gan De, and Shi Shen alone became the foundational works of the stellar canons. All present-day correspondences between the twelve celestial stations and terrestrial regions, the associations of the five planets and constellations with the celestial stems, earthly branches, and directions, and the agreements and differences among the stellar catalogues of the six schools are, in essence, all developments from their arts. The failure of celestial divisions and terrestrial regions to correspond has occasioned doubts since antiquity. There were books on this in ancient times, but they are now lost. Only the Tang monk Yixing’s account of the Milky Way, mountains, and rivers has found acceptance among learned gentlemen. He held that the celestial images suspended in heaven have their roots on earth. Stars and territories are linked through their essential qi, rather than tied to particular directions. His prognostications and measurements take mountains and rivers as boundaries, rather than relying on provinces and states. This is what distinguishes his account from those of the other schools.
There are three approaches to the apparatus for observing heaven. The Xuanye, or “Expansive Night,” has a name but no method; the Gaitian, or “Canopy Heaven,” has a method but no verification. Thus only the Huntian, or “Spherical Heaven,” comes close to the truth. Yet Wang Zhongren attacked it, while Ge Hong defended it, and opinions proliferated without agreement. Here again, Yixing’s account has found acceptance among learned gentlemen. He held that the ancients’ purpose in measuring the gnomon’s shadow was to regulate and circulate harmonious qi and assist things in attaining their proper conditions, rather than to determine the circumference and diameter of the celestial stations. Their purpose in valuing calendrical calculations was reverently to convey the seasons for human activities and respectfully to follow the patterns of heaven, rather than to decide whether the spherical-heaven or canopy-heaven theory was correct. title: 正德十二年會試錄
text:
君子當闕疑而不講此又其不泥於術數
者也愚之所聞於傳記者如此若其精微
之蘊則有司存焉而天人之際則為治者
之所當知不可以不悉也書曰天聰明自
我民聰明天明畏自我民明畏達于上下
敬哉有土言天人一理通達無間敬於民
者即所以奉乎天也又曰常厥德保厥位
惟吉凶不僭在人惟天降災祥在德言天
之禍福皆視夫人修吾德者即所以應乎
===
天也星者天之象也天垂象見吉凶聖人
象之則星文之變正天之所以警動乎人
君也而可以無畏哉此王安石之言所以
得罪於萬世也故因災而懼則雖有其變
而無其應高宗之雊雉宣王之旱魃是也
弗克畏天則殃咎從之而反得其常者君
子以為異魯宣公之大有年是也由是言
之有變不當以自棄無變不可以自喜亦
視吾德政之修否何如耳方今

punctuated: 君子當闕疑而不講，此又其不泥於術數者也。愚之所聞於傳記者如此，若其精微之蘊，則有司存焉。而天人之際，則為治者之所當知，不可以不悉也。《書》曰：「天聰明，自我民聰明；天明畏，自我民明畏。達于上下，敬哉有土！」言天人一理，通達無間，敬於民者，即所以奉乎天也。又曰：「常厥德，保厥位。惟吉凶不僭在人，惟天降災祥在德。」言天之禍福，皆視夫人，修吾德者，即所以應乎天也。星者，天之象也。天垂象，見吉凶，聖人象之，則星文之變，正天之所以警動乎人君也，而可以無畏哉！此王安石之言所以得罪於萬世也。故因災而懼，則雖有其變，而無其應，高宗之雊雉、宣王之旱魃是也。弗克畏天，則殃咎從之，而反得其常者，君子以為異，魯宣公之大有年是也。由是言之，有變不當以自棄，無變不可以自喜，亦視吾德政之修否何如耳。方今
translation_en:
…the gentleman should leave doubtful matters unresolved and refrain from discussing them. This, too, shows that he was not bound by technical calculations. Such is what I, in my ignorance, have learned from transmitted writings and records. As for their subtle profundities, there are officials charged with these matters. But the relationship between Heaven and humanity is something those who govern ought to understand; they must comprehend it fully. The Book of Documents says: “Heaven’s hearing and sight come from the hearing and sight of our people; Heaven’s manifest majesty comes from the manifest awe of our people. This reaches above and below. Be reverent, you who possess lands!” This means that Heaven and humanity share one principle, communicating without obstruction: reverence toward the people is precisely the means of serving Heaven. It also says: “Be constant in your virtue and preserve your position. Good and ill fortune fall unerringly according to the person; Heaven’s sending down calamities or blessings depends upon virtue.” This means that the misfortunes and blessings bestowed by Heaven all depend upon human conduct: cultivating one’s own virtue is precisely the means of responding to Heaven.

The stars are Heaven’s signs. Heaven displays signs revealing good and ill fortune, and the sage takes them as his model. Changes in celestial patterns are thus precisely Heaven’s means of warning and stirring the ruler. How could he fail to stand in awe? This is why Wang Anshi’s words earned him condemnation for all ages. Thus, if one becomes fearful because of a calamity, even though the anomalous sign appears, its corresponding consequence does not follow. The crowing pheasant in Gaozong’s time and the drought demon in King Xuan’s time are examples. If one fails to revere Heaven, disaster and blame follow; should normal conditions instead prevail, the gentleman regards this as anomalous. The great harvest in the time of Duke Xuan of Lu is an example. From this we may say that the appearance of anomalies should not cause us to abandon ourselves to despair, nor should their absence give us cause for self-satisfaction. It depends simply on how well we cultivate our virtue and our government. At present…

仁愛之所在亦或所以應天者有未能盡

translation_en:
…the sage sovereign reigns above, and his single-minded virtue inspires universal trust. Surely Heaven should accept it and manifold blessings arrive together. Yet throughout the prefectures and counties, uncanny portents arise one after another; in the capital region, floods and droughts occur in succession, just as your illuminating question states. This certainly manifests Heaven’s benevolent concern. But might our ways of responding to Heaven also fall short of fully conforming to antiquity? Why is this so? What troubles the realm is the exhaustion and impoverishment of the people. Today, construction in the imperial palace—the celestial Gouchen and Purple Palace—and works undertaken by the northern gates and the Palace Treasury send supervising commissioners along the roads in an unbroken procession of official caps and carriage canopies. Thus, in what is called ‘not encroaching upon the farming seasons,’ we may fall short of antiquity.

Another concern is the excessive number of those who eat without performing useful service. Today, titles and ranks are bestowed to excess without restraint, while hereditary stipends increase and never diminish. Thus, in what is called ‘having no positions at court obtained through undue favor,’ we may fall short of antiquity.

The neglect of military preparedness on the frontiers and the depleted condition of the troops are especially troubling. Yet the sources of extortion at military headquarters and the pursuit of undeserved credit in commanders’ offices cannot readily be stopped. Thus, our management of military affairs falls short of antiquity.

The annual receipts of the imperial treasury [?] cannot cover its annual expenditures. Soldiers and civilians hauling and transporting grain endure every kind of hardship, while along the capital’s thoroughfares, people living in splendid houses and eating fine food are everywhere to be seen. With such a gulf between hardship and ease, our establishment of enduring fiscal arrangements likewise falls short of antiquity. As for all such matters, in the wind…

text:

以致異矣况其多耶執事有憂時體國之
心有畏天命悲人窮之意詢謀所及盖惓
惓焉而愚以為窮災變之端則天道遠而
難見論消弭之術則人事近而可修將修
人事孰有切於伊臯之告其君者乎而愚
既陳于前矣誠能於此加之意焉不以民
視民而以天視民不以天視天而以心視
